This study delves into the generalizability of two-layer neural networks for calculating the eigenvalues of the Schrödinger equation in multi-dimensional space. Employing methods rooted in theoretical statistics, we treat and analyze the trainable parameters of the neural networks as the model's hyperparameters, which must be selected before training. In accordance with this approach, we establish the asymptotic ranges for the magnitude of the errors in the trained models' output when compared to the actual eigenvalues, as well as the probability of such errors occurring. These findings are demonstrated to be feasible under real-world conditions where the order of eigenvalues varies, a scenario that is proven to be impossible using traditional Monte Carlo sampling methods. Furthermore, our study shows that the neural networks can produce accurate results with small samples, a capability that is exemplified through numerical computations involving the discrete logonorm and the harmonic oscillator problems. This study's generalizability framework is versatile and can be adapted to other multi-layer neural networks. However, it is crucial to note that the choice of regularization parameters presented here can be challenging to interpret, a shortcoming that may also affect other deep learning-based methods. Nonetheless, one potential solution to this issue is to incorporate an adaptive optimization method for the hyperparameters into the model training process. This study is instrumental in advancing the understanding of neural networks' generalizability in the context of physics-based problems, a field of study that is gaining significant traction globally. Moreover, its analytical methodology is pioneering in the field of theoretical statistics, a capability that could also be applied to solving other multi-layer neural network generalizability problems. A readily accessible implementation of the framework for calculating the generalization error is available through the open-source repository known as $\mathtt{gesr2lnn}$. Our strategy draws on the approach taken in a study by S. Booss-Bavnbek and J. An operator theoretic linearization is a common approach in linear problems, yet this specific scenario is complicated by the potential's ill-behavior at infinity and the lack of a bounded potential. Our linearization strategy relies on an approximate inverse of the wave equation's coefficient, and we rely on the Fourier decomposition of this approximate inverse to eliminate issues related to its non-smoothness. Once we have successfully linearized the equation, we can use the compact resolvent to establish the scattering theory for the original equation. The compact, short-period orbit of K2-138 is comprised of five transiting planets, which displays an extraordinary pattern of simultaneous short-period transit multiplicity. This unusual configuration makes it an ideal candidate for examining resonant planetary configurations. Through a detailed analysis using transit photometry and spectroscopy, researchers have determined the properties of the planets, revealing a surprisingly small radius for the largest planet and multiple possible solutions for the orbital periods and eccentricities among the planets. Further investigation into the possible resonant interactions among the planets using dynamical calculations indicates a resonant chain involving planets p(b) through p(c) that aligns with astronomical observations and theoretical findings, and it is suggested that planet p(d) may be unbound. The presence of this resonant chain raises the possibility that the system may undergo thermal evolution, leading to a destabilization of its planetary system. Nonetheless, the predicted remaining lifetime of the resonant chain is estimated to be tens of billions of years, suggesting a significant remaining period before the system destabilizes. It is hypothesized that the initial formation of the planets likely arose through an instability of a disk ring due to its barotropic mode instability, followed by further processing of the planets via migration and interactions that ultimately produced the observed resonant configuration. These findings represent the shortest known example to date of planetary resonances, and they provide crucial insights into the intricacies of planetary formation mechanisms. Based on the calculated period ratios, the resonant chain is believed to correspond to a 3:2 resonance chain, and it is predicted to be observable for at least another 300 million years before dissipating. The system's properties have significant implications for its potential effects on its host star, with calculations estimating that the planets may cause a cumulative decrease in the star's spin period of up to 1.6 million years before the resonant chain dissipates. Moreover, researchers have identified several observable signs that can confirm or refute the predicted remaining period of the resonant chain, which includes an impending decrease in the transit period of planet p(c), a rising number of transits for planet p(b) that will occur in 71 million years, and a recurring transiting configuration of planets p(a) and p(c) that will recur every 11,800 years. This leads to a new characterization of the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality. Furthermore, we develop a novel action of the affine Weyl group, which we obtain by combining the automorphisms of the local Lusztig--Vector space with a modified version of Lusztig's action, and prove that this action corresponds to the yet unknown action on the standard $U_q(\mathfrak{g}_)$-module when applied to the Whittaker functor. Utilizing atomic simulations, our research investigates amorphous ices, focusing on their structural transformations when subjected to varying pressures. In contrast to traditional ice formation theories, our results indicate that crystalline and glassy ices coexist in a broad pressure range. This is evidenced by the presence of multiple stable crystal structures and glassy states, each with its own distinct density. We also find that the transition from a lower-density crystal to a higher-density glass is characterized by the formation of localized molecular vibrations without significantly altering the ice's density. While our findings are consistent with observational data from planetary science research, they diverge from some experimental and molecular dynamics model results, highlighting the need for further studies in this area. In particular, considering the complexities of ice II, IV, and VI structures may be essential in replicating the results from high-pressure experiments and computational models. By accounting for these structures' inherent complexities, our research may contribute to a more complete understanding of how water transitions from a liquid to a solid state under extreme pressure conditions. Formal proof libraries serve as a collective memory for validated theories, but their full potential is not yet realized in their ability to influence and guide research. We investigate how central aspects of proof development, represented by key concepts within the Mocha framework, evolve over time across the Isabelle Archive. Through a historical analysis of these patterns, we seek to address two questions: (a) Can empirical research uncover underlying trends in how proofs are created and researched? and (b) Can these insights lead to the development of tools that foster more effective collaboration and research within the community? In particular, we aim to improve the SearchProof tool to facilitate research and development of novel strategies by analyzing and visualizing the Archive's content. Initially, we focus on the Archive's methods (proofs), but we also plan to expand our study to encompass other aspects, including the structure of proofs, the relationships between individual contributions, and the context of proof development. Ultimately, our goal is to empower the Isabelle community to leverage these patterns and drive innovative research in verified software development, which in turn may lead to the realization of the Archive's full potential. In this study, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the Archive's structure, exploring various aspects such as the relationships between individual proofs, the dynamics of proof development, and the evolution of concepts within the library. In addition, we present SearchProof, a tool that facilitates research by allowing users to explore the Archive's content through proof trees, and improve it by enhancing its functionality of searching strategies. Through an empirical investigation of the Isabelle Archive's structure, we uncover patterns and relationships within the library and demonstrate the potential of empirical research in shaping the development of formal verification tools and infrastructure. In the future, we plan to extend our study to other important aspects of the Isabelle community, including the context of proof development, the relationships within the community, and the impact of our findings. In particular, we aim to continue the development of SearchProof by integrating it with a visual exploration system for proof trees, and by complementing it with a tool for cost-based recommendation, which recommends verified proof strategies to the Isabelle community. In addition, we plan to promote the utilization of the Archive's collective knowledge through data mining and natural language processing, which may lead to a shift from the current verification paradigm towards semi-automation. In the long term, we aspire to establish a cycle of growth, where automated tools foster innovative research, which in turn advances the verifiable software development paradigm. Their properties as rotating solutions of the modified Einstein field equations are examined. These rotating black holes have a prolate shape with a single horosphere. A subgroup of a group has a "near exponential remainder" growth when it has a specific set of distinct subgroups that collectively account for nearly all other subgroups. It's been established that any subgroup of a finite group with a considerable share of its subgroups meets this criterion. Building on this, we now show that all such subgroups of finite groups possess a higher rate of growth. Moreover, there are infinite groups where every subgroup meets this specific growth criterion. Interestingly, we found an infinite group where the ratio of its center to the rest of its subgroups significantly approaches 1. These findings answer a previously posed question and complement earlier work by Guriyev. Our method also helps resolve a longstanding conjecture concerning finite groups. Nonetheless, an open issue remains: determining if every subgroup of a finite group, regardless of its properties, possesses a near exponential remainder growth. In addition to these results, we present an alternative proof of a previously known theorem using our growth model. Lastly, we introduce a collection of highly symmetric groups that exhibit rapid growth. These highly symmetric groups include projectsive linear groups, Hall's hypercenters, and the Hall-Janko group, among others, unless they possess simple centers. It's also discovered that the ratio of a group's centre to the rest of its subgroups can be very close to 1 for some of these highly symmetric groups. Specifically, this is true for the projective linear groups of dimensions 2 and above, the Hall-Janka group, the Heinehold group, the McNinch-Yamaguchi group, among others. These findings were achieved using a model that measures highly symmetric group growth. Moreover, we discovered that the satz group possesses a near exponential growth characteristic, which is a distinct finding when considering only its simple centre. Finally, we give an alternative proof to a previously known theorem about highly symmetric group growth using our model. We've introduced a model that expands the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation to a star-shaped graph structure, accounting for internal resonances within the edges and internal resistance within the points of intersection. The interlinked edges allow information to be transmitted in both directions, yet the internal resonances can lead to instability in the system, particularly in the transient state. To explore the long-term stability, we've investigated the internal resistance affecting the internal points, and found that a critical value applies when three edges converge. Below this threshold, the system becomes asymptotic to a steady state, using Lin's characteristic frequency function approach, whereas above this threshold a broader class of solutions is observed, prompting the occurrence of internal resonances and transient behavior. To study this behavior, we've employed a spectral theory based model, and through a regular approximation, we've identified the existence of multiple internal resonances and a correlation between amplitude and frequency. Lastly, through a Hausdorff dimension computation, we've established the measure of these resonances, showing that their density decreases as the star-shaped graph order increases. An alternative method to study this behavior involves a regularized approximation, starting with the analysis of a specified measure that describes the density of resonances along the edges. The interplay of these resonances is then observed through a spectral shift function, influencing the long-term behavior of the model. Notably, we've demonstrated the existence of multiple internal resonances within the transient state, and through a regular approximation, we've established the long-term behavior of the model: for a certain class of solutions, we've proven that they remain stable, using an integral representation approach; for another, we've shown the occurrence of chaotic behavior, using a spectral operator approach, and that the set of these solutions has a measure that depends on the order of the star-shaped graph. In the end, we've compared our findings with the results of a numerical simulation. A collaborative filtering system predicts user preferences by identifying patterns that connect users to similar items. To do this, we use a dual feature allocation model that assigns a unique feature set to each user and an item, with the constraint that only one feature set is assigned per user or item. This model allows us to discover shared feature sets among users and items, which we use to make predictions for users without a history of interactions. Specifically, we calculate the probability of a user liking an item by counting how many times their shared feature sets appear together. Experimental results show that this approach outperforms existing methods in terms of predictive accuracy, especially for users with few interactions. Additionally, the system scales efficiently, as only the shared feature sets need to be stored, not individual interaction histories. Furthermore, we demonstrate the system's ability to explain recommendations with a simple method that identifies the most relevant features within each shared feature set. To showcase its utility, we provide a web page with recommended movies based on their associated keywords. To the best of our knowledge, this approach to collaborative filtering has never been documented in literature. In addition, the related concepts of dual models and latent feature allocation are discussed. Also, existing collaborative filtering systems are reviewed, with a focus on their predictive accuracy, scalability, and explainability. Finally, publicly available data sets used to test and validate our system and methods are identified. Our analysis indicates that our system achieves state-of-the-art performance, with the added benefit of being interpretable through the explained recommendations feature. Moreover, we observe that existing collaborative filtering systems fall short in three key areas: predictive accuracy, scalability, and explainability. While top-performing systems achieve impressive predictive accuracy, they do so at the cost of storing a complete interaction history for every user. Conversely, systems designed for explainability have high processing requirements to generate predictions for every user. Our system, on the other hand, strikes a balance by investing in both predictive accuracy and scalability while also providing transparent explanations for user preferences. Specifically, our system achieves 0.718 average precision on the MovieLens dataset, outperforming all other methods while using significantly less data storage – a mere 9GB, as opposed to 1.3TB for the simplest interaction-based model. Similarly, our system outperforms other methods on the Netflix dataset in terms of predictive accuracy, storage requirements, and complexity. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the primary factor limiting collaborative filtering systems from reaching their full potential is scalability, with many systems failing to efficiently utilize available resources. This paper presents a tutorial on using direct transcription for control design through a case study involving noninvasive ventilation for multiple patients during the COVID-19 pandemic. Due to concerns about ventilator shortages during the pandemic, hospitals have had to consider ventilating patients who are not critically ill, increasing the demand for ventilators. Furthermore, patients who do require ventilators often need to be supported for an extended period, further increasing the demand. A significant design issue arises when trying to control systems that include nonlinear subsystems with multiple degrees of freedom, compounded by the need to prioritize the well-being of patients who are not in critical life-threatening situations. To address this, we propose a general strategy for control design and subsequently apply it to a specific patient ventilation scenario. We utilize the open-source MATLAB toolbox mupad for efficient model usage and demonstrate a successful design through patient ventilation. Our approach results in significant cost reductions, with each patient requiring a ventilator now needing only 42 minutes of ventilation time, as opposed to 15 minutes, allowing for a higher patient throughput. Additionally, we showcase the efficacy of the proposed control strategy in a simulation environment. Our belief is that this tutorial will serve as a valuable resource for control design through direct transcription and could be adapted for various other applications, including medical, industrial, and environmental problems. We identify the "deck clusters" of $f^n$, which consists of the pre-images of $f^n$, for nearly all values of $n$. The identification is made possible by solving the "branching equation" for $f$, which allows us to parameterize the "bifurcation points" of $f^n$ in terms of $f^{n-1}$. We utilize a recent results by Remondini and the third author on the "topological invariance" of these bifurcation points to conclude that the deck clusters of $f^n$ have a geometric interpretation as a branched cover of the Riemann sphere to itself, except when $f$ has a "resolvent" with a zero in the complex plane. In this exceptional case, the deck clusters of $f^n$ have a more intricate structure, which we also describe in detail. Traditional training in supervised learning can be viewed as an extension of this process, where labels serve as an initial partial model and a weighted average of predictions is taken to produce the final model, considered successful when it generates the correct output for a given input. The process of adjusting weights to achieve a successful model is analogous to propagating changes in a specific direction guided by the partial model and observations from the training set. Our research demonstrates that this process can be seen as the reflection of general adjustments, derived from the theory of change propagation, which is based on the principles of general delta lenses. A notable benefit of this formulation is the ability to identify and investigate underlying assumptions about the functioning of this process, as well as to develop tools that enable the application of various strategies for change propagation and to explore their differences. Our research was conducted while exploring the connection between supervised learning and the broader concept of change propagation, which allows for the simultaneous modification of multiple systems with adaptable structures, as well as an integrated analysis of various observations that form the foundations of the training process. This research develops and applies a uniform stationary phase estimation method for oscillatory integrals with phase and amplitude functions within certain smoothness classes. The method involves establishing uniform estimates for the oscillatory integrals by classifying the phase function's critical points into stagnation points and regular points. For phase functions with lower smoothness, different estimates are employed to account for phase function variations, which ultimately yield uniform oscillatory integral estimates. The derived estimates can be applied to solve hyperbolic partial differential equations, such as the inverse scattering problem for the heat equation and the Whittaker equation. Furthermore, an application is made to derive uniform stationary phase estimates for a class of oscillatory integrals over oscillating domains. The underlying reasoning relies heavily on techniques involving change of variables, the vanishing momentum argument, and properties derived from phase function phase and amplitude analysis. The phase function's phase and amplitude analysis techniques developed here are, in fact, general results that can be employed in various oscillatory integral contexts. The research provides smoothness condition comparisons for class I and II phase functions and introduces new results for class III phase functions. Specifically, distinct smoothness conditions are required for phase and amplitude when it comes to class I and II phase functions, which inherently include the assumption of a non-degenerate critical point. In contrast, a limited smoothness condition is imposed on the phase function in this research for all types of phase III. The research presents a smoothness condition comparison table that can be applied to class I and II phase functions, detailing the minimum required smoothness conditions for phase and amplitude. The research presents a set of sufficient criteria for class III phase functions to be treated equally to smooth phase functions. Lastly, a set of general recipes for deriving uniform oscillatory integral estimates is provided, along with specific examples applied to phase III. The research provides a comprehensive set of references for phase function phase and amplitude analysis and oscillatory integral estimates and includes an addendum section that addresses open research questions regarding generalised phase functions. The research demonstrates that complete phase and amplitude information can be obtained from a singular stationary phase estimate. The derived estimates can be applied to phase III to solve the mentioned research question. Moreover, a complete set of references for phase function phase and amplitude analysis is provided in the revised version of this thesis. The research provides a correct and comprehensive analysis for the phase and amplitude properties for solutions of the heat equation using the method of stationary phase. The solutions exhibit linear phase and amplitude, which contradicts previous research claiming exponential phase and amplitude for solutions of the heat equation.

A straightforward iterative method is proposed to approximate the steady-state distribution of a rarefied gas flowing through a channel with varying cross sections. By assuming molecules follow a Boltzmann distribution, the velocity components are calculated through a sequence of Poisson integral calculations, starting with an initial velocity profile. As a recognition of the iterative method's potential limitations, such as convergence and computational efficiency, an alternative approach utilizing a finite difference scheme for solving the Boltzmann equation in the spatial domain is also presented. Although the alternative method demands additional CPU time due to 2D iterations and memory requirements, it is argued that this is a reasonable trade-off for attaining a more accurate solution in a relatively small number of iterations. Furthermore, it's acknowledged that while the alternative method requires around 50-100 iterations, which is still a relatively small number, it may take hundreds or thousands of iterations using the basic iterative method, resulting in significant CPU time. In an effort to accelerate the basic iterative method, a pre-conditioning technique is introduced. By pre-conditioning the velocity profile, it's shown that this can significantly reduce the required number of iterations to a manageable 20-30, closely matching the number of iterations for the alternative method. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods, the accurate velocity profiles for molecules flowing through a specific two-stage Knudsen layer are reconstructed from thinly partitioned domains using either 2 and 3-dimensional models. By comparing the results to the exact solution of the Boltzmann equation, it's shown that the proposed methods are capable of producing highly accurate solutions in a relatively small number of iterations, outperforming previous research which obtained the solution in around 300 iterations. In an effort to verify the accuracy of the 2D approach through comparisons with existing methods, the pre-conditioned basic iterative method is also applied to reconstruct the velocity profiles for molecules flowing through a specific two-stage Knudsen layer using a broadly used model, failing to accurately match the exact solution. By identifying the source of the failure, it's shown that modifying the model to better match the exact solution can accurately reproduce the desired solution. In an effort to visually validate the obtained velocity profiles, the particle distribution is simulated and photographed for the specific two-stage Knudsen layer in 3-dimensional models as well as using the pre-conditioned basic iterative method. By comparing the results to the accurately calculated velocity profiles, it's shown that the proposed methods are capable of producing highly accurate solutions that closely match the visually observed particle behavior in 3-dimensional models.

Determining similarity between datasets is a significant challenge in information retrieval. Recent advancements have focused on comparing graph datasets, but concerns about data confidentiality in server-based systems drive the need for a method allowing clients to maintain their data privacy. A new concept, called the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy, is introduced to compare graph datasets while protecting its structure. This discrepancy metric is the magnitude of the largest value in the Gromov-Wasserstein matrix that results from combining the graph's distance information, and it can be used to compare graphs locally on networks such as Facebook and LinkedIn without exchanging direct data. To protect user privacy in the graph analysis process, Local Differential Privacy is applied by adding noise to graph labels on clients before sending them to the server. A decoupled algorithm is then used to compute the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy, and it involves graph processing on clients and inference on the server. Our research, involving over 230,000 graphs from Facebook, 40,000 graphs from LinkedIn, and 100,000 graphs from YouTube, demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy metric in the presence of noise. Moreover, the proposed approach exhibits sensitive graph label retrieval capabilities while achieving an almost perfect similarity search accuracy. Our results also show that the proposed Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy metric outperforms other similarity metrics in terms of accuracy and efficiency. A comprehensive experimental study is presented in this paper, demonstrating the proposed approach, experiment design, and results. Our work contributes an algorithm for graph similarity search and retrieval in the context of distributed graph datasets while ensuring the privacy of the graph structure. Our approach maintains a balance between search accuracy and label retrieval rate, and it outperforms other metrics in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, the proposed Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy metric has a minimal error rate of less than 0.00006 and an average processing time of under 0.1 seconds per graph, and it exhibits better results than other metrics such as GW-DP, SAST, and Token-Ratio. We publicly share our code and data with the community to support the graph similarity search and retrieval research community. Our work has the potential to support various data processing tasks that utilize graph similarity as a building block, and it can contribute to a wide range of applications in information retrieval and machine learning. The Transit Feed Specification (TFS) enables seamless real-time access to public transportation schedules and routes. Although TFS feeds can be generated synthetically, acquiring feeds for a long period of time is often impractical and costly. Lack of a comprehensive training dataset for TFS feeds hinders the success of deep learning (DL) models. This study establishes a universal model to predict any point in a TFS feed using time series data and scheduled stops. The proposed solution outperforms conventional time series prediction methods and establishes new benchmarks for TFS feed simulation. The study provides an open-source implementation and all necessary data for replication and validation. Furthermore, the research highlights potential avenues for improving predictive accuracy in TFS feeds using DL models. By diverging from the traditional approach of directly using prototypes to recognize novel categories, we instead developed a novel model, the Repeated Fine-tuning Model (RFM), which effectively utilizes prototypes as initial positions to start training on novel data, thereby significantly improving its recognition performance. A split graph, defined as the combination of two distinct sets $\{v\}$ and $W$, is formed by directing all edges from $v$ to $W$. The semi-transitive property in a graph $G$ indicates the absence of directed cycles of length 3 or more. The primary goal of this study is to investigate the minimal directed split graphs that satisfy this semi-transitive property. Through the examination of directed paths of length 2, we develop a framework for classifying the minimal directed split graphs that meet this semi-transitive requirement. Specifically, we establish a precise characterization of these minimal directed split graphs that have 3 or fewer vertices in the set $W$. Additionally, for split graphs with 4 or more vertices in the set $W$, or in case $|W|=1$, we provide another characterization of the minimal directed split graphs that satisfy this semi-transitive property. As a consequence of our investigation, we derive a constant upper bound on the number of edges present in the minimal directed split graphs that meet this semi-transitive requirement. The described classification is realized through the use of automata theory. The edge upper bound can be attributed to a simple in-degree-based criterion. The theoretical validity of our findings is supported by the presentation of accompanying experimental results. The study further investigates the semi-transitive property in directed acyclic graphs, highlighting its application in semantic web applications. The provided classification is realized through the integration of our theoretical findings with the existing literature in this area. The study concludes by examining the semi-transitive property in directed graphs that possess the hereditary property of being bipartite. A precise characterization of the minimal bipartite split graphs that satisfy this semi-transitive requirement is developed through the examination of directed cycles of length 3. The study is concluded by opening up two unresolved problems. The associated code is available through the repository directed-split-graphs. Two important combinatorial optimization problems, the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem, serve as key applications of various robust optimization techniques. This paper showcases that exact solutions can be obtained under certain conditions and highlights the benefits of using a powerful, state-of-the-art local search method to solve these problems effectively. This local search method, known as non-convex short path maximization, demonstrates impressive computational capabilities, with the ability to find a global maximum in a relatively short time when a maximum flow in a specific graph can be determined. Notably, our experiments show that our approach outperforms existing approximate algorithms for the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem, with the added benefit of being easily adaptable to solve the Set-Union Knapsack Problem. Moreover, our method exhibits strong practical performance, with a runtime of less than a second capable of producing a 20% improvement over the current best-known approximation for datasets with up to 5,000 items. Furthermore, our approach is highly flexible, with the ability to easily integrate it into existing search algorithms, as well as be applied to various related problems that serve as crucial tools for data streaming, such as the Set-Union Covering Problem and the Set-Union Knapsack Problem with Item Priors. Our experimental results highlight the effectiveness of our technical contribution, with a maximum coverage rate of 0.4685 on standard test datasets, representing a 23% improvement over the current best-known approximation. Our method also shows promising scalability, with the ability to produce high-quality solutions within a second for large datasets with up to 50,000 items. Despite our local search method being pseudo-polynomial, we were able to overcome polynomial runtime limitations by leveraging a state-of-the-art binary search implementation. However, further improvements to the computational efficiency of our approach are needed to expand its applicability to more complex problem instances. Our method's current drawbacks include its inability to handle edge cases due to a relatively simple design and the lack of theoretical guarantees of optimality. Nonetheless, our experimental results demonstrate that our technical contribution, the non-convex short path maximization local search method, yields the best-known approximation for the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem to date. Ultimately, our study illustrates the importance of further research in local search methods that can tackle robust optimization problems effectively. Until then, our approach remains the current state-of-the-art algorithm for the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem and a valuable tool for solving related problems. Churn prevention is a critical concern for online service providers, and accurate prediction of customer churn is essential to informing predictive models and preventing customer loss. In the context of online gambling, sudden withdrawals from betting can indicate potential problem gambling, which is regulated in regulated markets. Studies on gambling churn typically concentrate on one-time churning behavior, and there's a shortage of research on recurring churn patterns among less active or 'dormant' customers. We seek to fill this gap, analyzing customer data from an online gambling operator to examine distinct churn behaviors. By comparing one-time and recurring churn patterns, our research revealed differences in demographic characteristics and betting behavior. Specifically, we found that recurring churn users retained relatively high levels of engagement, whereas one-time churn users displayed more varied behaviors. Notably, while one-time churn users made infrequent but substantial wagers, recurring churn users engaged in steady but minor betting activity. Our analysis further indicates that incorporating features related to dormant periods is essential for accurate churn prediction. Interestingly, it appears that less active customers are less likely to experience notable periods of inactivity before transitioning to churn behavior. By exploring correlations between betting patterns and churn in distinct timeframes, we were able to identify unique characteristics associated with one-time and recurring churn. Finally, our research reveals that feature embeddings, particularly those related to betting intervals and status, emerged as crucial elements in predicting both types of churn. With our findings, online service providers are better equipped to address problem gambling by targeting distinct demographics and behaviors, and to inform retention strategies for less active customers, potentially by promoting campaigns tailored to their typical betting intervals. Moreover, these insights can inform responsible gaming policies by identifying specific demographics and betting patterns indicative of potential problem gambling among inactive customers. Ultimately, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of customer behavior, revealing that less active customers may comprise a significant yet overlooked segment. By acknowledging and addressing this group's unique behaviors, online gambling operators can refine their models and strategies to prevent customer loss and promote healthier gaming habits. The increasing popularity of cycling as a commuting method corresponds with a rising number of fatalities due to cycling hazards. To address this problem, researchers have been developing systems that utilize on-motorcycle sensors and real-time data to warn cyclists of impending dangers such as blind corners and hazards. Notably, there has been significant progress in utilizing sensors and computer-vision technologies to automatically generate cycling routes with integrated risk alerts. Our paper focuses on the design of a comprehensive system that combines computational models, computer vision, and contextual data to automatically identify potential risks on the cycling route in real-time. The proposed system incorporates the existing 'RouteMap' system, which uses satellite imaging and geographical data to provide directions, along with two advanced components: 1) a computer-based system that uses available video footage to estimate the geometry of the road and predict potential risks, and 2) a real-time sensor equipped safety system that provides real-time updates on any detected obstacles or hazards. Our paper outlines the implementation details of the RouteMap system, introduces the geometry-road predictor, and evaluates the effectiveness of the real-time safety system using actual cycling data. The resulting application not only assists cyclists in navigating safer routes but also collects valuable data that can be utilized for informed urban planning, such as identifying areas that require infrastructure upgrades to enhance road safety. The proposed system showcases a cutting-edge example of Technology-driven Urban Planning, where city authorities can collaborate with technology-savvy cyclists to create a safer urban environment. Our research demonstrates that advanced technologies like computer vision, geographical data integration, and sensory systems can address pressing city problems and foster a collaborative relationship between city authorities, residents, and the organizations providing these technologies. The proposed system exemplifies a strong use of computational methods to gather and utilize user and city data for more informed decision-making in urban planning. This method involves defining a concept of "nearness" between a robot's trajectory and a predetermined path, and using this definition in a geometrically-inspired approach with the robot's trajectory serving as a geometric barrier to prevent collisions. This barrier has an associated set of safe velocities, and by using control barrier functions, we can determine the maximum safe velocity for the robot. However, the uncertainty in the robot's surroundings could cause the set of safe velocities to disappear, so we use fuzzy logic to mitigate this issue by allowing the robot to temporarily deviate from its original path. We present multiple scenarios where this method is useful such as the presence of obstacles or uneven terrain, and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulation results involving a quadrotor and a ground vehicle. Ultimately, this research aims to align the outputs of deep learning models with the expected natural transformations of images, making our models more resilient to malicious manipulation. Although our work primarily focuses on visual challenges, we believe that similar techniques can be applied to other domains where characterizable input-degradation models exist. By achieving this, we are closer to developing systems whose outcomes make ecological sense. Furthermore, we are working towards a future where deep learning models can be utilized in various critical applications, such as autonomous vehicles, without being controlled by manipulative forces. Yet, despite our best efforts, we have yet to completely remove adversarial inputs from such systems, leaving the elimination of these inputs as a key task requiring further research. Given the relatively recent emergence of several crucial challenges in machine learning, such as robustness, fairness, and explainability, we are working to uncover the underlying one-to-many mapping between inputs and outputs, thus enabling us to prevent or correct unjust biases. As advancements in terms of data availability and analytical models occur, we are improving our comprehension of the underlying mechanisms driving learning and making the outputs of deep learning models more transparent and interpretable. Ultimately, this research aims to align the outputs of deep learning models with our moral standards, thus bridging the gap between justice and the digital realm. The classical Segal-Bargmann theory in quantum mechanics is extended to a Clifford algebra-valued formulation.  We start with a one-dimensional real Clifford algebra. The SB transformation is defined between a phase space and a Hilbert space of square-integrable functions on the real Clifford algebra.  We generate an extended Segal-Bargmann kernel, incorporating Taylor isomorphism elements, to establish isomorphisms among spaces of square-integrable functions on the phase space, its Fourier transform, and the Hilbert space.  The kernel's properties are defined in a Clifford algebra-valued setting, incorporating geometric norm, convolution, and a co-ordinate transformation linking the three spaces.  This extends the existing Segal-Bargmann theory in complex analysis to a more comprehensive framework.  It also includes elements of Clifford algebra-valued Hermite polynomials, which form an orthonormal basis in this new framework.  This research is a preliminary step towards developing a more comprehensive theory of Clifford algebra-valued quantum mechanics.  It also explores the potential application of this theory in relativistic physics and spin physics.  It further examines the connections between geometric norm, convolution, and co-ordinate transformations in this new Clifford algebra framework.  Many of the key concepts and properties from the classical SB theory are carried over to this new Clifford algebra context.  However, some of the key concepts and properties from the complex SB theory are lost in this translation or appear in new and complex forms.  This is largely due to the inherent properties of one and two-dimensional real Clifford algevas.  It is noted that the phase space is non-commutative, whereas the SB transformation and the Hilbert space are commutative.  This is not the case in the complex SB context.  Notably, the SB kernel and its adjoint are conjugate complexes of one another in the complex context, but they are real in the Clifford algebra context.  The kernel's properties are investigated under various conditions, and it is noted that it serves as an unitary transformation between the three spaces.  Many of the key properties from the complex SB theory are lost in this translation or appear in new and complex forms.  This is largely due to the inherent properties of one and two-dimensional real Clifford algevas.  It is observed that the SB kernel and its adjoint exhibit quasi-hermitian properties in the Clifford algebra context. The notion of pathwise conditioning of a Gaussian field is introduced and explored, with the underlying inspiration being the pathwise conditioning for random variables. In the context of Gaussian fields, this concept can be viewed as the random medium property, where the indexing set of the random variables becomes a point index. We prove that a Gaussian field enjoys the random medium property in two distinct scenarios: when it is the result of conditioning a standard Gaussian process with continuous samples to a sigma-finite index set, or when it is a homogeneous Gaussian process with independent samples across subfields that share a finite index. These conditions are further analyzed to reveal that subfields with independent samples can only be sigma-finite in circumstance. Additionally, an alternative characterization of Gaussian processes with the random medium property is presented through the concept of hypercontractive conditional excess joint independence. Moreover, an error estimate for approximating a Gaussian process with the random medium property using quasi-monotone functional methods is provided, which also implies the extension of well-known approximation theorems for Gaussian processes to the field level. These theorems hold particularly significance in circumstance where subfields have independent samples. Finally, an example illustrates that the pathwise conditioning of a Gaussian field can differ from the conditional Gaussian field resulting from standard Gaussian process conditioning. Moreover, an investigation into potential numerical applications of these theorems in the Monte Carlo method framework reveals that pathwise conditioning can sometimes lead to improved convergence rates, although this depends on the specific algorithm utilized. A comprehensive Monte Carlo method incorporating both conditioning techniques has been implemented for two real-world examples: a stochastic partial differential equation modeling a biological invasion and the linear complementarity problem, with source code available at the provided repository. Our numerical experiments suggest that in certain instances, approximating a Gaussian field through pathwise conditioning can be beneficial, whereas in other cases, conditional Gaussian fields may perform superiorly. Ultimately, a dual analysis of these theorems, taking into account both theoretical and practical implications, is conducted. From a theoretical perspective, an extended application of well-known approximation theorems to the Gaussian field level is realized through the use of quasi-monotone functionals, while from a practical standpoint, a deeper comprehension of the random medium property and its approximate properties can be achieved by analyzing the underlying Gaussian fields. Moreover, an alternative characterization of Gaussian processes with the random medium property through the hypercontractive conditional excess joint independence is achieved. These results contribute to the advancement of Gaussian field theory, encompassing both theoretical and practical advancements, and may also spark future research in the field

Challenges in spatiotemporal predictive learning arise from the need to analyze motion patterns across different spatial and temporal dimensions while considering various factors such as orientation, speed, and acceleration. Existing methods are limited in their ability to (i) capture dynamic changes in all three dimensions of motion, (ii) handle irregular and non-uniformly sampled data, and (iii) address the scarcity of labeled data, all of which are essential for real-world applications like weather and traffic forecasts. To address these limitations, we introduce ModRNN, a generic framework that enables a comprehensive understanding of spatiotemporal patterns by characterizing motion as a dynamic triad of orientation, speed, and acceleration. It achieves this by leveraging a bidirectional neural network that extracts features from both spatial and temporal dimensions, and uses a conditional random field to improve performance by incorporating a self-similar mechanism. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that ModRNN outperforms existing baselines by effectively generating accurate forecasts for both 2D and 3D predictions. Notably, our framework achieves success in predicting three-dimensional motion patterns, thereby showcasing its potential to tackle complex spatiotemporal tasks. The source code of ModRNN is available at https://github.com/MayflyProject/ModRNN. Additionally, the pre-trained models can be downloaded at https://github.com/MayflyProject/ModRNN-projects. We're interested in protecting sensitive data's lifetime within a execution scope. Existing static type systems cannot effectively analyze dynamic runtime environments and heap allocations. As a result, they struggle to reliably guarantee data safety across all execution scenarios. Our approach develops a novel dynamic type system that effectively manages dynamic memory access and controls data flow through function calls and operations. This type system is implemented using JavaScript within a browser context, with a specialized library providing compile-time implementation options for performance optimization. Our evaluation, conducted across multiple benchmark suites, demonstrates the performance and efficiency of the implementation. Furthermore, a thorough analysis of potential security vulnerabilities reveals the benefits and limitations of the implemented strategy. Overall, our study provides an in-depth understanding of the challenges and potential approaches to managing dynamic memory access and data flow control, particularly in browser-side programming. The research was presented at the ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation in June 2022. Belief propagation (BP) decoding for this subcode has been found to converge or enter an infinite loop. A new decoding method called the BP list decoder (BP-LD) has been developed to address the lack of guaranteed convergence for BP on the polar subcode. By reducing the maximum variable-to-information ratio of a polar code $\mathcal{C}_0$ below one using subcodes of specific structures, the new decoder can successfully decode polar subcodes $\mathcal{C} \subseteq 2^{\mathcal{C}_0}$ with high efficiency. The new decoder's performance was evaluated through simulation results, demonstrating superior error-rate performance and lower average decoding iterations in comparison to non-successful BP decoding. The decoder's average number of iterations was investigated as a function of the code parameter $\epsilon$, the desired list size $L$, and the subcode parameter $\eta$. Simulation results showed the potential for the BP-LD to successfully decode polar subcodes with high $\eta$ values, an impossible task for pure BP decoding. Furthermore, the decoder's time complexity was shown to be linear in $n$, the code length, and proportional to $L$. The decoder's memory requirements remained constant at $O(n/\log(n))$. The decoder's exceptional performance at extremely high $\eta$ values makes it the first known decoder to successfully decode polar subcodes with high $\eta$ values. Generating synthetic cell shapes poses a significant challenge due to the complex interactions involved, processing the vast amounts of cellular data required for representation seemingly intractable. Our approach tackles this problem by employing implicit neural representations (IRs) that enable us to model cell shapes via compact, trainable networks. In a pioneering step, we develop an IR-based framework for cell shape modeling that leverages annotated cell segmentation images and corresponding cell classification labels. By integrating a classification head into the IR and employing a classification loss during training, our network is capable of producing class-specific generations. To evaluate our method's generative capabilities, we performed a fan-out experiment demonstrating the potential applications of our approach. Our results demonstrate that the knowledge embedded in the IR is versatile and can be utilized for various tasks, processes that were unseen during training such as cell segmentation. Our implementation of the IR-based framework, named irf, along with the corresponding cell segmentation dataset 'SynCells' is publicly available on github. Our work lays out a novel foundation for the creation of synthetic cell shapes, exploring the boundaries between supervised and unsupervised learning, and advancing visible and understandable explainability in neural networks through the use of visual loss functions and simple diagnostic tools. Ultimately, this research contributes to the essential development of synthetic cell generators that could significantly boost our comprehension of cell dynamics and development, ultimately benefiting our understanding of living organisms. Our proposed method has successfully passed preliminary tests in a range of applications including motion prediction, shape transformation, and exploring cell diversity. These resources, data, code, and network weights are freely accessible at https://github.com/alexk1l2l3(irf) and https://github.com/alexk1l2l3(SynCells). Blind, low-vision, and other print-impaired individuals still struggle to access printed documents, despite advancements in document scanning technologies. Our research explores the underlying reasons for this ongoing challenge, focusing on the difficulties encountered by print-impaired individuals when trying to navigate scanned documents. We found that such individuals face considerable problems because current document formats fail to provide necessary navigational elements. As a result, they often rely on cumbersome methods such as using Braille labels or feeling the page. Our study shows that there is a clear need for future research to develop methods to make scanned documents accessible to print-impaired individuals, and we propose the term 'document navigability' to describe this area of study. We also outline several potential research directions, including exploring the role that image-based techniques, such as tactile signatures, could play in enhancing navigational capabilities. Ultimately, our goal is to facilitate the collective development of methods and tools that can aid print-impaired individuals in efficiently navigating documents via various channels including visual, auditory, and tactile. With such collaboration, we aim to eliminate the current obstacles that prevent print-impaired individuals from effectively utilizing scanned documents. 

The document scanning process, although seemingly straightforward, poses challenges for print-impaired individuals due to its unintended side effects and imperfect results. These difficulties become particularly evident in environments where print is more prominent, such as educational, cultural, or informational settings. In such situations, the print-impaired individual may find themselves forced to resort to Braille or tactile navigation methods, and this can be a source of great frustration. The problem of accessing printed documents has not been completely resolved despite advancements in document scanning technologies, primarily because of the lack of universally accepted standards for document design. As a result, the layout and content of documents vary significantly, affecting their navigability in distinct ways. The goal of our research is to identify effective strategies for making scanned documents accessible to print-impaired individuals by understanding the broader context of document design.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, rectifies the limitations seen in BERT. Moreover, XLNet incorporates key aspects from the advanced autoregressive model, Transformer-XL, thereby achieving substantial pretraining improvements. According to comprehensive evaluations on a wide array of tasks, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across various tasks, with notable success on long-range dependency tasks such as question answering and text generation. Furthermore, XLNet outperforms Transformer-XL when run under similar computational constraints, thereby demonstrating pretraining advantages on various downstream tasks. Our approach involves integrating planet and star spectra, then accounting for scattering and absorption by the planet's atmosphere. The potential detectability of these features could be enhanced by future transit spectroscopy missions like the James Webb Space Telescope and PLATO, as they respectively identify more targets for analysis and provide valuable data for modeling planet atmospheres. A mathematical model describing the swimming dynamics of forficatus is developed, which shows that this lightweight centipede swims using a combination of oscillatory movements in its legs and longitudinal body movements. Similar to other animals that swim near the surface of water, forficatus's swimming motion can be classified as a type of boundary swimming, where the movement of the body across the water surface generates forward motion. A laboratory study on forficatus's walking behavior when submerged in water, as opposed to walking on a completely dry surface, shows that when walking under water, each leg moves in a different phase, resulting in an irregular gait pattern that actually aids the centipette in overcoming drag when swimming near the surface of water. This unique form of movement is not observed in other animals that swim near the surface of water. A mathematical model describing forficatus's swimming dynamics near the surface of water is developed and shows that this form of movement is actually stable and efficient, where the movement of the body across the water surface generates forward motion. Research into El Ni\~no's various forms is growing, with a focus on Pacific Ocean rainfall patterns being well documented, but the impact of these forms on global precipitation patterns remains underexplooration. This study examines the connection between different ENSO flavors and global precipitation patterns, particularly during rainfall and drought periods, through an analysis of precipitation data from 40 years. The results show distinct global and regional precipitation patterns linked to the three main ENSO flavors - Modulation of Asian Monsoon, Modulation of African Monsoon, and Modulation of South American Precipitation Patterns. These patterns were identified using a combination of two statistical methods - partial least squares regression and Bayesian probability estimation. The findings reveal how different ENSO flavors leave unique marks on global precipitation, paving the way for an improved understanding of how ENSO impacts life on Earth and potentially leading to better forecasts of ENSO's effects. This study contributes to a more detailed understanding of ENSO's complex and multifaceted nature, with potential applications in research on ENSO-driven ecological changes and ENSO prediction. The methods used to analyze the data are available for immediate use and adaptation in studies on ENSO-driven ecological changes and climate variability and change research. The data interpretation is provided at a 1x1.5$^{\circ}$x1$^{\circ}$ latitude-longitude grid resolution, providing insights to scientists and policymakers. The analysis is further supported by a multiscale climate analysis, with a focus on small (Africa), medium (Americas), and large (Asia), regional and global scales. The study's scientific contributions total 8 and undergoes rigorous peer-review, with a review score of 92/100. The study's outcomes have been confirmed by independent research for two of the ENSO flavors, with potential for confirmation in the remaining flavor. The study's scientific significance is supported by its impact factors of 2.53 and 3.11 in its respective publication years. The associated data is available for immediate download from https://doi.org/10.21943/2DWSKVL/DJZOCQ. The data's original credit is given to the ERSD 2020 database and the TIERES project. Traditional graph representations, whether Euclidean or geometric, are inadequate for encoding the complex hierarchy of a taxonomy. In contrast, hyperbolic space models, which have been shown to effectively represent trees, can also learn noisy data into meaningful representations. A level of theoretical accuracy comparable to electronic structure methods is achieved through employment of the pairwise convolution-corrected Statistical Associated Liquid Theory model. The predicted interaction energies, geometries, and energy density distributions correlate well with high-level ab initio calculations, with the accuracy augmented by an electrostatic potential-based correction method when solvents are considered. The model's capability to account for external electric fields in molecular pair interactions is demonstrated. Cyber-Physical Systems require a high level of resilience to withstand disruptions in their control loops, caused by the failure of sensors, malfunctions in control software, or issues with actuator functionality. Resilience in CPSs involves selecting and configuring backup components to maintain system functionality despite such failures. This paper presents a framework based on temporal logic to model different approaches to resilience and evaluate their effectiveness. It proposes an STL-based framework allowing for the specification of backup strategies through reformulations of original system properties. The framework's validity and its design methods are substantiated through a case study using the physical model language PML. A tool has been developed to automate the conversion process and implement the framework's methods. The benefits of using this approach over traditional UML-based methods are also discussed. The framework can manage various types of backup components, from fully-usable backups to temporary substitutes, and even component redundancy. This research aims to provide a foundation for the formal design and verification of CPSs with multiple backup strategies. It furthers current discussions on formal methods in CPSs by introducing a rigorous framework for specifying and realising backup strategies. The framework's rigour enables the formal verification and validation of CPS design. This research makes the STL2PML tool available for converting design specifications, as well as a model library containing 25 CPS designs with multiple backup strategies, to promote discussion and further development. The framework's source code can be found at https://github.com/cq01/STL2PML. The design models can be accessed at https://github.com/ResCPS/distributions. Through the combination of various observations of identical fields with radio telescopes, we have gathered and analyzed a massive dataset.  It contains information on the properties of sub-millijansky radio sources, specifically their sizes and luminosity.  By comparing our results to larger, nearby radio source sample, we have established a distance at which their sizes start to differ noticeably.  We also found evidence suggesting smaller, low-flux radio sources have thinner fuel reservoirs than larger, high-flux counterparts.  An analysis of their power and energy relationships revealed no significant differences.  Furthermore, we have estimated the average sizes of sub-millijansky radio sources in two large, nearby radio source sample and discovered they have an average energy similar to a study of highly luminous radio sources.  An examination of their power and energy relationships revealed significant correlations.  Also found were similarities in the ratios between radio sources' sizes and flux densities between our sample and a study of highly luminous radio sources. This paper seeks to examine the potential association between fractals and Gausson processes in the context of consistent dynamical systems.  Fractals are studied under the Mandelbrot-Drinksbacher-Nagel self-similarity criterion, while Gaussons are defined by their inverse variance self-similarity property.  Four fractal measures are outlined which capture the fundamental properties of a system's potential energy.  These measures include the fractal dimension, the radial radial autocorrelation length, the Radon-Nikodym derivative, and the surface-to-volume ratio.  A system is dynamically consistent if its potential energy meets certain criteria, notably if its Radon-Nikodym derivative is nonnegative.  Upon investigating free fields on the flat space and a five-dimensional de Sitter space, the relationship between these measures is determined to be nontrivial.  Calculations of key fractal measures for free fields on the flat space and de Sitter space are carried out with perturbation theory used to confirm the consistency of these measures in both systems.  Furthermore, the inverse variance self-similarity property of Gaussons is linked to a key fractal measure, namely the surface-to-volume ratio, which is nontrivial in both de Sitter and flat spaces.  Consequently, the inverse variance self-similarity property of Gaussons is incompatible with a fundamental property of quantum field theories, namely dynamical consistency.  Thus, the characteristic scales of quantum field theories, which exhibit inverse variance self-similarity, extend only to the Planck length.  Beyond this length, the behavior of these scales becomes statistically nonlocal, rendering their prediction to be impossible.  An argument is presented to show that these length scales represent an intrinsic quantum uncertainty, analogous to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which applies to quantum fields as well as quantum particles. A recent advancement in 3D point cloud localization utilizes the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation of 3D point clouds as a central component. The efficacy of NDT-based point clouds has been further enhanced through the application of a novel Transformer architecture, which leverages a patch-based strategy to enable the efficient processing of high-resolution point clouds. Following pre-processing that incorporates both range imaging and color normalization, the 3D point cloud is transformed into an NDT representation via a kernelized density estimation algorithm. Subsequently, the generated NDIs are segmented into region-based units and arranged in a grid-like pattern of patches. Building upon this novel representation, a depth-wise multi-layer perceptron (DMLP) is employed for initial localization, which is then integrated with a patch-wise Transformer module comprising a sinusoidal position embedding (SPE) and a depth-wise attention mechanism (DMA). Upon receiving the combined local features from the DMLP-DMA module, a top-stage non-linear layer produces a fine-tuned pose estimation. Experimental validation of the proposed approach on the S3DIS dataset yields superior performance, with an notable enhancement of 2.1% and 1.3% in overall accuracy relative to the competing SLAM3D and Atlas networks, respectively. Notably, the proposed architecture exhibits a notable reduction in computational complexity, displaying an 8.7 times decrease relative to the Atlas network. Finally, extensive evaluations utilizing a range of point cloud resolutions demonstrate the proposed architecture's ability to efficiently handle large-scale 3D point clouds, which proves to be a crucial factor of performance. Therefore, the presented approach is versatile and adaptable across a range of possible 3D point cloud-based applications. Establishing reliable, large-scale connectivity between brain regions, particularly in the resting state, remains a crucial goal in systems neuroscience and functional neuroimaging. Building on prior research, we assessed the statistical significance of functional magnetic resonance imaging data in a dataset comprising 52 participants and identified potential methods to enhance measurement accuracy. Our analysis explored the effect of combining individual and group data on measures of connectivity strength and network organization. The results demonstrate that functional connectivity can be consistently established across multiple scans from a single participant. Furthermore, our findings suggest that using a combination of scans yields more reliable metrics than individual scans, while functional connectivity in group analyses is stable with four or more participants. The observed outcomes align with the theoretical underpinning of measurement theory, allowing us to predict accuracy rates based on the number of scans and participants. The development of a general approach for assessing and refining functional connectivity in large datasets may, therefore, contribute to optimizing research design to establish reliable and valid measures of brain network structure. Recent advancements in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained significant attention, 
mainly driven by the vast availability of datasets in multiple languages, including
Indo-Aryan languages such as Marathi and Gujarati, which are commonly used in social 
media interactions in India. Although RPEs have demonstrated effectiveness in processing
monolingual monoscriptal texts, their application in code-mixed CMRPE is challenged
due to the diverse nature of word positions across individual languages. In this research,
we address the limitations of RPEs through APESTO, a novel positional encoding framework
that adapts to the statistical patterns of switching points in code-mixed texts. Our experiments
reveal that APESTO-based models including BERT, XLM-R and FinoNLP achieve enhanced
performance on CMRPE tasks, as gauged by the WNUT2018 dataset. Our analysis indicates
that APESTO's performance is closely linked to the frequency distribution of switching points
in individual languages. A script-level analysis of our results also yields intriguing insights
into language script-specific patterns of positional correlations. Moreover, APESTO's code
is freely accessible on GitHub, including our fine-tuned BERT-Large-MN models for CMR, GM and HM classification. Our research is an extension of similar works in CMNLP, including a related paper published in EMNLP 2020. To overcome the non-convex problem of maximizing the mutual information, this research proposes an alternative optimization method that first determines the user indices via a group LASSO algorithm. A convex approximation is then used to derive an closed-form solution for the remaining variables. Key advantages of this method include its ability to handle a high number of users with linear complexity and its capacity to outperform existing schemes such as LASSO and SDP-based approaches, as demonstrated through its favorable comparison with ZEROTFOR in terms of performance and complexity. Additionally, this study presents a precise analysis of the cardinality of the obtained Gramian matrices, providing a tighter bound that surpasses the existing LASSO bound and thus reduces the probability of incorrect user selection. Furthermore, this research presents a precise characterization of the achievable rate achieved by the proposed algorithm, showing it to be complementary to the previously established LASSO-based method. In Vertical Federated Learning, where data ownership is divided, participants collaborate to train a unified model by concatenating their local models. However, this framework's reliability on data owners to secure participant data allows an adversary to potentially leak sensitive user information in the event of compromised data storage or stolen models. 
Our study investigates several threats to VFL's privacy: one attack focuses on personally identifying user contributions from stored model updates while another involves reconstructing sensitive user data using a compromised model; 
Both attacks are able to achieve success with relatively low computational requirements; 
We also look at some possible privacy losses in popular VFL algorithms; 
Further, we propose an informal rule for gauging the safety of VFL's privacy practices; 
Lastly, we outline possible solution approaches for mitigating these threats. 
The outcome of our research is an informal benchmark for estimating the extent of VFL's privacy risks, as well as preliminary strategies for lessening these risks. 
The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/ucb-imla/vlm-attack. 
The outcome of our study is an essential warning to the VFL community: without additional steps, there may be considerable privacy degradation even in scenarios where data are not shared. 
Also, an attack might succeed even in scenarios where model updates do not contain sensitive information. 
Therefore, additional steps are necessary to guarantee robust privacy in VFL scenarios.

This research focuses on developing robust, differentially private methods for learning distributed decision trees through a Bayesian framework. The two-stage Bayesian approach first initiates model construction by selecting data partitions, followed by learning the partitioned decision trees. The resulting algorithm, called DP-DTL, uses differential privacy to derive a reliable model from a private learning process of decision trees on separate data sets. The method's composition property in relation to privacy and accuracy was investigated, with specific analysis of its effects on predictive accuracy and the required gradient norm. The evaluation demonstrated that DP-DTL exhibits nearly the same predictive accuracy as its non-private counterpart in various data configurations, with the only loss incurred by differential privacy shown to be positively correlated with the desired level of privacy. Additionally, DP-DTL's performance was compared to other private learning algorithms through a controlled experiment, with the results indicating significantly enhanced accuracy when compared to a private decision tree learning algorithm based on $\ell_1$-regularization and equivalent or superior performance when compared to a private learning algorithm that utilizes noisy gradients at the tree level, with the only loss incurred by differential privacy positively correlated with the desired level of privacy. An extension of DP-DTL in terms of robustness to data corruption was also presented, with the method's susceptibility to adversarial data manipulation shown to be positively correlated with the desired level of privacy. Finally, an extension of DP-DTL in terms of parallel processing capabilities was presented through Sy-DP-DTL, with the method's differential privacy analyzed in conjunction with its enhanced parallelism and predictive accuracy improved by its ability to utilize multiple processing units. The evaluation demonstrated that Sy-DP-DTL's only loss incurred by differential privacy positively correlated with the desired level of privacy and its improved parallelism resulted in better predictive accuracy in various data configurations. With these contributions, several implications for the reliability and the theory and practice of differentially private learning were derived. An related software implementation can be found at the repository https://github.com/jayjayweng/Differentially-Private-Distributed-Decison-Trees.

Interpreting the semantic meaning of a given SQL query is a crucial aspect of databases. The task is particularly challenging due to the varied combinations of key elements in the query, such as the mix of precision and ambiguity in referencing database tables and columns. Current top-performing models often rely on pre-trained models, analyzing the query's surface structure from left to right, but this approach falls short in accurately understanding the query's underlying structure. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a novel auxiliary task that helps determine the reference paths within a query by analyzing joint statistics across a dataset. The auxiliary task demonstrates significant improvements on the SPARTA benchmark, achieving 76.3% accuracy in interpreting semantic meaning. The full implementation is available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/allenai/semantic-parser. Additionally, we've contributed a new dataset, the SQLdev 1.0.5 dataset, containing 50K SQL queries, which provides 5.7x more examples than the SPARTA benchmark and offers 2x more tables and columns to enhance model robustness.
