FastAC incorporates principled statistical methods, such as an iterative singular value decomposition, to create reliable factors and handle large datasets efficiently. Evaluation with real-world multimodal data from the ISA platform demonstrated the superiority of FastAC over existing tools like Autominer. This led to the development of M-ar-K-Fast, an extended version of FastAC that can handle complex factor structures. M-ar-K-Fast is a comprehensive tool for extracting robust and interpretable factors from multi-domain data, facilitating autonomous component analysis and decision-making. Its versatility allows for its current application in data enrichment and future use in autonomous systems. M-ar-K-Fast has been published as an open-source tool to support the creation of autonomous systems. FastAC was selected as the top tool overall, reflecting its superior performance. This study examines M-ar-K-Fast's capabilities in the absence of ground truth. FastAC was compared against Autominer, generating the FastAC-L version for analysis. M-ar-K-Fast was then applied to four real-world datasets, including the CArma, Mackey-Glass, SMD, and SMD2 scenarios. Using FastAC and FastAC-L, M-ar-K-Fast was able to discover 95% or more of the underlying components in all datasets. FastAC produced the FastAC-L version, reducing the detect rate to 47%, highlighting its improved performance in the analysis. FastAC's results closely resembled the known component structures of the datasets, with the exception of minor alignment discrepancies. This further establishes FastAC as the preferred method for achieving reliable component analysis. FastAC is currently the preferred tool, with FastAC-L its closest alternative. Our system overcomes this limitation by analyzing real-time Twitter data in a map view, utilizing color coding to indicate incident likelihood and applying a statistical method to gauge probability. The proposed algorithm uses a multi-modal distribution consisting of normal and Gamma probability distributions to differentiate between expected activity and abnormal activity. Research into quantum feedback guidance has garnered significant interest due to its implicit restriction on input states. All input states are either guided or rejected. This work examines the necessary conditions for quantum feedback guidance in continuous-variable systems, revealing that state guidance is inherently tied to Wigner negativity. Additionally, we present a practical approach for designing quantum feedback controllers that can accommodate a broader class of input states without rejection. This involves transforming the original system into a new one with an enlarged Hilbert space, allowing for greater flexibility in selecting input states. We demonstrate this method in a coherent linearizer example, enabling it to handle a wider range of states than would be possible with an ordinary quantum feedback controller. Our findings may lead to the development of more general and versatile quantum feedback controllers in the field of quantum engineering.

When the seeds are not uniformly distributed, a flag indicator is used to decide whether to use a long or short seed in the privacy amplification step. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in a semi-metric space, are classified into two distinct categories: the curves that can be re-parameterized to have uniform speed, and those that cannot. We demonstrate that a curve is of the non-uniform speed type if and only if it is associated with a Bertrand parabolic vector field, thereby leading to a new definition. We further establish that certain types of one-order contact curves are of the uniform speed type if and only if they are associated with a Bertrand parabolic vector field, and we provide several initial conditions that are sufficient to guarantee this property. Additionally, we explore and demonstrate the applicability of these principles to higher dimensional spaces (three dimensions and beyond). Finally, corresponding principles and applications are identified for space-like and light-like curves, respectively. As an application of these findings, we demonstrate that semi-geodesics are of the uniform speed type if and only if they are associated with a Bertrand parabolic vector field. We also investigate the geometry of semi-geodesic curves in a two-dimensional space, specifically the regions in which a Bertrand parabolic vector field is unique, and provide key insights into the properties of semi-geodesic curves, such as their local convexity, concavity, and flatness depending on the characteristics of this unique vector field. Moreover, we demonstrate that a semi-geodesic curve is of the non-uniform speed type if and only if it is associated with two distinct Bertrand parabolic vector fields, and identify key principles related to its local properties based on these distinct vector fields. We also establish that a semi-geodesic curve is of the uniform speed type if and only if it is associated with two distinct Bertrand parabolic vector fields, and its geometry for any dimension (three or more) is consistent with its geometry for a two-dimensional space, specifically regarding its local properties such as convexity, concavity, and flatness. Finally, corresponding principles and applications are identified for light-like geodesics. We demonstrate that a light-like geodesic is of the uniform speed type if and only if it is associated with two distinct Bertrand parabolic vector fields, and its geometry for any dimension (three or more) is consistent with its geometry for a two-dimensional space, specifically regarding its local properties such as convexity, concavity, and flatness. (The corresponding findings for a one-dimensional space are not applicable as a Bertrand parabolic vector field is not uniquely determined.)

This is achieved by first obtaining the Fourier transform of the process's semigroup, then using Ito calculus to derive the desired distribution. spin in two distinct scenarios: when the mass difference between dark matter and ordinary
matter is negligible, and when dark matter is significantly heavier. It is demonstrated
that highly accelerated dark matter can increase its scattering rate, particularly for
particles with significant spin. The consequences of this process on dark matter are then
evaluated, showing that high-speed, spin-dependent interactions may be necessary to
explain certain weak signals detected in experiments. This possibility could be
confirmed through future experiments that search for similar interactions using accelerated
laboratory particles. Furthermore, it is suggested that high-speed, spin-dependent
interactions may be able to explain a discrepancy in another experimental result, the
ratio of $^{148}Nd$ to $^{144}Nd$ in the terrestrial atmosphere. If these ideas are
correct, it would imply that dark matter is significantly heavier than previously
thought. As a result, it is proposed that experiments focus on a specific range of
parameters that incorporate the effects of dark matter acceleration and increased
spin-dependent interactions. This investigation is unique in comparing one- and
two-dimensional scattering processes, emphasizing the significance of dark matter
acceleration and spin in these scenarios. Additionally, it is the first study to examine
the influence of gravitational forces on spinning dark matter particles using numerical
simulations. The concept of accelerated dark matter is explored further in a related
study, in which numerical simulations are used to examine the spatial distribution of
interacting dark matter within the solar system. If these theories hold, it would imply

properties and potential interactions. This investigation is unique in considering the
possibility of accelerated dark matter, and it is proposed that experiments focus on
this theory, which better explains existing data and could be confirmed by future
experiments. A accompanying paper contains detailed information about numerical
simulations used in this investigation. This research is part of a larger series of
studies that utilize data from global atmospheric sampling to explore concepts of

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from programming and cognitive sciences to establish a method for assessing the understandability of algorithms. This involves developing a composite model of human cognition that learns a given algorithm and tracks the difficulties of comprehension. These complexities are represented by points on a cognitive complexity map. The resulting metric, the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS), serves as a rating system for algorithmic interpretability. The CCS is illustrated using a simple algorithmic solution for identifying individuals with COVID-19 symptoms, in addition to a more complex scenario involving actual patient data. The study highlights the advantages of this measure, demonstrating that CCS can effectively capture the understandability of algorithms. It also demonstrates its potential by identifying key factors that contribute to difficulties in comprehension and offering suggestions for improving algorithm clarity. Furthermore, CCS is shown to facilitate the comparison of multiple algorithms in terms of their interpretability. All the necessary code and data can be accessed through a dedicated repository. This work marks a significant step towards developing a common standard for evaluating the understandability of algorithms using a scientifically grounded methodology. Potential applications of this research involve building upon a shared platform a community of interpretable machine learning developers can leverage to enhance their models' transparency. This initiative has the potential to reshape the learning environment, promoting research into algorithms that are easier for humans to comprehend and develop training programs that enhance learning abilities. By promoting a data-driven culture, this project can facilitate the creation of data-driven education systems that focus on enhancing human cognitive capabilities. Similarly, this technology has the potential to be adopted in various industries, including business sectors that are leveraging algorithms to enhance customer experience, scientists using AI in life-science-research, or companies developing trustworthy autonomous systems, among others. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, which makes estimation more complicated. We suggest a technique to overcome this issue by employing a Gaussian covariance to reparameterize the Poisson process. This technique allows the parameters to be estimated independently. Notably, the parameter representing extreme event variability is correlated with the parameters governing the tail of the extreme event distribution, but this does not impact its asymptotic behavior. Our study evaluates the reparameterization technique's efficiency in estimating extreme event distribution parameters and considers two potential applications: using Bayesian inference with varying priors distributions and constructing extreme event confidence intervals. We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic Casimir pressure on a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field. This scenario gives rise to a Casimir torque acting on the particle. We find that the torque is most pronounced when the particle achieves specific energy levels, known as Landau levels, and that its magnitude is directly correlated with the magnetic field and the particle's charge. Additionally, the torque exhibits variations based on the particle's charge state and charge distribution, and these variations are most evident at higher magnetic field strengths and larger values of the fine structure constant. To enhance the security of Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems, it's crucial to protect against covert attacks on feedback control loops. Previous research has focused mainly on detecting overt attacks that alter system parameter values. In contrast, this research investigates stealthy attacks that manipulate system behavior without altering its parameters. We utilize a system's transfer function to represent the stealthy attack, demonstrating its root cause. Our analysis reveals that a specific set of system characteristics dictates whether such an attack is feasible and what parameters would be necessary to achieve it. To address the detection difficulty, we propose an effective predictive monitoring method. We illustrate our method through a numerical case study verified using a simulation. Our simulation compares the proposed monitoring method with existing approaches, showcasing its practical applicability in preventing stealthy attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this research initiates effective predictive monitoring methods against stealthy attacks on fundamental LTV systems. It also sets the groundwork for applying these methods to more complex Subsea Lifting systems. Lately, Subsea LTV systems have gained significant interest from researchers and industry experts due to their vast applications. As the success of stealthy attacks in the material and numerical validation demonstrates, our approach has far-reaching practical implications that could be exploited by malicious entities, posing a significant threat to the safety of critical infrastructure. In particular, we have found that it is possible to carry out stealthy attack on LTV systems by manipulating the Step Response, an attribute that is typically considered innocuous. In the future, we suggest applying our monitoring method to other applications, such as predictive maintenance. Additionally, we propose adapting the concepts of stealthy attacks to other areas of autonomous systems, promoting future research in effective predictive monitoring methods against stealthy attacks and stealthy attacks on predictive control systems. A patent has been filed for the monitoring method presented in this research. The research has also received the first-place prize at the 2021 ML4CS workshop's "Attacks on Machine Learning" competition. The associated materials can be found at: https://bitbucket.org/ucy_cns/research_2021/src/main\_tree/ucy\_cns\_2021.11.17. Automatic summarization has advanced significantly with the integration of graph-based algorithms, enhancing summary quality. Despite its prowess, previous studies have predominantly focused on English, leaving other languages behind. A major challenge hindering the application of graph-based algorithms for non-English languages is the scarcity of annotated data required for model training. To address this issue, we introduce a ground-breaking method, GAE-ISumm, which can automatically produce high-quality summaries in lesser-known languages with minimal human intervention. GAE-ISumm relies on pre-existing low-fidelity summaries and performs entity recognition, part-of-service identification, and summary generation through an innovative hybrid network that integrates deep learning and graph adjustment. By incorporating an entity ranking module, GAE-ISumm produces accurate and comprehensive summaries. Additionally, our findings indicate that GAE-ISumm outperforms traditional text-rank based approaches. Furthermore, the summaries generated by GAE-ISumm demonstrate qualitative superiority, embodying the inherent characteristics of human-created summaries – namely, redundancy and coherence. To further establish the generalizability of our model, additional sets of summaries were generated for two underserved languages, namely Urdu and Urdu-Arabic, and the results indicate that GAE-ISomm can effectively summarize text in any language without requiring any form of regularization. Utilizing deep learning, a custom quantization module can be designed to optimize the error rate of a target MSK signal, without relying on complex mathematical calculations. This paper aims to fill this gap by examining various aspects of the algorithm's behavior and examining its replacement with alternative components. We specifically investigated these five key areas: memory representation, fitness function, selection process, dynamics of evolution, and stack tracing. Our findings indicate that a guiding function and the algorithm's iterative process are crucial to its effectiveness, but the specific approaches used do not greatly impact the outcome. Furthermore, we discovered that incorporating additional elements such as extra system state fields and input data does improve the algorithm but is not always necessary. Ultimately, this research provides insights that can help inform the development of future evolutionary algorithms for creating detailed system state snapshots from crash reports. The management of quasiparticle defects within doped semiconductors is a long-standing enigma of great importance due to its potential links with thermally induced transitions and the emergence of unusual electronic states near the Fermi level. By utilizing scanning tunnelling spectroscopy, the spatial distribution of core electronic states surrounding vibrational gaps in the optimally doped and charge-optimal MgxBa1-xCu3O6-$\delta$ was investigated. The results reveal the existence of two distinct organization patterns of core states: a square grid arrangement in the optimally doped sample and a square arrangement with 90-degree rotations in the charge-optimal sample. These findings provide direct evidence for a transition from a uniform lattice to a rotated grid arrangement. The phenomenon can be explained by the fragmentation of a uniform lattice due to the increase in core state density as well as the disappearance of small circular clusters. Notably, this transition bears similarities with a known first-order transition in NiAl2O4 near its antiferromagnetic critical temperature and may also be related to a previously unidentified transition in La1.85Sr0.15CuO4-$\delta$ that occurs near its structural and magnetic phase transition temperature. If this transition were to occur near the percolation threshold for superconductivity, it may impede the development of high-temperature superconductivity. Moreover, the transition may be a common mechanism for the formation of unusual nonhomogeneous electronic states observed in the presence of antiferromagnetic or structural phase transitions in high-temperature cuprate superconductors. The phenomenon could potentially be used as a diagnostic tool to investigate other transitions in doped semiconductors and related materials that have undergone structural or magnetic transformations. By employing high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy, the research opens up the possibility of using scanning tunnelling microscopy to investigate the fragmentation of quasiparticle condensates and the formation of coherent electronic condensates that form upon doping semiconductors. If this approach were to be broadly applicable to the entire class of high-temperature cuprate superconductors, it may provide significant insights into the role of fragmentation in the development of superconductivity. Moreover, the methodology could be used to investigate the disappearance of small circular clusters in various materials that have undergone structural or magnetic transformations. Notably, the technique could be developed to detect similar phenomena in molecular materials, which may be related to transitions in high-temperature cuprate superconductors that occur near the percolation threshold for superconductivity

Adaptive interaction in human-conversational systems is crucial for sustaining conversations. Measuring the level of adaptation, or entrainment, that a system displays is, however, a complicated task. Most existing methods for assessing entrainment rely on manual, labor-intensive annotation processes. This study investigates whether unsupervised AI techniques can be relied upon to detect entrainment. We've successfully used an unsupervised autoencoder to recognize instances of entrainment from audio recordings and have demonstrated the validity of this approach through a comparison of human annotations and the model's predictions. The results show that the unsupervised method successfully identifies entrainment and, notably, also accurately captures the intensity or level of adaptation evident in the data. This unsupervised model has significant implications, particularly for evaluating entrainment in human-conversational system interactions automatedly. Furthermore, this study provides insights into the model's performance based on various factors such as speaker similarity, dialogue coordination, and speaking time. The analysis reveals the model's sensitivity to these aspects, suggesting areas for improving the model's precision. Ultimately, this study presents evidence suggesting that AI-driven methods could be used to detect entrainment in human-conversational interactions, including those involving human-conversational systems. You can access the pre-trained model through https://github.com/AllamMohan/Unsupervised-Entrainment-Detection. Additionally, this study is a part of a larger research initiative examining the various modes of adaptive interaction that are observable in human-conversational system interactions, including, but not limited to, entrainment. Classifying every frame in a video into distinct actions requires a sophisticated temporal segmentation approach that previous studies have shown to be difficult when training only occurs in relation to the frame's specific class. To improve this process, our proposed technique employs two self-supervised models that bypass the need for explicitly labeled data. The first model generates crisp segment boundaries from raw videos, while the second model refines this information using a multi-modal, semi-supervised approach that combines frame and fine-grained semantic segment features. A proprietary loss function enables these models to jointly identify meaningful actions and their corresponding temporal durations within each video. As a result, our technique outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on challenging datasets such as 60 Minute Recap, ActivityNet, and THUMOS-24. The code for our method is openly available at https://github.com/dianneWC/SSCAP. When applied to the task of action detection, our technique achieves top results on ActivityNet and THUMOS-24 when evaluated using established metrics. The analytical findings from our study shed light on the effectiveness of specific loss functions in action segmentation and provide valuable insights for future research in this domain. Additionally, our technique has practical applications in creating engaging video summaries where users can seamlessly transition between distinct actions within each segment. The corresponding video is available on YouTube at https://youtu.be/dRrL9l8a4Og. Further examples are provided in the accompanying paper. (Source: arXiv:2202.01617)

Current educational tools for teaching software testing provide comprehensive feedback but are limited in their ability to simulate real-world scenarios. To address this, educators can encourage students to create and share software tests as an alternative form of feedback. This practice provides students with an immediate understanding of their peers' skills in software testing but may also lead students to focus solely on writing tests rather than learning the subject material. To explore the effectiveness of this approach, we compared the performance of two groups of students. Those in the treatment group received feedback in the form of sample solutions from their instructor, while those in the control group were encouraged to provide feedback in the form of answers to a call for participation. Our results indicate that students who received feedback in the form of sample solutions performed better in a follow-up assessment than those who were encouraged to provide feedback in the form of answers. However, our data also suggests that students who shared feedback in the form of answers showed greater engagement and sense of community, and were more likely to continue learning software testing. This study provides evidence that can be used to inform the effectiveness of different approaches to providing feedback in the software testing domain. Domain adaptation is a challenging task in deep learning where adaptation occurs without access to the target domain's label space. One subvariant of domain adaptation, source-free adaptation, prohibits the use of target domain labels but instead allows the collection of synthetic annotation from an additional unsupervised source. However, this alternative source presents its own issues, such as differences in annotation distributions and semantic gaps, necessitating statistical correlation between the two domains. Furthermore, this alternative source may contain information not relevant to the target domain, requiring a response modification technique to address. To resolve these challenges, we suggest Hypothesis Shift, a novel framework composed of multiple deep neural networks, each capable of generating different label hypotheses for the target domain. By selectively utilizing these hypotheses, Hypothesis Shift is able to mitigate domain differences and bridge the semantic gap, as well as adapt to the target domain's label space based on the available synthetic annotations. Our proposed HS4SA, an implementation of Hypothesis Shift for source-free adaptation, boasts superior performance across multiple datasets and outperforms existing domain adaptation methods by achieving up to 97.53% accuracy. Our project's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/fuqianghu/HS4SA. Additionally, additional details about our method have been included in the appended study, including the corrigendum in arXiv version arXiv:2301.00171. Importantly, HS4SA's performance is revealed to be significantly influenced by its interior neural networks. Consequently, an important implication arises: the underlying mechanism of hypothesis shift can be further studied by neural network designers with potential for enhancement. To the best of our knowledge, this neural network-based investigation of hypothesis shift is a novel contribution, thereby offering valuable insights to the research community. As an example of such investigation, we provide a worthy counterexample that can guide hypothesis shift developers towards improving their creation, potentially resulting in an advanced version. Moreover, through our research, we establish an essential link between generalization and adaptability, thereby offering valuable lessons to deep learners and neural network designers. In this framework, fission occurs outside the core, with fuel atoms fragmenting into highly reactive fragments that release energy through subsequent collisions. Currently, gas core reactors remain unexploited for nuclear propulsion due to an unaffordably large number of collisions needed for a significant portion of fissionable material to undergo fission. To overcome this limitation, a system is described where liquid metal fuel is circulated and contained by magnetic forces, reducing the number of collisions required for fission and enabling a more efficient and viable gas core reactor for propulsion systems. Such an system would offer a high specific impulse and high specific thrust, along with various benefits in different applications of flight modes, including a capability to function for extended periods of time in low power mode, sustain high power for an extended period in medium power mode, and achieve rapid acceleration in full power mode. Background:  A crucial component in the detection of rare particles and their origins is the tracking of astroparticles. To accurately identify and follow these particles, experimental projects regularly make use of massive data sets incorporating information on simulated astroparticle interactions, which, however, can significantly increase the scale of available data, posing a substantial burden on data analysis processes. Addressing these challenges is the primary objective of our study. 

Methods:  The paper introduces an innovative neural network architecture that efficiently incorporates domain-specific knowledge to forecast the positions of astroparticle interactions. To achieve this, we utilize knowledge-utility networks, specifically designed for domain-informed policy optimization (DIO) methods. 

Results:  We demonstrate the efficacy of our domain-informed neural network across three distinct training settings. Notably, the domain-informed approach yields a substantial reduction in the average positional error when positioning muon interactions in the range of around 70-87%, in comparison to standard neural network models. 

Conclusion:  The study showcases the domain-informed technique's potential for enhancing neural network performance on complex, physics-related tasks by streamlining the training process and yielding more interpretable outcomes. To further facilitate the adoption of domain-informed domain policy optimization methods in the field of astroparticle research, we have released related source code and data sets publicly available at https://github.com/DeepPhysics/Astroparticle_DIO.

Quantum matter exhibits diverse topological properties, classified by their bulk and boundary characteristics. Our study focuses on a particular theory for bulk and surface states in topological insulators with high-order boundaries. Using a new mathematical technique, we show that the surface properties of these insulators remain stable even when they are imperfect, while their bulk properties are resilient under specific disorders. Conversely, we discovered a previously unidentified phase displaying both bulk and surface properties in the presence of disorders. This phase exhibits a unique boundary that separates two distinct topological insulators. Our results should be observable in experiments using various methods such as transport measurements, optical or acoustic microscopy, or by inspecting the system's band structure. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the intricate relationship between bulk and surface properties in topological insulators, especially in those with high-order boundaries. While bulk properties can withstand some disorders, other bulk properties emerge in the perfect system, and are triggered by disorders when intermediate disorders are introduced. Moreover, we show that the surface properties can stabilize in two distinct types of disorders, one that divides the bulk into two distinct phases and another that splits the bulk into three distinct phases. These remarkable connections between bulk and surface properties are the hallmarks of a newly discovered topological phase displaying both bulk and surface properties in the presence of disorders. This new phase is the first to be predicted to exhibit both bulk and surface properties in the presence of disorders, and it is predicted to be realized in systems of two coupled 2D topological insulators with high-order boundaries. Such a system can be constructed using coupled quantum dots, or as a light-matter system consisting of two 2D photonic insulators with high-order boundaries. This study introduces advanced techniques for analyzing the movement of vortices in a fluid flow on a two-dimensional plane, and we find that the equation of motion for a single vortex is a functional stochastic differential equation (FSDIE). Our approach for solving this type of equation is adapted from a method originally used to research the pricing of financial instruments. By applying mathematical results equivalent to a FSDIE to two different types of vortex motion, one with deterministic and the other with random starting points, our methods allow for the calculation of the average distance between two vortices. We also investigate the effects of external interference on a single vortex, using numerical methods to demonstrate our findings. Furthermore, our methods can be extended to research the motion of multiple vortices by utilizing the idea of "condensing" to simplify the analysis. Ultimately, our methods allow for the simulation of realistic scenarios where vortices interact with each other due to their motion. Although our numerical examples focus on the motion of vortices in a fluid flow, the techniques used are generally applicable to any situation in which the motion of objects can be modeled as an SDE and can provide valuable insights for a wide variety of areas. It is anticipated that these methods may also be used in other fields such as molecular biology and finance. Such potential applications are discussed in Section 1.4. Moreover, our methods allow for the integration of physical and biological experiments by researching the properties of rare molecular events in mathematical models. A detailed explanation of these methods and their potential applications outside of the context of vortex motion is provided in the author's thesis, which is available for viewing. The work presented in this study is the researcher's final project, supervised by Dr. Stephanie Peter, and Dr. Scott A. Romans is the second reader. A summary of this study is provided below: Notwithstanding significant advancements in the theoretical and numerical modeling of 2D fluid dynamics in the last century, the complexity of real-world 2D fluid dynamics remains an unsolved problem. The reason for this is that 2D fluid dynamics is a component of a larger system of interest - the 3D fluid dynamics surrounding the 2D plane. The motion of 2D fluid dynamics is consequently affected by external interference from surrounding 3D fluid dynamics. The discrepancy between idealized models of 2D fluid dynamics, which assume no external interference, and actual 2D fluid dynamics, which assumes the opposite, is the main obstacle to accurately modeling real-world 2D fluid dynamics. In various life science applications such as cell tracking and behavior analysis, 
time series analysis poses a significant challenge due to the large amounts of data involved.
The problem is complicated by the presence of noisy and irregular measurements which can result in distorted signals.
These complexities necessitate the development of techniques that can handle short and dimensional-rich sequences efficiently.
A suitable approach to address this need is deep learning, which can learn optimal features for accurate prediction when provided with the correct guidance.
However, most existing methods are unsupervised and suffer from the problem of mode collapse, where multiple distinct features are mapped to a single representation, resulting in the loss of valuable information.
To overcome this limitation, we present TEOARGA, a novel supervised deep learning model that utilizes output activation to remove redundant features and achieve an accurate, compact representation of temporal sequences.
By leveraging the knowledge of expert annotations via a gradient-based approach through expert network, TEOARGA surpasses the performance of existing unsupervised deep learning methods by a considerable margin.
Its effectiveness in handling noisy and irregular sequences with limited expert guidance positions TEOARGA as a robust supervised representation learning solution for temporal sequence analysis.
With its successful application in multi-modal behavioral analysis, TEOARGA demonstrates its potential as a leading technique in various temporal sequence-related tasks.

Reinforcement learning agents can use partially observable environments by incorporating a belief space into their framework. Typically, researchers utilize the Kalman filter, which is limited to dynamic systems with observable states and linear noise, exceeding practical limitations. By contrast, we demonstrate that a simple neural network, consisting of a one-way recurrent model with hidden, uniformly distributed states, can effectively learn an accurate probability distribution over the hidden states from the observed variables, even in highly non-linear scenarios with random noise. Notably, we found that this belief distribution converges to a fixed point after an infinitely long sequence of steps. Furthermore, we analyzed the characteristics of one such fixed point, while also identifying the necessary conditions for existence and uniqueness of the other fixed points. Lastly, we explored the policy iteration algorithm in the one-way recurrent model and discussed potential areas for further investigation. Our results present novel tools for the analysis of one-way recurrent models and have significant implications for the development of practical algorithms in the field of reinforcement learning. However, a long-standing challenge has hindered the development of such measures - a lack of standardized evaluation procedures. This work presents the challenge's findings, introducing a new evaluation dataset and procedures, evaluating ten state-of-the-art methods across human visual perception and deep learning standards. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that existing algorithms still fall short of being effective in practice, suggesting potential benefits from their integration with other detection methods. The stochastic processes experience a shift towards a stochastic process related to an adjusted degenerate elliptic operator, with a nondegenerate diffusion component, largely due to a constant factor. Metastability is then analyzed within this context, specifically in cases involving incomplete controllability, which typically occurs in such scenarios. Two main scenarios are investigated: stabilization of the stochastic process near its natural boundary and stabilization at an artificial boundary resulting from a combination of boundary and internal obstacles. The occurrence of an intermediate metastable state is determined by the limit of the ratio of the adjustment time and a characteristic time scale of the stochastic process. If this ratio tends to infinity, numerical results suggest that metastability should decrease, and an estimate can be derived using homogenization theory for the nondegenerate diffusion component of the related operator. This analysis is performed without relying on the ergodic eigenfunctions of the operator and provides estimates comparable to those obtained through the ergodic eigenfunctions. Notably, our findings concerning stabilization near the natural boundary are relatively strict and more precise than those obtained through the ergodic approach, while the reverse holds for stabilization at the artificial boundary, with the exception of a scenario involving reflection invariance of the boundaries and a specific sign condition for the potenial, in which case the occurrence and duration of metastability can be assessed with greater accuracy using the ergodic approach. These observations highlight the benefits of considering adjustments to the time scale rather than the typical exit time in analyzing metastability in these scenarios. Additionally, the study demonstrates that under specific conditions, the metastable state can be identified as a stable steady-state solution of the adjusted stochastic process, which may not necessarily be the case for stabilization near the natural boundary. Lastly, the study shows that when the adjustment is extensive enough, the stochastic process exits the intermetastable state in a direction determined by a degenerate elliptic operator, which marks an improvement over the limitations of incomplete controllability, while still allowing for control at an artificial boundary. This study focuses on the impact of intense magnetic fields on nuclear matter, investigated using the lowest order constraint variational method with a specific phenomenological nucleon-nucleon interaction. Variations of the nucleon mass, caused by strong magnetic fields, are accounted for in our calculations, utilizing different values of the magnetic field strength (σ) ranging from 0 to 3 times the critical nuclear density. Results indicate that increasing the magnetic field results in a decrease in the saturation density of the system, accompanied by reduced binding energies and an increased compressibility. Furthermore, the effect of magnetic fields on the pairing properties of nuclear matter was explored through calculations of the singlet and triplet pairing energies, showing that these energies respond differently to varying strong magnetic fields. At a density corresponding to normal nuclear density, pair energies were found to exhibit a non-linear decrease with increasing magnetic field strength, contrasting the linear decrease observed at higher and lower densities. Ultimately, our research suggests that intense magnetic fields may facilitate the formation of dipolar clusters within nuclear matter. Additionally, calculations of the magnetisation and energy density contributions from spin and kinetic components are presented. All calculations were carried out at a convergence level of higher than 90%. Findings were also validated through comparison with existing studies on the subject. The present study represents the initial application of the LOCV method to investigate dipolar clusters in nuclear matter under strong magnetic fields. Due to computational constraints, we were unable to explore other aspects of dipolar physics in this work. Nonetheless, future research aims to address these limitations by employing the projected variance method to study T and T-odd correlations within a nuclear medium exposed to strong magnetic fields. This approach will enable us to investigate novel physics associated with magnetic fields, breaking spin symmetry, and T-odd symmetry within a relativistic mean field formalism. To tackle these limitations, we plan to develop novel code that can accommodate a Gogny-type phenotype of nucleon-nucleon interactions. Historically, the LOCV method has been implemented using phenomenological interactions, whereas the projected variance method has been developed using phenomenological interactions as well as microscopic interaction. Notably, our earlier work has revealed that the microscopic interaction is not required to explore novel physics. For example, studies have demonstrated that pairing symmetry is highly dependent on the specific structure of nucleon-nucleon interactions. Therefore, unless theoretically justified, the use of phenomenological interactions is entirely sufficient to explore the aforementioned limitations. Federated learning offers a decentralized way to train complex models by sharing minimal data, reducing communication time, and preventing data leakage. 
However, training on sparse models still requires large amounts of data, necessitating increased communication. 
Our solution, DP-REC, tackles this challenge by developing a communication-efficient technique for sharing direction information in k-nearest neighbor regression, an essential building block for popular machine learning protocols such as Federated Proximal Projected Gradient Descent and Federated Rational Subgradient Descent. 
First, we adapted the KP-PGD protocol to use k-nearest neighbor regression instead of full dataset regression to minimize communication time. 
Next, we found a way to compress the labels of local training data without affecting the model's performance. 
Finally, we evaluated the efficiency of DP-REC by comparing it to other popular protocols including Federated Averaging, Federated Proximal Projected Gradient Descent, and Federated Rational Subgradient Descent, using synthetic datasets on various parameters. 
Our experiments show that DP-REC achieves a significant decrease in both communication time and data size with minimal performance loss, making it an efficient method for the inference process of FL. 
Moreover, DP-REC's ability to handle large datasets with numerous features, such as breast cancer and diabetes datasets from open datasets on KDnops, without compromising model performance. 
This versatility and efficiency make DP-REC a suitable method for the inference process in FL. 
Our solution utilizes the Python programming language and several open-source libraries, including PyTorch, TorchCluster, DeepCluster, KDnops, and DP-SAG, which are all freely available at this GitHub repository. 
Lastly, we discuss several potential enhancements to our protocol, such as the use of parallel processing to speed up computation and the application of DP-SGD with binary data to further reduce communication time and improve model robustness against data breaches. 
Our solution and related research are expected to have a significant impact in the field of decentralized machine learning and robust privacy preservation. 
This research is still ongoing and the findings have not been formally published yet. 
Several related work is also being investigated that might enhance our solution and contribute to the body of literature on the topic.

We develop a model to describe the conceptual hierarchy of players and introduce a new concept of sufficiency for information. We prove that any player using this hierarchical structure can be treated as if they use complete information specific to each layer. We also establish conditions under which this hierarchical structure achieves the best possible outcome among all types of incomplete information in multi-layered games. Additionally, we provide an original example illustrating the practical application of our theoretical findings. Furthermore, we show that our results also apply to larger sets of players with different levels of information. Finally, we investigate how players interact with each other in multi-layered games of incomplete information. We identify a type of equilibrium that takes into account the cognitive characteristics of players and prove it is the most effective type of interaction in such games. We also demonstrate that this interaction is even more effective when players are homogeneous in terms of their cognitive characteristics. We base our theoretical findings on a mathematical technique called \epsilon-equivalence, which is used to define the different levels of information that players may have. To validate our theory, we also provide computational examples that compare the effectiveness of various interactions in multi-layered games of incomplete information. These examples demonstrate the practical application of our theoretical findings. These estimates can be achieved at a relatively low cost if there is adequate data available and appropriate analytical tools employed. Discovering hidden patterns in data is a key challenge in machine learning that is more effectively tackled by algorithms capable of analyzing complex patterns in data itself, rather than through pre-defined parameters. We have developed a set of algorithms capable of performing unsupervised clustering and classification of data, which is independent of user input and can be applied to any type of data that can be mapped to a geometric space. By utilizing a quantum computing architecture based on superconducting qubits, our approach offers the potential for faster processing and higher scalability than traditional methods. We have demonstrated the efficacy of our algorithm with real-world data sets from various fields, and show that it is resistant to errors in data. Additionally, we propose an alternative version of our algorithm that incorporates additional user input, allowing for semi-supervised learning with reduced user involvement. Experimental results indicate that our approach is capable of achieving optimal performance with minimal user input. Due to its architecture, our algorithm is capable of processing more complex input data compared to existing methods. Overall, our approach marks a significant step towards applying quantum computing algorithms directly to real-world problems in machine learning. We anticipate these algorithms to be utilized not only in the quantum computing era but also as inspired solutions for classical computing systems. The algorithms and related tools have been made publicly available.

A recently developed non-sequentially structured TTS model called FastPitch offers improved computational efficiency in speech synthesis.  Initially, the FastPitch model provided limited control over its pitch parameter, with significant deviations from the desired pitch for every unit of pitch alteration.  Subsequent research demonstrated that by applying a normalization technique to the pitch parameters, the pitch range could be expanded, significantly enhancing the model's controllability.  However, applying the normalization technique resulted in a minor loss of the natural characteristics observed in speaker-dependent corpora.  To address this issue, we implemented an optional module known as pitch augmentation that modifies the speaker-averaged pitch range rather than the naturally occurring pitch variations.  As a result, the incorporation of this module preserves the speaker's distinct pitch variations while offering improved controllability to the FastPitch model.  Our experiments involved training the model on a large dataset of publicly accessible speaker-features derived from a variety of corpora.  Through a comprehensive analysis that incorporated a combination of subjective and objective evaluations, we confirmed the significant advantages offered by the newly implemented pitch augmentation module.  Specifically, the results indicated an approximate 60% reduction in the discrepancy between the desired and actual pitches for sentences with extended pitch variations (those exceeding 20 semitones), while also demonstrating minimal adverse effects on speech quality and articulation.  Furthermore, the analysis revealed that the pitch augmentation module was highly consistent and reproducible, with results that were nearly identical when applied to sentences with short and intricate syntax.  Ultimately, the fastpitch model equipped with the pitch augmentation module provided the capability to generate speech at any desired pitch level while maintaining its inherent speaker-specific characteristics and timbre.  Our implementation of the pitch augmentation module represents a major breakthrough in speaker-agnostic TTS models, and we intend to make the relevant code and audio samples publicly available.  Moreover, our objective evaluation revealed that the pitch augmentation module was highly generalizable, with successful applications possible on speaker-agnostic TTS models trained using a variety of corpora, even those distinctly different from the corpus used in our study.  As such, the code and ideas behind this innovation could be readily integrated into other speaker-agnostic TTS projects.  Finally, the results of our evaluation indicated that the pitch augmentation module was highly scalable, with applications possible on a computing cluster to process large quantities of speaker-features in a distributed environment.  Specifically, the results suggested that the pitch augmentation module could be applied to millions of speaker-features within a period of less than 2 days

This paper introduces Hopper, a multi-hop spatiotemporal deep learning framework, 
designed to enhance internal data flow through sequential refinement steps.
The Hopper architecture achieves this through sequential expansions of its internal state,
utilizing a transformer-based approach for efficient handling of the expanded dimensions.
We evaluate Hopper on spatiotemporal prediction tasks such as weather forecasting and
human action recognition, leveraging its scalability and extendibility properties.
The framework's current implementation on a GEForce GTX 1060 graphics card takes 
approximately 0.5 milliseconds for each forward pass involving a single hop.
The accompanying code is available on the repository at https://github.com/satya777/Hopper.

This research presents a fuzzy k-means algorithm with variable feature weights (FKM-VFW) for clustering high-dimensional data. Since large data sets are typically spread thinly across multiple dimensions, our approach adjusts the influence of each feature on a cluster in proportion to the entropy of its members, reducing the negative effects of dominant features. Evaluation metrics such as the Silhouette coefficient and entropy were used to assess the effectiveness of FKM-VFW, which was compared with traditional fuzzy k-means and two recent variants. Our experiments demonstrated that FKM-VFW produces better clustering results than its predecessors, as evidenced by the Silhouette coefficient and an entropy metric, which measures the homogeneity within compact clusters and the separation from others. Notably, the algorithm was developed with the intention of producing interpretable clusters from the output of pre-trained machine learning models, such as support vector machines and random forests. Furthermore, our study provides a framework for evaluating the quality of clusters produced by any fuzzy k-means variant using multiple clustering metrics. Moreover, our approach demonstrates its ability to enhance the accuracy of breast cancer clustering when applied to the MRI scans of patients, which have been segmented using the Auto-encoder-Convolutional Neural Network (ACNN) method. The implementation of FKM-VFW has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. The results of our research were obtained using the MR breast cancer dataset, which can be accessed through the http://www.med.ulster.ac.uk/ research/our-research-areas/computational-intelligence/clinical-aids/ clinical-aids.html website. The algorithm was verified using 30 trials with 10 patients per iteration, which confirmed our findings. The evaluation metrics showed that the FKMs outperformed its predecessors on most of the datasets used. The results of our research are available on the GitHub repository at: https://github.com/MalikAyub007/Variable-Fidelity-Weighted-Fuzzy-k-Means. The repository includes the data used in our research. The inter-cluster and intra-cluster Silhouette coefficients for our approach were found to be higher than those of its competitors in most cases. Notably, the ACC, SC, RC, PR, FP, and FN metrics were used to measure the effectiveness of the fuzzy k-means variants. The number of clusters (k) was set to 2 to prevent bias in the evaluation process, as recommended by earlier research. The DC index was not used in our assessment due to the predominantly binary nature of the clusters produced by the ACNN method.

Mixtures of experts, a type of network architecture where multiple expert networks are combined through a gating network, have long been recognized for their potential in efficiently handling large datasets. However, the typical training process for these networks often gets stuck in local optima due to its gradient-based nature. In an attempt to overcome this limitation, previous research proposed various pretraining and fine-tuning procedures, but these workarounds are either computationally expensive or achieve only marginal improvements. Under the assumption that the mixture of experts meets certain depth and width requirements, as well as that the gating network outputs satisfy a condition known as the "orthogonality" property, our research presents two novel algorithms that directly tackle the mixture of experts' parameters through an optimized iterative procedure. Unlike previous solutions, these algorithms are both efficient and effective, and are capable of consistently producing high-quality solutions that are well-suited for handling large datasets. Our research also reveals that the pretraining-and-fine-tuning workflow can be viewed as a special case of our second algorithm, where the expert networks are trained independently from the gating network, resulting in suboptimal performance. In addition to these findings, our study includes applications of the mixture of experts to various complex datasets. Our algorithms have been made publicly available on the website at the following URL: https://github.com/Info-Naples/MoE_Algorithms. Our research demonstrates that the mixture of experts is capable of efficiently and effectively learning high-quality solutions for complex problems, thereby opening up its potential for practical applications in areas such as data classification and function approximation. Ultimately, our study is a contribution towards the development of scalable machine learning architectures. Specifically, our research is an advancement on the works of several top conferences, including ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR. In this paper, an in-depth analysis of factors affecting transferability is provided. Specifically, we challenge two widely accepted agreements within the deep learning community: firstly, that convolutional neural networks are universally superior to recurrent networks, and secondly, that using fine-tuned models for feature extraction is the standard practice. Our experiments reveal that these agreements may not hold under certain circumstances. For instance, a recurrent neural network outperformed a convolutional neural network in our benchmark, and surprisingly, fine-tuning the batch-norm layer yielded better results than fine-tuning the entire model. These findings are valuable knowledge that researchers and practitioners in the field of deep learning can benefit from. These tasks must be executed in a specified order, making it challenging to adapt and often forcing developers to recreate the setup process each time the application's dependencies evolve. A solution to this problem can be found in containers like Docker, which encapsulate an application and its dependencies, but a notable absence in current container platforms is a compact and safe method for managing the execution order of setup and Teardown steps during the container's lifetime. To address this limitation, we have developed a new container-based framework, Universal Orchestration Container, which decouples the orchestration of applications from the underlying container platform by introducing the concept of a container factory. This framework comprises three key components: the Universal Container, the orchestration component, and the Setup/TearDown execution component. Our proposed container has an average execution time less than 0.1 seconds and a constant memory consumption, showcasing its high performance and resource efficiency. To further reduce execution time, we can leverage an asynchronous Teardown execution approach, which does not affect memory consumption but shortens the Teardown phase by 10% on average. Our experiments demonstrate that the new container outperforms traditional container platforms, with the extra setup time paying off significantly in complex applications with a large number of dependencies. Furthermore, the introduction of an asynchronous Teardown implementation significantly accelerates the execution time of applications during the Teardown phase, leading to a notable time savings of 30% on average in a complex-use-case scenario. This innovative framework decouples the orchestration of applications from a specific container platform by introducing the concept of a container factory, which generates containers safely at runtime. Our framework's decoupling advantage enhances portability, allowing a given application to be executed across various container platforms without modification. Moreover, the framework's resource efficiency and high performance make it suitable for use in a wide variety of applications, even those with many dependencies. Finally, the framework's safety features, such as memory isolation, ensure that the application's interactions with the virtual machine do not cause errors. To validate our approach, we conducted a study demonstrating the framework's high performance by showcasing its average execution time of less than 0.1 seconds and constant memory consumption (plus a small overhead) on average. Adaptive Normalization Scheme (ANS) is a data encoding technique that adapts to the distribution of its input data by adjusting the normalization factor. Unlike a traditional normalized encoding, ANS doesn't rely on a predetermined variable for normalization and instead calculates the normalization factor from the input data. We present a more robust method to determine the normalization factor, which we call'max entropy encoding ANS', in which the normalization factor is optimized to achieve the highest possible entropy of the normalized data distribution. Our findings indicate that this iteration leads to better representation of the original data and enhanced lossless coding performance. Furthermore, we discovered that the max entropy encoding ANS produces quasi uniform probability distribution of the normalized data, which contributes to better coding outcomes. Additionally, our algorithm outperforms previous normalization schemes such as Shannon entropy encoding and Mohan et al.'s normalization scheme both in terms of data representation and coding efficiency. Nonetheless, it's worth noting that the difference in coding performance between this algorithm and Shannon's is relatively minor. In summary, our research reveals the benefits of ANS in terms of both data representation and coding efficiency and we present theoretical arguments for its capability to effectively encode both continuous and discrete probability distributions of data elements. It's acknowledged that ANS isn't suitable for encoding large datasets because of its computational intensity. Thus, this thesis presents the results of experiments conducted on various natural image datasets. It's hoped that the proposed algorithm will inspire researchers to combat the shortcomings of traditional normalization methods and develop more efficient techniques in the future. In terms of future work, it's suggested that additional algorithms be developed to enhance the computational efficiency of ANS while maintaining its current level of performance. Such an effort could ultimately contribute to the development of a more robust image encoding paradigm. In the interest of contributing to the future development of the field, the source code for our experiments has been made publicly available on the CVpedia knowledge base. It's through collaborative sharing of knowledge and research that we can collectively advance the field of image encoding. The dielectric properties of micro- and mesoporous materials are influenced by the characteristics of their pore systems, including surface charge and the movement of ions. This insight is especially crucial in the study of cement-based materials, where capillary pore systems dominate, affecting the materials' overall dielectric behavior. An experimental investigation examined the dielectric properties of a high-pH cement paste at various ages through comparisons with a collection of simplified, porous ceramic samples having different surface areas and amounts of isothermally adsorbed sodium nitrate. Sodium nitrate was employed as a model for surface charge, facilitating an examination of its impact on the dielectric properties of the pore liquid. Data from the dielectric property measurements allowed for the calculation of key parameters, including surface conductivity and interfacial dielectric potential. Notably, the results indicated that dielectric properties are primarily determined by surface conductivity. This finding is attributed to the presence of high-conductivity phases or surfaces that, when in contact with a high surface area of a dielectric material, significantly enhance the dielectric response due to these surfaces. A conceptual model was developed to explain the dielectric response of the pore liquid, considering the combined effects of bound charges, free ions, and surface conductivity. The model was used to estimate the ionic concentrations in the pore liquid and surface conductivity. Notably, the total sodium nitrate concentration was found to be the sum of the amounts bound at the surface and those dissolved in the pore liquid. This insight into the solution chemistry was attributed to the dielectric properties being influenced by the surface conductivity rather than the total sodium nitrate concentration. The study provides novel methods for estimating the interfacial dielectric potential, surface conductivity, and total sodium nitrate concentration in cement-based materials. The research offers the first measurement of the surface conductivity of cement-based materials, revealing that the surface conductivity can reach remarkable levels, up to 15 S/m, which is essentially determined by the high ionic concentrations in the pore liquid. The study's findings can contribute to the advancement of numerical models simulating the dielectric properties of cement-based materials by including parameters such as surface conductivity, bound charges, and material surface area, thus facilitating their practical application. By analyzing the redshifts of background quasars, scientists detect the gravitational influence of unseen haloes that have stopped or slowed the advancement of cosmic fluids. This effect is quantifiable through the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest correlation functions, which contain precise information about the linear coefficients of pressure and viscosity, as well as nonlinear characteristics such as the average neutral hydrogen density and its fluctuation amplitude. In this study, we employed a mock dataset to demonstrate that fluctuation amplitude can be determined independently of the mean hydrogen density. Furthermore, we developed a statistical approach that utilizes a $3\sigma$ confidence interval to set a limit on the underlying signal-to-noise ratio and recover nonlinear parameters such as their standard deviations and nonlinear correlation coefficients. This variability in state dynamics is referred to as state complexity. Measuring state complexity is crucial in optimizing the network for its desired performance. This work proposes a theoretical framework for comparing and evaluating metrics of complexity in Boltzmann machines by examining how they align with the generative model of artificial neural networks. Various information-theoretic measures of complexity, including one recently developed, were assessed based on their alignment with the underlying model of artificial neural networks. A detailed examination of how one of these measures of complexity, subsequently referred to as Lempel-Ziv complexity, depends on system size was also conducted. A similarity between this measure of complexity and the theoretical measure of state complexity derived from the Hamiltonian was identified. Consequently, Lempel-Ziv complexity of artificial neural networks can serve as a suitable proxy for measuring state complexity. Moreover, Lempel-Ziv complexity involves significantly lower computational demands than the theoretical measure of state complexity derived from the Hamiltonian. Consequently, Lempel-Ziv complexity offers an efficient way to gauge the state complexity of artificial neural networks. In our experiment, a group of four individuals could effectively direct a swarm of robots to perform specific tasks within a 3x3 grid layout. Upon initial implementation, our system demonstrated an accuracy of about 85% in task execution, as measured from the robot's perspective. Our study aims to contribute to the continued development of swarm robotics by addressing the prevalent issue of limited and inefficient interaction between humans and robots. Future research will focus on refining the hand signal recognition algorithm and exploring methods to enhance the clarity of swarm-level intentions for the human operator. Additionally, elements of coherence among the robots will be incorporated to streamline interaction. Our associated project, $d$RONI$, is accessible at https://d-roni.go-ing.io. The code for our study can be found at https://github.com/going-com.github/roni-swarm-interaction-2022. Lastly, the visulations from our experiment are hosted on https://goto-ing.io/roni-swarm-interaction-2022. To the best of our knowledge, our work constitutes the first attempt to apply sequential RNN-based hand signal recognition in a decentralized setting. Our approach effectively addresses the challenging task of learning distinct commands within a condensed timespan and filters out irrelevant information, allowing the system to function through efficient feature extraction. Ultimately, this study represents an important step toward enabling seamless, meaningful communication between humans and a swarm of robots. The study aims to assess the efficacy of model merging in enhancing the accuracy of blood cell classification. Initially, the team trained high-performing neural network models for identifying four distinct white blood cell types: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, and eosinophils. By combining these models' probabilities, the researchers demonstrated improved results, specifically for eosinophil and monocyte classifications, with minimal negative impact on neutrophil and lymphocyte classification accuracy. The optimized model achieved superior validation performance compared to a pre-trained, converged ensemble of models, with significantly lower loss and increased accuracy above 90% for all cell types. Furthermore, the team applied the model probabilities to contribute to the development of an automated, rule-based system for annotating large-scale microscopic images. Notably, the study explores the effectiveness of model merging in achieving better overall performance. While the method doesn't alter the models themselves, it offers a viable strategy for enhancing neural network-based classification models without the need for model refinement or retraining. Additionally, the study provides validation and training loss plots for the merged model, specifically to provide a detailed analysis of the merging process. The analysis reveals that model merging can be an effective method for achieving better performance. A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary road. However, this approach has a drawback: it's marked by a pronounced oscillation in the driving Hamiltonian. To address this, a new approach has been proposed, allowing the realization of a quantum benchmark, such as the Mott insulator to superfluid phase transition, with minimal oscillations in the Hamiltonian. By developing a method to approximate the protective, guiding path, a way to reduce the magnitude of these oscillations has been achieved. To validate this strategy, a variational approach was employed, using a projected gradient descent method to optimize a suitably constructed cost function. To facilitate experimental design, the method was applied to a simplified model as well as the Hubbard and Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonians. Our results demonstrate that the proposed strategy is an effective means of achieving smooth, protocol-driven transitions between quantum states. Moreover, we've shown that our strategy is robust against realistic (e.g., trigonometric) perturbations and can be used to optimize costly Hamiltonians. To facilitate future research, the code used in our study has been made publicly available. Our results suggest that the proposed strategy could be used to improve the efficiency of quantum initialization methods. Moreover, the study highlights the utility of gradient-based methods in quantum optics research. A public code repository containing the code used in this study can be accessed at https://bitbucket.org/krithika32/variouscddr. For instance, applying our approach to a (1, 1) Hubbard chain allowed us to achieve a level of ground state fidelity of approximately 100% without needing to sample from the thermal state multiple times. To the knowledge of the study authors, this technique is an innovative means of leveraging variational methods in quantum optics research. A related paper discussing the implementation of the strategy in a atomic lattice has been published, while an extension of the strategy to handle multi-dimensional systems has also been explored. Furthermore, a related study has successfully implemented a new protocol, known as time-constrained protocol, which constrains the driving Hamiltonian to be parameterized as a function of time alone, thereby improving the efficiency of the supporting, auxiliary road. To achieve such an improvement, a method to reduce the magnitude of oscillations in the driving Hamiltonian was developed. To validate this strategy, the method was applied to a theory Hamiltonian as well as the Hubbard model and was successfully implemented both in theory and in experiments involving ultracold atoms. To address this inconsistency, this paper presents a novel, reference-less algorithm utilizing the WRGB color space to achieve natural image appearance on a specific display, taking into account scene irradiance and factors influencing color appearance. The proposed algorithm improves upon existing methods by providing more consistent results and accurate WRGB values, enabling effective RGB mapping. Comparative analyses and practical applications demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm over other techniques. Additionally, this research provides an in-depth review and comprehensive discussion on the principles of human color perception and their relevant applications in digital image processing, especially in the field of tone mapping. Lastly, a related issue concerning fast changes in scene color temperature is thoroughly investigated and an efficient solution is proposed. The proposed algorithm has been successfully implemented in the Adobe Camera Raw software, an essential tool for image processing and editing. The method allows users to view original camera images in their native color state and then adjust the image to a specific appearance, all while preserving accurate color temperature characteristics. Moreover, this technique provides a significant time-saving benefit, requiring only a few seconds to process a hundred M-byte image, a remarkable achievement considering the need for fast interaction. The speed and efficiency of the method make it well-suited for frequent use in image processing and editing applications. A novel laser-plasma framework is developed to investigate photon-photon collision phenomena. Initially, an introduction to high-energy photon physics and the inherent limitations of traditional methods is provided. The feasibility of generating extremely intense, sub-meV photons through laser-plasma interactions is demonstrated, and a framework is introduced to study extreme photon-photon collisions. The treatment is comprehensive, covering all participating photons and particles, and includes a formalism for calculating joint probability distributions based on a plasma's radiative properties. The utility of this approach in examining novel phenomena, such as photon collision-induced egress, wave generation, and pair creation in intense electromagnetic fields, is discussed, with a focus on wave propagation in the joint photon-photon phase space. The framework is dubbed "Laser-Plasma Photonics with Quantum Effects" and is denoted as LPPQE. The article delves into the theoretical underpinnings of LPPQE and presents two novel phenomena that can be studied using this tool: extreme photon-photon collisions and quantum pair creation in vacuum induced by ultra-powerful laser and bremsstrahlung interactions. The framework is designed to facilitate research into a wide array of laser-plasma phenomena, empowering physicists to comprehend and predict the intricate interplay of particles and photons within and beyond the plasma environment. The study offers a new perspective on plasma, urging researchers to explore the underlying physical mechanisms driving the production of plasma-based photon sources, including free-electron lasers, and to harness these devices for a comprehensive investigation of high-energy photon interactions. The work is an exhaustive examination of the fundamental principles, a comprehensive review of the state-of-the-art in laser-plasma physics and photon physics, and an innovative prediction of future breakthroughs in the field of LPPQE. The study advances the field of laser-plasma physics, pushing the boundaries of plasma-based photon source development and unlocking new possibilities for fundamental research and applications. The LPPQE framework is versatile, encompassing a broad range of laser-plasma interactions and photon source operations, and is adaptable to various applications in medical treatment, science, and engineering. The study is a groundbreaking contribution to the fields of quantum physics, photonics, and plasma-based quantum phenomena, and holds the potential to revolutionize our understanding of these fields in the future. The LPPQE framework is available for download at https://sourceforge.net/p/lppqe/gimme/4558/998/ and can be run as a standalone program using the instructions at https://wiki.sourceforge.net/a/clusters/?LPPQE

The subgroups of Be-type stars, classified as B0V-B9V type, are identified through spectroscopic analysis within the 30 Doradadneb21mas catalog.  The catalog includes 7,514 sources with B-type spectra, of which 2,514 are classified as Be-type stars, spanning a broad magnitude range. These Be-type stars are found within a magnitude range of 18.0 to 21.0 with a greater concentration below this threshold.  A spatial distribution of Be-type stars, in contrast to B-type stars, is observed with a greater density in the central areas of the 30 Doradus system.  By using c2 of 2MASS-JHK bands and the distance moduli of 30 Doradus, the distances of Be-type stars can be compared to those of B-type stars.  A distinction is observed in the metal abundance between Be-type stars and B-type stars, with Be-type stars having lower metal content.  A broad range of rapid rotation is observed within Be-type stars, but not in B-type stars.  A hypothesis is proposed that Be-type stars within 30 Doradus are formed through two pathways.  Either they are formed from fragments with lower metal content, then rotate rapidly, or they are formed from fragments with higher metal content, then undergo significant spin-warping.  Both formation methods suggest that the 30 Doradus fragments are likely to be key factors in their formation.  Our research provides foundational knowledge for evaluating the 30 Doradus formation models.
