Many current advanced distributional approximations in machine learning are based on maximizing a variational lower bound that learns optimal parameters for a chosen distribution family, typically one that is exchangeable (symmetric) by nature. Nevertheless, exchangeable distributions sometimes fall short in capturing essential context information, leading researchers to rely on increasingly complex models that can accommodate more context. Our paper presents a practical technique to introduce context-dependent variations of popular exchangeable distribution families without compromising the model's identifiability or adding unneeded complexity. This approach involves a simple non-parametric transformation using a disentangling mechanism based on mutual information. As a result, we can create more effective variants of popular distribution families, such as the Gaussian and reverse identity flows, as well as the Fully Exchangable Variational Autoencoder (FEVA). Our empirical findings show that these improved models surpass their exchangeable counterparts across various benchmark tasks. Furthermore, the disentangling mechanism used here also enables a new, more robust method for detecting and removing noise from existing data sets, one that is independent of data labels and operates by filtering out redundant information. This method is directly related to properties of mutual information, is easy to implement, and is capable of handling large datasets under memory constraints. Working with categorical data for regression analysis can be complicated, especially when we're dealing with a large number of variables. To overcome these challenges, we've developed two new methods - Category Obfuscation and Categorical Forward - that use the group lasso framework to efficiently perform regression in categorical data. Our first approach involves converting categories into binary variables and then applying the group lasso for faster computation. This allows us to seamlessly integrate categorical features into the existing lasso regression model. The second method, Categorical Forward, pre-determines the optimal coefficients for categorical variables and then uses the lasso to refine his results, providing a more accurate coefficient estimation. Through simulations and case studies, we found that our proposed strategies often produce better outcomes than traditional techniques, such as Category Encoding and Forward Selection. This is particularly the case when dealing with a large amount of data in high-dimensional scenarios. Our research finds that the Categorical Forward method yields coefficients that are closest to the true values, while the Categorical Forward method has an impressive ability to identify the most important features with remarkable precision. Encourisingly, the false positive rate in this approach is found to be relatively low, indicating a higher signal-to-noise ratio. Ultimately, the performance of our models is revealed through application to a real-world disease risk prediction study, where our proposed strategies are shown to be highly effective. This is particularly the case when the number of variables exceeds the sample size, as the performance of our models is found to be nearly uniform across different scenarios. To facilitate replication and testing of our findings, the code used in this research has been openly published on the GitHub repository, accompanied by a data visualization supplement. In various industrial devices like medical equipment and aerospace tools, the failure of an operating system can have catastrophic consequences.  In such cases, embedded real-time systems often rely on specialized operating systems, implemented as part of the device's firmware.  However, managing multiple versions of these systems can be difficult, particularly when developing medical equipment that requires FDA certification, as developers must demonstrate the system's ability to meet real-time healthcare standards.  To address these challenges, we've introduced the T-Visor, a hypervisor designed to provide services for embedded real-time systems.  Implemented on the Xilinx Zynq UltraScale MPSoC, which combines CPU and FPGA capabilities, the T-Visor hypervisor enables us to partition resources and ensure reliable system functioning.  By testing its compatibility with the FREEDOM-RTOS, we've demonstrated the T-Visor's ability to meet real-time standards and streamline the development process of multi-platform embedded systems.  With its fully-integrated FPGA region, the T-Visor is able to allocate system resources and virtualize hardware components with high precision, in addition to providing services for interrupt management, virtualized clock management and I/O virtualization.  By dividing hardware resources into separate virtual sections, the T-Visor is able to efficiently manage performance, safety and development costs.  To evaluate its performance, we conducted a real-time testing experiment that compared the T-Visor's functioning with and without virtualization capabilities.  The results indicated a minimal delay in virtualization, with the T-Visor meeting all necessary real-time standards in our evaluation.  By integrating the T-Visor with its multi-level configuration and resource partitioning design, we've achieved a reliable, high-performance embodiment of an embedded real-time hypervisor, capable of meeting the stringent requirements of aerospace tools, medical equipment and other critical systems.  Our investigation into the T-Visor's properties revealed that through the T-Visor's separation of processes, fewer constraints are placed on the use of hardware components and system memory.  The T-Visor's ability to manage virtual clocks and interrupt requests ensures an additional, safe layer of system functioning, while its efficient I/O virtualization capability preserves system performance.  The integration of our T-Visor with its integrated FPGA interface achieves an optimal balance between software portability and FPGA design flexibility.  The T-Visor's programming of its interface, its FREEDOM-RTOS installation and testing, as well as its development and debugging tools are all freely available

A novel method for reconstructing the 3D structure of cities using images is presented, specifically for generating wide-angle panoramic views of a scene. The approach assumes that a biased gradient prior exists due to the influence of gravity, and this bias is mathematically defined for the first time in terms of image orientation on a sphere. To accommodate the bias, a modified panoramic joining problem is formulated as a nonconvex energy minimization problem. Various mathematical and computational solutions to this problem are proposed, and one solution is discretized and tested using synthetic and real-image data. The results show that the proposed approach effectively handles the bias and reconstructs high-quality 3D structures from wide-angle images. In comparison to previous methods, the proposed approach requires fewer images to achieve similar results, and it is more resistant to low-quality images. Additionally, the computational time for the discretized solution has been significantly reduced using a parallel computing approach. Overall, the performance of the proposed approach is evaluated, and it is demonstrated to be a useful tool for generating high-quality panoramic views of scenes from various sources, including RGB images. The source code of the computational solver is freely available online for the community to use. The approach described here has been published in a journal called IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI) in 2021 and has been used in other related research published in 2022. A 2nd place challenge prize was awarded to the researchers for participating in the 2021 KITTLIENS 3D Challenge competition. The source code is located at https://epsrc.mod.ac.uk/docs/evaluation.html and the challenge results are located at https://git.ws.oic.rs/epsrc/AIC21_KITTLIENS_3D_Challenge_2021/README.html. Additional information is located at https://research.naiad.ai/panoramic-joinings/ and at https://research.naiad.ai/panoramic-joinings/Challenge. The researchers have also used the solver to compute 3D structures for cities using aerial views from Google Street View: an article located at https://research.naiad.ai/panoramic-joinings/ is provided for further information on this project. The Google 3D structure compute city list is located at https://research.naiad.ai/panoramic-joinings/. The bias in the gradient prior is a widely influential factor that affects various computer vision problems, and this study has successfully demonstrated its impact on a particular task.

Despite achieving tremendous success in controlled laboratory settings, model-based reinforcement learning approaches struggle with real-world disruptions. This study develops a method to enhance model-based reinforcement learning for complex systems with potential flaws. By incorporating a probabilistic estimator for the policy's continuity, we establish a well-defined link between policy quality and the smoothness of its underlying model. This smoothness guarantee is then used in a model-based policy search algorithm, which accounts for the uncertainty associated with the system's parameters. Experimental validation on a robotic manipulation task demonstrates that our proposed algorithm offers robustness in the presence of external disturbances, outperforming existing model-based reinforcement learning techniques. Furthermore, the results show that our method is more energy-efficient compared to partially observable model-based reinforcement learning approaches. This research presents a framework for quantifying the link between a policy's quality and its smoothness, which can be leveraged to ensure the reliability of model-based reinforcement learning strategies. This framework may also be applied to other model-based reinforcement learning algorithms for improved robustness and scalability. What's more, the approach does not require modifications to the policy's architecture, making it suitable for practical utilization. This is presented in a series of empirical studies that demonstrate the efficacy of our method in a complex robotic context with numerous potential sources of instability. Notably, our method is tested against these uncertainties without any adjustments, which is a critical factor in ensuring its applicability to various applications. This study differs from previous model-based reinforcement learning research in several key ways. Initially, our method focuses on ensuring the regulator's smoothness in parameter space. This distinction is significant because ensuring Lipschitz continuity is typically more challenging than proving the regulator's smoothness in the input domain. Additionally, our approach is centered on a model-based policy search algorithm, which is distinct from direct model-based reinforcement learning algorithms. This study explores the theoretical underpinnings of our method, starting with a review of existing research that ensures the regulator's smoothness in parameter space. This is followed by a presentation of a probabilistic model-based policy search algorithm, which is validated through empirical studies in a complex robotic context with numerous potential sources of instability. Finally, our method is compared to other model-based reinforcement learning techniques that do not account for the uncertainty associated with the system's parameters. This comparison highlights the advantages of our approach, which is more energy-efficient and requires fewer parameters (three vs. twenty-five). The notion of stabilization in diagram categories is a key concept that can be utilized in various ways, and it's particularly significant in categories involving directed graphs. When working with multi-layer diagrams in a diagram category with an action, there are different methods for applying stabilization, which can lead to conflicting outcomes. Nonetheless, using the formalism of coloured operads, it's possible to find a common pattern where these different methods for stabilization converge. In the context of diagram categories with a symmetric structure, there are corresponding symmetric diagram categories, and stabilization plays a crucial role in identifying universal objects within these categories. Moreover, incorporating a functorial structure on these diagrams leads to the concept of slice algebras, and in the case of coloured operads, it's possible to extend this concept to higher dimensions. Lastly, incorporating coloured objects into operads results in the notion of algebra bundles, and further generalization yields the concept of cobordism groups, which can be seen as a particular case of slice algebras in the context of coloured operads. Operads involving coloured objects that are not coloured in colour 0 possess more flexibility and allow for more possibilities, and their concept is particularly significant in the context of classical cobordism, where it's possible to omit the case involving no colours. As such, the concept of algebra bundles serves as a significant interpretation and expansion of the concept of genus in classical cobordism. In addition, the concept of algebra bundles in the context of operads also encompasses a broad range of other concepts related to cobordism, such as Thom complexes, formal groups, and quantum groups. In other words, the concept of algebra bundles serves as a unifying framework for relating these concepts to operads, which can be seen as a particular case of slice algebras in the context of diagram categories. In order to demonstrate the utility of these concepts, we provide definitions and examples of cobordism in various algebraic contexts, such as quantum groups and formal groups, and show that the concept of stabilization in these contexts is naturally tied to the concept of a Hopf structure. Using the concept of stabilization in this context, it's possible to identify a fundamental object within this field, which is tied to the Drinfeld generator in quantum groups and the Loday word in formal groups. In addition to these findings, the text also serves as an introduction to the study of n-slice algebras in the context of coloured operads, which is a particularly significant area of research that is worth exploring in the future

We examine the reflexibility of quantum information in random tensor networks.
Research reveals that even in a random tensor network with a completely random configuration, there is a non-zero chance that two distant systems will share reflexibility.
To further illustrate this discovery, we used a specific random tensor network model that we introduced earlier and demonstrated that its reflexibility gap continuously declines as the distance between the systems grows.
This finding is particularly noteworthy since it holds without any upper limit on the network size or complexity.
Moreover, our research also shows that there is a threshold in randomness beyond which the reflexibility of isolated systems automatically implies reflexibility in the entire network.
This threshold is characterized by the average magnitude of random tensor elements being greater than the square root of the network size. 
These findings are validated by mathematical proofs and theoretical reasoning in the presented study. Moreover, an experimental demonstration of these concepts is proposed using quantum atomic ensemble technology. 
The results from this study contribute to our understanding of reflexibility in quantum information and its unique implications for quantum communication systems.

In various fields, including biology and complex systems, stochastic dynamics is a widely used method for modeling systems that incorporate randomness. This type of dynamics is often represented by nonlinear equations that include random variables such as Gaussian noise. Although numerous studies have employed stochastic dynamics, they often overlook a crucial aspect - the origin of heritable information - without addressing whether heritable information is inherently present in the system or if it's introduced externally. We examined this omission by investigating the ability of stochastic dynamics to generate and sustain information about future states, including heritable information. Using measures of mutual information, we performed comprehensive numerical analyses of stochastic dynamics with Gaussian noise, covering a range of parameters and different types of interactions. We discovered that, in general, systems with high self-interaction tend to produce self-corrrelation, while systems with low self-interaction tend to correlate with their past states. Additionally, we found that systems with weak interactions may generate limited yet lasting information, initially existing in earlier states. These results indicate that stocahstic dynamics with Gaussian noise can generate and sustain heritable information, providing insights into the creation of enduring patterns within systems. We observed similar results within a model simulating cellular signaling. Our research reveals the importance of noise in generating information, potentially resolving long-standing debates over the role of randomness in life's processes. We have made the raw data for our research available, including data for Figures 1-8, and the Python code for our calculations. Please see our Deposited Material for further details. The research expands upon previous work in one-dimensional systems and has broader implications for the measurement of tunneling durations in two-dimensional systems with spin-degenerate edge modes. Continual learning with an ensemble method can tackle issues of interference and obsolescence, but existing ensemble methods have limitations. Some require either prior knowledge of the tasks or a large number of parameters, making them less suitable for practical applications. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel method called Neural Structure for Online Ensemble Continual Learning (NOEC-L). This method consists of an online ensemble model with a neural structure that dynamically adjusts its layer and parameter configuration in response to each encountered task. The adaptive structure is achieved through the removal of unnecessary sub-networks, prevention of parameter sharing, and incremental updates of parameter distributions, all of which help to mitigate interference from previous tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that NOEC-L surpasses all other ensemble methods in a realistic setting, reflecting its success in achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets, including linear subclassing, reinforcement learning, and real-world scenarios. This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates regime-switching environments, characterized by individuals' willingness to take risks, in addition to standard financial factors. Using a linearly-decomposed approach and an adjusted Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, researchers derive an approximate Nash equilibrium. The approximation technique employs parameterization and the resulting equation is solved using a finite difference method, with convergence proven for both parameters and time. An extension of this approach is also presented for model misspecification scenarios. It is demonstrated that, when the regime-switching factor disappears, the approximation converges to the correct solution. Moreover, an extension of this approach is provided for two types of non-zero-sum games: mixed-moment and mean-variance games. It is hoped that this technique can be employed in practice by insurance companies to obtain actionable insights in such complex systems. An accompanying computational tool has also been developed for use by practitioners. The researchers test the technique on various examples, offering practical insights into how investment and reinsurance interactions are affected by various factors. Notably, results show that reinsurance interactions are influenced not only by reinsurance parameters, but also by the convex risk-sharing parameter and the regime-switching parameter. An accompanying computational tool has also been developed for use by practitioners. The researchers test the technique on various examples, showing that reinsurance interactions are influenced by parameters such as reinsurance premium, the probability of claims for the insured and the insurer, and the coefficient representing individuals' willingness to take risks. An examination is also conducted into the technique's sensitivity. The researchers' numerical findings highlight the significance of considering regime-switching models in non-zero-sum games, particularly when there is a significant difference between the willingness of the insured and the insurer to take risks. Moreover, the impact of the two types of reinsurance models used in these examples on the approximation also reveal some sensitivity, with the mixed-moment model appearing to be more robust than the mean-variance model. These numerical findings offer valuable and systemizable insights into how investment and reinsurance interactions are affected by various factors, which can be of practical use to insurance companies. This research introduces a Precise Integrated Dual Adaptive (PIDA) controller, representing a significant improvement in Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controllers. The primary objectives of PIDA are to maintain stability and smoothness in the flight trajectory. To achieve this, PIDA employs a modified Lagrangian function and a novel genetic algorithm, known as the Genetic Filter (GF), to enhance the performance of the Pyquila flight simulator. The Pyquila simulator models the nonlinear dynamics of a quadcopter. The essential nature of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions is examined in depth.  It is demonstrated that the electromagnetic properties of nucleons and the properties of low-energy pion-nucleon scattering are in close relation.  A detailed microscopic analysis is applied to confirm these connections.  The significance of a pion-nucleon sigma term in relation to chiral symmetry is also explored and findings from a 2005 study relevant to hadron physics at very low temperatures and zero impact, as well as around the QCD phase transition point, are reinforced.  The sigma term associated with the strange quark is shown to be relatively small in comparison to the energy generated by pions.  The nature of the mass split between the $N$ and $\Delta$ resonances, which occurs at relatively low energy, is also examined and previous work indicating a significance role of $K$-mode coupling is reaffirmed.  A detailed examination of the energy range $0-360$ MeV, incorporating the effects of regularization in missing energy, draws upon observations of $\pi N$ cross sections measured in experiments conducted over a 50-year period. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS detector, the silicon pixel detector forms the forefront layer in the tracking system, responsible for identifying the starting point of particles' tracking paths. Although initially functioning across the entire collision point, the silicon pixel detector's functionality was restricted to a single nucleus during the LHC's first phase due to limited readout capabilities. Subsequently, a subset of pilot blades with full readout functionality enabled researchers to assess the detector's performance during this phase. Using pilot blade data from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions in 2015-2016, this study analyzes the reconstruction of pilot blade hit lists, including their efficiency, point resolution, and track hit patification efficiencies. Utilizing Gaussian envelope simulations, the effects of pixel occupancy and charge are also modeled and incorporated into the analysis. Notably, the analysis reveals that the bulk of reconstructed track points exhibit an accuracy of less than 1.5 micrometers, with approximately 80% of reconstructed track points demonstrating an accuracy of less than 1 micrometer. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that the majority of reconstructed track points beyond the collision point (forward track points) exhibit an accuracy of less than 1.5 micrometers. Also, the analysis reveals that the majority of reconstructed hit list match rates between the forward and backward hit lists provide a match rate of greater than 99%. These findings from the LHC's first phase provide essential validation of the CMS pixel detector's functionality and serve as an important indicator of the detector's expected performance during the LHC's second phase. The validation also provides essential knowledge for assessing the detector's functionality during future phases. The analysis will be shared at the LHC's Week 2017 workshop. By examining the function maps of various models, such as the single-hidden-layer Gaussian network, the single-hidden-layer sigmoid network, and the two-hidden-layer sigmoid network, both with real and complex inputs/outputs, it has been possible to demonstrate the equivalence of function maps across different model architectures. This has far-reaching implications, demonstrating the ability of weight sharing models to achieve better performance, potentially leading to more compact models with improved interpretability. Furthermore, our research reveals that using complex-valued outputs can lead to higher representational capacity compared to using real-valued outputs, which could have significant implications for applications. The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to revolutionize the detection of low-energy nuclear recoils.  It is characterized by an exceptionally high sensitivity to recoil energies, low energy thresholds, minimal readout noise, and sensitivity to nuclear recoil direction. The principle behind PALEOCCENE involves exploiting the interaction between a laser and the 771 nm absorption band of Yb+ centers in Yb2SiO5 when excited by 879 nm light. This results in an stimulated emission signal clearly distinguishable from uncorrelated dark counts. Notably, PALEOCENEs are directionally sensitive due to the requirement for conserved momentum, resulting in enhanced sensitivity to nuclear recoils. Theoretical projections indicate that PALEOCENEs should be capable of identifying single-crystal Yb2SiO5 devices with as little as 100 keV/c recoil energy and are robust against a wide range of backgrounds.  It is also anticipated that PALEOCENEs can be directional to at least several keV recoil energies with further optimization. Future research will investigate reading out the time and rate of PALEOCENE events to fully exploit directional sensitivity. Ultimately, PALEOCENE has the potential to be an extremely sensitive detector of nuclear recoils, making it an excellent candidate for neutrinoless double-beta decay and dark matter research.  It may also be applicable to studies of cosmic rays and low-energy astrophysical phenomena. The characteristic tree of a graph can be used to express its distance-based metrics. For planar graphs and minor-free graphs, a more compact representation of their distance-based metrics can be achieved by constructing a smaller tree, called a k-branching tree. A recent study showed that a planar graph's characteristic tree can be approximated within a constant factor for any k greater than or equal to 3. In this research, a planar graph's distance-based metric can be approximated within a constant factor using a k-branching tree for any k. Also, minor-free graphs' distance-based metrics can be exactly represented by a tree with the number of leaves equal to the number of nodes in the original graph. A novel variational autoencoder modification, termed the 'deep generative encoder', employs an innovative approach to represent complex data, characterized by its self-referential structure that enables backpropagation, unlike traditional fully connected generative models. When enhanced with Bethe approximation, the deep generative encoder exhibits three significant improvements over standard generative models: it boldly infers its own parameters, firmly stands by its representations and steadfastly resists overfitting. Experimental outcomes have validated the deep generative encoder's superiority across a range of datasets. Moreover, we have successfully integrated its underlying technique, termed 'inverse message passing', into various standard generative models, thereby enhancing their functional correspondence to standard generative models and yielding enhanced performance. Our work is made freely available on github with the intention of contributing it to the machine learning community. Furthermore, our accompanying video provides a visual illustration of the deep generative encoder's representations that begin unintelligible but gradually become increasingly meaningful with continued training. Lastly, through the creation of a game that harnesses the deep generative encoder's representations, we have successfully obtained human validation of its elevated understanding of its inputs over the course of only 1000 iterations of training. In particular, we found that the deep generative encoder's self-learning mechanism exhibits a notable 'cognitive surge' around 800-1000 iterations where there is substantial improvement in human readability and coherence of its representations. Following further training, the deep generative encoder's representations continued to demonstrate remarkable precision and continued to exhibit a high degree of semantic coherence. Importantly, the deep generative encoder's elevated understanding of its inputs was found to be highly stable, exhibiting very little variation across various different initial conditions for training. In summary, our innovative approach to representation learning through the deep generative encoder provides a robust computational mechanism for gaining insight into the structures that underlie complex data, and the technique as a whole represents a significant breakthrough in the field of machine learning. The game page provides a nightly update that reflects the current state of the deep generative encoder's representations, and visitors may find that the representations are more or less coherent than what is reported here.

Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile molecules. We utilized the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of the ALMA telescope to examine the molecular emissions of CO, CS, C2H5CN, and H2CO in the 41-minute lightcurve of the comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) on March 4-5, 2016. The data indicated the presence of three distinct molecular emissions: a centered ring structure for CO and C2H5CN emissions and a shell-like appearance for CS emissions. A combination of a molecular emission region and a continuous disk of H2CO was observed. By analyzing the spectral lines, a gas concentration of approximately 3.0 x 10^18 cm^-3 was estimated for CS and 2.0 x 10^18 cm^-3 for H2CO. The lightcurve revealed distinct light patterns for CO and CS emissions, with CO peaking at the north-east and CS at the south-west. A south-western region of the comet's brightness center was also detected for H2CO. By correlating the data with a 3D ray-traced model, a variety of scenarios were generated to explain the emissions' patterns. The presence of a dispersed source of CS was proposed, suggesting that the emissions observed were not from a single homogeneous layer but rather from a more intricate structure. A comparison with other cometary data revealed CS emissions from C/2015 ER61 were significantly lower than those in other comets like 51P/Hutao and 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. The data further indicated CO emissions from C/2015 ER61 were less intense than those in C/2013 A1 (Sostero). The study represents an essential step in understanding the origin and evolution of small comets and provides valuable insights into their volatile loss mechanisms. The survey provides a necessary foundation for future studies of this class of comets and aids in planning future observations of emerging comets. The data presented serve as a crucial starting point for future ALMA observations, encouraging ongoing investigations into the science of cometary emissions. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a pre-trained or manually crafted voice model. The method is straightforward to implement, requiring the same computational resources as its supervised counterparts. However, it yields comparable, if not superior performance, across the entire speech spectrum, according to both subjective ratings and objective measures. Specifically, our synthesized speech is reported to demonstrate up to 0.3 mean opinion scores (mos) greater consistency with human speech, as well as a 6 dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio (snr) matching. A comprehensive evaluation is presented on the Librispeech corpus, a comprehensive dataset spanning 20 hours of speech from public domain audiobooks. Similarly, our technique proves effective on a 100-hour subset of the corpus and on a 56-hour dataset of conversations. Moreover, our technique is shown to be adaptable to various voices and use cases with minimal retraining. Specifically, our technique is effectively applied to voices not previously heard during training and is used to create speech for a range of spoken languages using a single English-based voice model. Lastly, our technique is used to automatically generate speech for individuals with speech disorders such as dysphonia via a simple voice conversion process. All of the research is conducted using open-source software and data and is made publicly available. Furthermore, our technique is used to generate a comprehensive speech dataset, a high-quality audio archive spanning 275 hours, a $US. 12. 10 million investment, a 12-fold return on investment from the initial data gathering costs, a debt-to-revenue ratio of 0. 86 and a 0. 93 ratio of revenue to operating expense. To account for the limitations of practical devices, we establish a general framework for the signal-to-noise ratio, and then develop an optimization method to design the phase shift matrix of the RIS under two different secure criteria. The proposed solutions involve an approximation technique that enables efficient implementation, and we demonstrate their effectiveness via numerical experiments. Compared to a baseline approach that dismisses the negative effects of hardware defects, our method can achieve improved signal-to-noise ratio values and satisfy the RIS's phase shift constraint. Notably, the performance enhancements are more pronounced in scenarios with intense signal distortion. Overall, this research highlights the importance of considering the limitations of practical devices in the context of secure communication design. Additionally, the proposed method offers a promising solution for optimizing RIS performance in various communication systems. Finally, our work via Fig. 7 has shown that the RIS can be leveraged to counter an aggressive eavesdropping attack by reducing the signal received by the eavesdropper or increasing the noise impact on the eavesdropped link. This creative application of RIS is reminiscent of classic countermeasures used in communication systems. We introduce a type of noncommutative countable principal bundle with a twisted structure, derived from a free action of a countable group on a unital C*-algebra, extending traditional definitions to the noncommutative context. Building on this concept, we examine the geometric significance of noncommutative principal bundles with this twisted structure, and demonstrate their equivalence to foliations without leaf schemas, thus falling under the category of irrational subalgebras. Moreover, we establish the existence of a universal bundle associated with each action, encompassing several pre-existing noncommutative bundles as special instances. This framework allows us to construct a range of examples, including noncommutative bundles corresponding to actions on full Fock spaces and symmetric Fock spaces. The resulting topological properties of these examples are investigated. Specifically, we demonstrate that some noncommutative fiber bundles feature locally regular elements while the universal bundles do not. Additionally, we show that some families of isometrically faithful actions generate regular elements, and in particular, faithful actions on compact Gelfand-Neumark spaces do not result in regular elements. Lastly, we address the challenge of verifying interiority in noncommutative geometric settings. To achieve this, we introduce a definition of interiority for subsets of C*-algebras via local operations and prove its equivalence to several distinct, more algebraic representations of interiority. Furthermore, we show that for certain subsets, specifically those containing the unit, the interiority definition aligns with the standard topological notion. To exemplify the utility of this definition, we show that for actions of certain groups, such as those inducing Krulltopos on the corresponding functor categories, the set of strictly outer elements forms a dense subset. By applying the AST approach, a black hole in a disc-like environment would appear as a ring of negative mass, which could be positioned at the equatorial plane of the black hole's shadow. According to the AST, the gravitational field of a source is repelled by a surrounding disc-like structure and influenced by the number of discs present. For a single disc-like structure, the gravitational field experiences repulsion when facing the disc and attraction in the perpendicular direction. For two co-rotating discs, the gravitational field exhibits a repulsive relationship, which reduces with increasing age of the discs. For a black hole surrounded by two co-rotating discs, the secondary peak in the radial temperature distribution potentially acts as a thermal barrier, which could explain the origin of bipolar outflows and the disc-like structure of the X-shaped wings observed in the polar image of the black hole in M87. Moreover, the presence of two co-rotating discs around a black hole results in a repulsive gravitational interaction between the two discs, which may lead to a decrease in their ages, which could explain the young appearance of the disc-like structure of the X-shaped wings observed in the polar image of the black hole in M87. Lastly, the theory suggests that the two discs-like structure of the quasar 3C 75 has a north-south symmetry, which is in the direction of the black hole's rotation axis. The rapidly expanding science of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) has garnered significant interest over the past decade. Despite initial mysteries surrounding their optical counterparts, recent discoveries of associated galaxies and tight constraints on FRB emission wavelengths have paved the way for in-depth investigations. To further explore this area of research, our study provides a comprehensive analysis of 13 FRBs, leveraging 10 telescopes across radio, optical, infrared, and X-ray spectrums to detect their emission beyond radio frequencies. By cross-referencing X-ray data and establishing a lower bound on optical flux within 2 months of their radio bursts, our findings reveal that 11 of the 13 studied FRBs exhibit faint emission rates, with two possible scenarios emerging: (1) deep extinction may obscure optical emission from host galaxies; (2) a significant fraction of FRBs might experience prolonged emission periods, necessitating the monitoring of these events repeatedly over extended periods. These findings underscore the importance of multi-wavelength observations and potential near-far IR emission from cloud-covered galaxies. Moreover, our study indicates that an optical telescopic follow-up of candidate FRBs should be conducted promptly, within an hour of their initial detection, to increase the likelihood of a successful observation. The optical flux upper limits we derived correspond to luminosity densities of 10^4 - 10^7 GHz, with two FRBs exhibiting notably higher values (10^6 - 10^7 GHz), suggesting the possibility of inverse Compton scattering by electrons probing the interstellar medium at kiloparsec scales. Notably, our study also set constraints on repeating FRB activity linked to 2020 November 20A, 2021 March 19, and 2021 August 24 FRBs, with repeat times of at least 188, 52, and 204 days, respectively, consistent with circular delay paths. By examining the interplay between radio and optical emission from these events, our study indicates that such phenomena could offer valuable insights into magnetic field complexity in the interstellar and intergalactic media. Ultimately, our research highlights the potential for in-depth optical and optical-infrared observations of FRBs to reveal new physical properties and mechanisms governing these enigmatic events. For instance, the significant optical emission from FRB 20121124A may be attributed to an abundant far-IR-emitting gas, potentially present within 0.01 parsecs of its host galaxy, indicative of a highly dense star-forming region. Language generation models have gained popularity, but they currently lack a way to see what they're typing. To address this, we've come up with a straightforward way to let language models "look" at images while generating text. This is made possible by integrating an image decoding tool directly into the model, allowing for text generation that's guided by images. By testing different methods of integrating this tool, we found that using features from specific parts of images is more effective than other approaches. This is the first time an image decoding tool has been used to guide the entire text generation process, and our experiments show that it's possible for models to "look" at images while generating text. The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we also practically apply to the Zec blockchain for successful deployment on the Zec blockchain under the name 'ZecRing'.
Our security evidence, developed in a generic setting, assumes an organized group of attackers attempting to breach the anonymity of transactions and RingCT users, which we addressed by creating a new type of linkable ring signature that retains the same size as standard RingCT but offers twice the level of security protection as previous variants.
The Delegated RingCT scheme achieves a notable reduction in computational complexity for non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs when compared to conventional RingCT, with computations taking less time and requiring fewer CPU cycles on the network.
A comparative analysis between Delegated RingCT and Conventional RingCT is presented based on performance metrics such as computational complexity, network efficiency, and overall performance, which highlights Delegated RingCT's advantages over Conventional RingCT across these dimensions.
In a study examining Delegated RingCT's practical performance, we carried out various experiments which showed that Delegated RingCT outperforms Conventional RingCT by means of all performance metrics considered.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique for training deep neural networks with quantized weights. Named AskewSGD, this method iteratively refines the optimal search space for each parameter until convergence. As a result, AskewSGD achieves significant reductions in computation, memory, and power consumption, while still performing comparably to stochastic gradient descent on large models and outperforming it on smaller models. AskewSGD's efficiency stems from its straightforward implementation, low overhead, and ability to leverage existing SGD-based training procedures, making it easily adaptable to various neural network architectures and training protocols. Furthermore, AskewSGD's optimization properties enable us to provide theoretical guarantees for its performance, including a guaranteed upper bound on its suboptimality relative to the best possible quantized solution. In addition, we showcase AskewSGD's performance by applying it to convolutional neural networks for image classification and regression tasks and evaluating it on small, state-of-the-art models for image recognition and language processing. AskewSGD's results demonstrate a substantial improvement in power efficiency, with some models experiencing up to 10 times faster training times while occupying 2 to 20 times less memory than state-of-the-art quantized training methods. AskewSGD's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sterian/AskewSGD. In experimental settings, we also compared the performance of AskewSGD against two recently proposed optimization techniques for quantized neural networks: PACT-SGD and SQTahoe, as well as a recently proposed method for binary neural networks: BinarySGD. Our results reveal that AskewSGD's performance outshines these approaches, with AskewSGD's performance comparable to PACT-SGD, AskewSGD's performance comparable to binary SGD, and AskewSGD's memory efficiency surpassing SQTahoe. Ultimately, AskewSGD emerges as a robust optimization technique for applied neural network quantization, with extensive empirical results validating its efficiency, performance, and trustworthiness on a wide variety of models and training protocols. The results suggest that AskewSGD presents itself as the most up-to-date optimization technique available today. A comparative analysis of AskewSGD's performance against PACT-SGD, SQTahoe, and BinarySGD is also presented in this work. Understanding natural language relies heavily on knowledge about the world's facts, 
and language models have made significant advancements in generating text given a 
set of facts, but they still struggle to verify whether a given text aligns with 
those facts. To address this challenge, we introduce a new framework for verifying 
textual coherence with pre-existing information. Since existing large language models 
are not designed to evaluate statements for accuracy, we created a new dataset and 
a novel disassembly method for structuring sentences and facilitating fact-based 
verification. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through a newly 
developed fact verification task. When applied to a range of models, including 
pre-trained transformer models and language models specifically trained to support 
multistep reasoning, our results show that incorporating our disassembly method 
improves their performance by an average of 4% relative to working solely with 
unstructured text. To support further learning and assessment, we also provide an 
interactive tool for visually breaking down and reassembling sentence structures. 
This research aims to bridge the gap between text generation and text validation, and 
we make our model implementation and interactive tool available to the public at 
https://github.com/allenai/disassembly4verification. We also release our new FactVerif 
dataset for supporting further development of text validation capabilities in 
language models. The FactVerif dataset can be found at: https://allenai.github.io/disassembly4verification. 
Ultimately, our goal is to train highly capable language models that not only 
create coherent text but also confirm its accuracy based on underlying facts. 
Verifying text accuracy is vital, and our disassembly framework aims to facilitate 
textual analysis and comprehension by breaking down sentences into structured, 
logically connected components. To this end, we are releasing the structured 
disassembly of all sentences in the English Wikipedia and publishing an API for 
accessing these structured sentences. This API, along with our disassembly tool, is 
available at: https://disassemblytool.herokuapp.com. 
Our accompanying video illustrates how the disassembly of a sentence is 
constructed and the benefits of using this method for enhancing model performance in 
a text validation task. The video can be found at: https://youtu.be/8_auRk3GZ7Y. 
By using the disassembly tool to break down sentences, we can determine which parts 
of the text contribute most significantly to the verification of underlying facts.

To create a reliable generative model using high-quality hidden representations from a neural network, we suggest an alternative to existing generative adversarial networks. Our proposed framework, Hidden Space Conditioning Networks (HSCNs), wraps the generator in a hidden layer and connects it only to the input layer, maintaining the original discriminator design. This setup allows for better integration of the discriminator and generator, especially when dealing with memory-based discriminators. Unlike other conditional GANs that scatter conditional information throughout the network, HSCNs concentrate conditional information in the input layer, making training more efficient. By doing so, HSCNs can be seen as an efficient way to pretrain a conditional GAN. Our experiments successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of HSCNs in enhancing both visual and semantic generation quality in 2D images. Additionally, HSCNs provide significant improvements to Semantic Image Synthesis, an intricate generation task, outperforming other established semantic conditioning methods. A widely applied method for the evaluation of posterior distributions, named nested sampling, continuously generates samples from the posterior distribution, prioritizing regions with the highest likelihood. The success of nested sampling significantly depends on a step selector that chooses the next sample, determining the efficiency and accuracy of the method. Different step selectors have varying strategies and can be categorized into likelihood-based, distance-based, density-based, and polyhedral-based approaches. In this paper, several step selectors are compared, including PolyNorm, PolyBall, PolyHypersphere, PolyPyramid, PolyDomain, PolyDomain2, and PolyDomain3, in addition to Demeter and Sorter. The performance of these step selectors is evaluated under controlled and realistic conditions, also accounting for their complexity via a new metric called the selection efficiency. Given its superior performance, Demeter couple with Sorter, named DemeterS, is made freely available for general use. The source code is accessible at the provided repository address. In distance labeling, each vertex is assigned a set of labels that allows any two vertices' distances to be calculated in constant time, regardless of their direct connection status. Our research builds on previous works and presents an algorithm to construct a fault-tolerant distance labeling system for planar graphs, where the label size remains constant at O(log^2 log log n) with a set of faulty vertices allowed. This algorithm can handle up to a specific percentage of vertex failures (approximately 3.5% for a general case and 4% for an optimal scenario) and provides an accurate distance calculation between any two vertices. Additionally, we propose a more efficient algorithm with a reduced label size of O(log^2 log n) and an increased tolerance to vertex failures (up to half of all vertices in a set of n vertices). This more efficient algorithm can be used in applications where low overhead and fast processing are crucial, such as in systems with limited hardware resources and data streaming scenarios. Our research also highlights the importance of the set of faulty vertices' geometry in relation to the vertex failures, with the optimal scenario involving vertices that form a specific, non-standard polygon in the plane. This unique shape, a 4-gon with certain vertices excluded, has interesting topological properties and influences the constant-sized label production. Our research also explores similar concepts in related problems. Depending on the specific application, our research provides different solutions that offer various trade-offs between efficiency, constant label size, and fault tolerance. This adaptability makes our research valuable for different applications. Our proposed algorithm for the fault-free distance labeling system has been implemented and applied to applications in geometry and information systems, demonstrating its efficiency and constant label size in these scenarios. In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to both external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. We calculate a temporal two-particle correlation function and observe oscillations that indicate a non-equilibrium phase transition. Utilizing a numerically efficient method of eliminating the microscopic details, we derive a compact expression for the frequency-domain two-particle correlation function, comprising contributions from both a semi-classical model and a damped Raman pulse scenario. As dissipation decreases, our findings align with experimental protocols employing time-of-flight imaging. Ultimately, we suggest a research strategy to investigate quantum phase transitions via fast-frequency modulation. The proposed experimental approach aims to capture a comprehensive view of the system by combining time-domain and frequency-domain findings. Automated out-of-distribution (OOD) detection has become a crucial capability 
for deployed machine learning models, given the potential for catastrophic 
consequences when applying them in real-world environments without such a 
capability. Various methods have been proposed in the literature. This work 
explores the utilization of distributional Gaussian processes (DGPs) for OOD 
detection, starting from a comprehensive analysis of available benchmarks 
suited for model comparison. Unlike existing benchmarks, we develop a more 
realistic evaluation metric that operates on a continuum between 
in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) data points. This is 
accompanied by a novel benchmark that features an extensive ID-OOD 
continuum, allowing for nuanced comparison of methods. Experimental results 
reveal that DGP-based techniques excelled in OOD detection, surpassing other 
state-of-the-art approaches. Further investigation into the reasoning 
underlying this excellence led us to conclude that DGPs offer benefits stemming 
from two key aspects: (1) the leveraging of predictive uncertainty 
estimates, (2) the capturing of divergent data representations. Consequently, 
DGPs prove adaptable and efficient in a wide range of OOD settings. Furthermore, 
we propose that learning id-ood continuum-based representations is an essential 
component for any model. Ultimately, we hope this work promotes the 
development of more comprehensive, continuous-scale OOD detection 
benchmarks.  You can download the code and data from  https://github.com/asharakeh/dgps-ood.  This research  has been  accepted at  ICLR 2021.

Counting the recurrence of cycling optical clocks is a fundamental operation used to measure time intervals. Yet, many clock systems operate outside of periodic cycling, requiring alternative strategies for time measurement. A statistical approach to analyzing optical clocks that don't follow a regular timing (non-oscillating) is presented here. The method involves rewriting clock signals so their patterns over time can be described using traditional statistical tools. This technique is demonstrated by studying a model of two interacting atoms that exchange a single photon with a light source (e.g. a laser), which often stops its regular timing cycle. By using this approach, the researchers were able to show how the distribution of time intervals between timing events changes in response to interactions with the surrounding environment (noise). Furthermore, the method allows for a single measurement to determine two distinct time scales: the average duration of timing events ($\tau_{\rm av}$) and the duration of individual events ($\tau$). The first scale represents a decoy time that is influenced by the entire system, while the second scale represents the inherent time it takes for the clock to change states and is influenced solely by the system itself and not by its surroundings. By studying how these two possible time scales differ, the researchers found that their findings are consistent with theoretical models of critical phenomena. This paper addresses the challenge of ensuring that services are delivered on time, particularly by managing network resources to prevent overutilization and minimize energy consumption in fog-supported Software-Defined Networks. Real-time applications require high network bandwidth and low latency, making them more susceptible to traffic jams and temporary disruptions. If service demands aren't properly managed, they could lead to network overutilization and increased energy consumption. To resolve this issue, a decision-making method is proposed for implementing Service Function Chains in real-time. This method includes algorithms for fault prevention, energy efficiency, and failure recovery, all of which are geared towards optimizing network resources and reducing energy consumption. The method is evaluated using various network scenarios, with results showing that it effectively prevents overutilization of network resources, saves energy, and provides high-quality services. Notably, the method achieves a 56% reduction in power consumption compared to a non-prevention approach. Furthermore, the results show that failure recovery only occurs in approximately 7% of cases, demonstrating its effectiveness in preventing failures. Overall, the service delivery process is significantly enhanced, with quality metrics like success rate and power consumption significantly improved. To validate the service delivery process, a series of experiments were conducted, which confirmed that high levels of success rate and power consumption reduction can be achieved. This, in turn, enables real-time service delivery with increased efficiency and reduced energy consumption. Moreover, the method boasts enhanced scalability due to its use of a scheduling database. Following a network switch, the method automatically adjusts its parameters at the fog node and scheduling database levels, allowing it to effectively manage changes in service demands at both nodes. In terms of computational complexity, the method performs optimally, with an average time complexity of O(n) and a ratio of execution time to real time of approximately 10^-9. Last but not least, the service delivery process effectively balances energy savings with success rate, demonstrating its capacity to optimize energy-efficient service delivery with high quality. In particular, when success rate and power consumption are both taken into consideration, the method achieves a weighted ratio of these metrics to energy savings of approximately 4.69. Conversely, the method achieves a ratio of these metrics to failure rate of approximately 3.57. Ultimately, the service delivery process effectively manages network resources while saving energy, making it a suitable solution for real-time Service Function Chain implementation. The method was demonstrated on the PSAT model with an experimental network of 312 nodes in continental Europe. The study ultimately suggests that the proposed strategy for CVR scheduling is efficient, reliable, and can be easily scaled up. Moreover, the method offers a level of flexibility as it relies only on the network admittance matrix, making it applicable to various distribution systems and network configurations. We investigate non-stochastic multi-armed bandits in the presence of an advisor that provides recommendations on unfolding sequences. While advisors can offer valuable insights when they know the reward functions of the bandit arms, they are often unreliable in real-world scenarios where this knowledge is not available. In our research, we address the practical issue of an advisor that, unlike classical settings, receives arm indices instead of reward functions and is subject to delays that can impact the advisor's recommendations. These arm-dependent delays result in non-iid recommendations even if the advisor has complete information about the reward functions. We address this challenging setting by designing a new algorithm called DELAY-AWAKE that efficiently takes into account the effect of these delays. Under the assumption that each arm has a unique reward function and a bound is given for the longest delay, DELAY-AWAKE is proven to achieve a cumulative reward of at least $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1)$, where $K$ is the number of bandit arms, showing an improvement of at least three orders of magnitude compared to the best previous results for bandits with dependent delays. Furthermore, we extend our findings to the scenario of multiple bandit arms with soft penalties and show that DELAY-AWAKE is nearly optimal in such a scenario, resulting in a significant improvement over previous research in this area. All our results are supported by rigorous analytical methods that result in the first analytically proven lower bound for bandits with dependent delays in the literature. In order to evaluate the effectiveness of DELAY-AWAKE, we carry out numerical simulations that result in a gain of at least two orders of magnitude compared to the best previous results for bandits with dependent delays. These experiments also result in a practical advisor that performs well in real-time scenarios with delayed recommendations. All our results are presented in two related papers, the first focusing on the analysis of DELAY-AWAKE in settings with dependent delays and the second presenting simulations of these results. In addition, we also obtained numerical simulations of classical bandit algorithms in a previous paper. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of elements in the normal closure $G^\varphi$. In this text, we demonstrate that a particular class of groups meeting this criterion includes, but is not limited to, the generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar group $A_{m,n}$ and the groups $GBS_{2,n}$. Furthermore, we investigate and explore the property $R_\infty$ in the direct product of these groups and in the nilpotent quotients of $A_{m,n}$ and $GBS_{2,n}$. It is shown that $A_{m,n}$ and $GBS_{2,n}$ themselves do not possess the $R_\infty$ property, but all nilpotent quotients of these groups and the direct product of $A_{m,n}$ and $GBS_{2,n}$ with an infinite number of copies of the infinite cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}$ meet this criterion. In addition to this, it is proven that $GBS_{2,n}$ and the direct product of $A_{m,n}$ and infinite cyclic groups meet this criterion universally. Lastly, the text examines an unsolved problem concerning property $R_\infty$ in groups and proposes a conjecture that aims to comprehensively answer this question. Several additional consequences of this conjecture are provided. The proposed conjecture would imply a complete and definitive answer to the question, indicating the result would be either that every group exhibiting property $R_\infty$ is comprised of or includes only stably finite groups, or that every group exhibiting property $R_\infty$ is comprised of or includes only groups that are operable. It is also shown that every group exhibiting property $R_\infty$ is comprised of or includes only groups that satisfy the Conjugacy Separation Property. As an additional finding, it is demonstrated that every group exhibiting property $R_\infty$ is comprised of or includes only groups that meet the conjugacy separability condition. Behavioral data in driving simulates real scenarios, yet there isn't an abundance of datasets that accurately replicate genuine driving conditions. Naturalistic driving studies have their limitations, as they often lack contextual information essential for behavioral analysis. To bridge this gap, we present the SceNDD: a dataset comprising multiple-camera recordings of participants driving in various situations. Our study showcases the importance of data representation in naturalistic driving studies. The acquired dataset contains over 38 kilometers of driving footage, along with corresponding labels for several critical events. The data is formatted to facilitate the application of attention-based neural networks, enhancing comparisons with simulation studies utilizing similar data representation techniques. Our analysis highlights the efficacy of this representation method and the potential for using the SceNDD to predict driving incidents. With its contextual information and robust nature, the SceNDD serves as a useful resource for researchers studying the psychology of driving and traffic dynamics. Our code and dataset are available for download on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/dendatasets/SceNDD. Moreover, an interactive web platform at https://sckennd.prismatic.net enables users to explore the data within a graphical interface. Our dataset and associated analysis address the limitations of existing naturalistic and simulated datasets, offering a novel and comprehensive understanding of driving behaviors. Ultimately, the SceNDD has the capacity to supplement existing datasets such as NATREC, NCDOT, and SHRP2. The compatibility of the SceNDD with multiple studies and potential extensions with additional sensor data make it an indispensable resource for the research community. Specifically, the SceNDD can address the limitations of datasets like HOTR, which lacks information on driving situations. Similarly, the SceNDD is more comprehensive than the DDC, as it includes data on multiple events. With its wide-range of situations and scenes, the SceNDD is an invaluable resource for training the tendo-layer of attention-based neural networks. Our study presents an optimized version of this layer, which outperforms state-of-the-art attention networks in the presence of driving data. Notably, the SceNDD is the first dataset to report on situations where the driver encounters an animal during their commute. Our study highlights the difficulty in predicting these events, which highlights the need for a more extensive understanding of potential situations where the data is collected. Finally, the SceNDD is an essential resource for the research community, offering a wealth of information for training attentional layers, which is particularly beneficial for applications in naturalistic driving

This paper introduces an improved variant of the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) algorithm for use in Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) transmission. The proposed model addresses two primary issues: reduced Cyclic Prefix (CP) length and hardware imperfections in amplitude and phase (HAPI). By taking HAPI into consideration, the power of the periodic catabolic vector's output and HAPI-powered interference are formulated as linear functions. A regularized least squares (RLS) algorithm is then applied to map the outputs of the RIS element input matrix onto its corresponding inverse. Subsequently, the modified ELM algorithm incorporates the projected outputs of RLS into its standard framework. Through both simulation and analysis, the novel RIS-ELM is demonstrated to outperform its pre-curated counterparts in terms of bit error rate (BER), particularly under conditions of both underutilized CP length and HAPI. Furthermore, the findings show that reduced CP length and HAPI have a synergistic effect on system performance. Notably, the loss in RIS-ELM performance relative to its optimal outcome can be mitigated through the deployment of an additional CP, despite the consequent decrease in spectral efficiency. Similarly, the introduction of a CP is found to be ineffective in counteracting the adverse impact of HAPI. Ultimately, the investigation suggests that the incorporation of both RIS technology and a refined machine learning method such as the one presented in this work is well-suited for the attainment of optimal performance in scenarios characterized by both underutilized CP length and HAPI. The Integral Variation Theorem is highly influential in the field of quantum information theory, defining a method to achieve optimal quantum discrimination between two channels without needing to analyze their individual properties. However, in this research, we demonstrate that a variation method exists that allows for optimal discrimination between quantum channels via a single measurement, independent of channel specifics. Furthermore, we illustrate that this method is achievable through non-projective measurements. Consequently, in this context, we refer to it as a multi-shot non-projective discrimination (MSNPD) method. Our research offers not only a new approach, but also a singular-measurement mechanism for optimal NPDPD methods, which has been lacking in the field. While various optimal multi-shot projective discrimination methods exist, our new method presents a way around channel-specific optimization for NPDPD. As an additional finding, our research indicates that MSNPD methods are applicable in scenarios where traditional NPDPD methods are not. Moreover, our study also delves into the challenges of generalizing this method for multiple channels. Despite this, in specific instances, our method presents a viable avenue for avoiding costly channel characterization, essential for traditional NPDPD methods. Our work's applications and extensions are extensively documented in a companion paper. The present study is visualized through 3D animations. The global COVID-19 pandemic has led to an unprecedented surge in cases and deaths, prompting nearly every nation to implement restrictive measures to slow the spread of the disease. As part of these efforts, many governments have adopted contact tracing mobile app programs aimed at minimizing the economic and health impacts of lockdown measures. While contact tracing apps may enhance public safety, their utility relies heavily on user adoption, necessitating balanced approaches that protect both individual and governmental interests. Specifically, this study examines the fine line between utilizing contact tracing apps to safeguard public health and compromising individual privacy, a concern highlighted by numerous high-profile breaches of COVID-19 contact tracing data. To address this issue, this research defines a problem analogous to the "Anonymity Problem" within the Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) model and proposes the "Coronavirus-SUS" (Coro-SUS) instance, distinguishing it from existing SIR model research by focusing on the "anonymity" of users within a contact tracing system rather than the "infection" and "recovery" processes. The authors then develop two algorithms, Self-Blinding (SB) and Distance-Based (DB), to solve the Coro-SUS instance. Finally, this research is extended to develop an efficient, distance-free algorithm, Balanced Anonymous (BA), addressing the inherent limitations of the SB and DB algorithms. The study's results, presented as pseudocode and analyzed mathematically, demonstrate the trade-offs between these algorithms in terms of user adoption, false positives, and computational requirements, paving the way for BA's potential integration into contact tracing services as a privacy-preserving solution. Overall, this research aims to contribute to the growing literature on contact tracing app privacy by proposing the Coro-SUS instance and developing the self-blinding and distance-based algorithms to address the evolving challenges of contact tracing in the post-COVID-19 era. Furthermore, this work is expected to lay the groundwork for future research on the rapidly evolving contact tracing landscape. The proposed algorithms are expected to be implemented in contact tracing apps, subject to the terms and conditions of their respective organizations. In the future, I intend to extend this research by addressing apps such as Google/Alphabet, COVID19 Trace, Cras, Care, CoronaRakett, COVID Trace, Contact tracing for Corona, Healthy Together, Healthy WA, COVID-19 Safe Entry, CDC Sage, Covid Safe Massachusetts, Covid Cares, Covid Good Neighbor, Exposure Notification, and the COVID-19 Tracking Project. In the field of classical computing, understanding how memory and computation processes coexist is crucial. Similar to this, research on quantum computing is focusing on understanding the intersection of quantum effects and neural network dynamics. Recent studies employing quantum simulation and experimental techniques have demonstrated that quantum effects can be observed in biological systems, and it's also evident that neural networks can exhibit nonlinear behavior. What's still unclear is whether quantum effects can be present in neural systems and how they impact the dynamics of networks. This paper discusses recent findings in this area. While there's currently no concrete evidence supporting the idea that neural networks necessarily rely on quantum behavior, experiments have shown that various nonlinear dynamics can emerge even at room temperature, and adjusting parameters can amplify these effects. Techniques such as spin pump current generation and pump-rectification have also been developed. These methods require further exploration but could potentially be applied to enhance information processing in neural networks. Finally, the advent of quantum neural networks is also a subject of current research. This paper summarizes recent findings and proposes new avenues for investigation, highlighting the need for more studies to fully understand the relationship between quantum effects and neural network dynamics. What's evident so far is that existing tools and techniques have provided significant insights but that much work remains to fully insight the intersection of these concepts. This study employs Hurwitz zeta functions to create novel instances of Ramanujan's equation for odd zeta values. To achieve this goal, we establish an adaptation of Gauss's duplication formula that is crucial in determining the expression for odd zeta values. Furthermore, by integrating the shifting theorem of the Hurwitz zeta function, we generate additional results that are considered significant. Ultimately, the obtained formulas are utilized to derive alternative proofs of a generalized equation introduced by Chudnovsky et al. for odd zeta values. This newly proven equation is characterized by simplified and regulable output. Consequently, the presented methods can be applied to develop a generalized version of Ramanujan's identity for odd zeta values. This endeavor yields an extensively broadened set of solutions to the equation $1+ 2^{s-1} + 2^{2s-2} + \cdots + 2^{s-1} = 2^{s-1}(1+2^{s-2} + \cdots + 2^{-s})$. Interestingly, the obtained results from the study can be seen as generalizations of various results that are closely related to the study by Chudnovsky et al. (2014) and are published in Integers. This study is in the process of being finalized. In addition, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of the output from the application of the formulas derived in the study and is designed to meet the requirements set forth in the MSc dissertation of the principal author. We define a specific form of equivariant elliptic cohomology for groups of automorphisms related to logical circuits, and demonstrate its generation in terms of a modified version of the Chern class that we call the logical fundamental class. This fundamental class is defined as the equivalence class of Chern class modifications across logical circuit transformations. This concept is applied in the study of free group algebras subjected to logical circuit constraints, resulting in novel cohomology structures. As an example of its utility, we compute the equivariant elliptic cohomology of projective spaces based on the coefficients of the associated algebra, which reveals intriguing connections to the study of monadic second-order logic over graphs. Specifically, we find an isomorphism between this cohomology structure and a monoid consisting of second-order logic operations applied to graph connectivity, which serves as an alternate perspective on known results. Moreover, we demonstrate that the equivariant elliptic cohomology of the projective space has a closed-form representation in terms of a generator associated with each group of automorphisms, which offers the possibility of further geometric interpretations of logical operations within this framework. This work, and the accompanying mathematical software code, offer mathematical support for the logical equivariant elliptic cohomology circle principle, which is a theoretical approach to the study of automorphism groups related to logical circuits. This code was written using the Swanson elliptic cohomology package and modified versions of the Tornqvist sigma algebra generation tool, as well as the Circe automorphism group generator. This work is a version of the author's PhD dissertation, which was initially submitted in 2020 for evaluation. It is primarily based on the related dissertation abstract by the author.
