Recent advancements in machine learning are paving the way for significant interactions between physics and computer science. This research explores the application of machine learning techniques to solve longstanding issues in algebraic topology, a branch of mathematics that has previously been difficult to compute. We examine the capabilities of deep learning methods for preserving topological properties in continuous datasets, such as persistent homology. This investigation applies mathematical concepts from algebraic topology to analyze the structure of implicit representations of scalar functions via formal homology. We use mathematical transformations to convert scalar functions into more easily manageable vector fields, which can be employed by machine learning models to predict properties. The ability to map function domains to lower-dimensional spaces serves as a diagnostic tool for monitoring the loss of topological properties in neural network models, which is particularly essential in physics. We demonstrate the potential of these techniques through a discrete version of Wilson's flow for quantum field theory. This research marks an early step toward integrating algebraic topology and machine learning to address fundamental problems in physics. As an example, we showcase the application of these techniques in quantum field theory where existing methods fall short. The development of new machine learning methods for preserving topological properties will facilitate a deeper understanding of the interplay between geometry, analysis, and topology in the context of physical systems. Furthermore, it is expected that these techniques can be broadly extended to other areas of physics. All the necessary technical details, including the mathematical framework and the implementation of the models, are provided to ensure that the results can be reproduced and to serve as a foundation for future work, as outlined in the appendix. The implementation details can be found in the repository at https://magma.math.unc.edu/PHY/. The PHY repository contains 18 notebooks, 14 of which detail the experiments, and 4 of which document the development of the methods. The primary experiment is a demonstration of the discrete version of Wilson's flow for quantum field theory. The development notebooks include an exhaustive analysis of the methods, which are designed to extend the capabilities of the neural network transformer model to handle scalar functions. The underlying mathematics of the method is based on the work of Kowalski-Glekler-Ullrich and the more recent adaptation of the method by the deep learning team at UNC. The implementation of the method is based on the more general framework for handling scalar functions developed by the team at UNC. The framework is designed to preserve the base geometry and is the core algorithm for analyzing the structure of the discrete and continuous datasets. The implementation details can be found in the repository at https://github.com

In preparation for the BESIII experiment's future measurement, we'll determine the $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^2)$ contribution to the angular distributions of $J/\psi$ production through the $e^+e^- \to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ processes at a energy of approximately $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV. Utilizing the massive gauge-invariant method with the charm quark wave function from nonrelativistic QCD (NRQCD) at the one-loop level, the derived prediction shows agreement with the leading-order (LO) result for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ within a 1-2% margin, and a Lo prediction for $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ with relative ${\cal O}(\alpha_s^2)$ errors ranging from 4% to 6%. The prediction also displays sensitivity to $\alpha_s$ and thus to the value of $\alpha_s$ at this energy. The obtained predictions will facilitate an accurate, order-$\mathcal{O}(10\%)$, next-to-leading correction to the angular distributions in the BESIII experiment's future measurements. Furthermore, the derived prediction for $q^2$ and $\cos\theta_c$ distributions at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ energy also agrees with the available QCD-corrected LO prediction for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and a Lo prediction for $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ with relative ${\cal O}(\alpha_s^2)$ errors ranging from 4% to 6%. and studies in natural language processing often overlook this characteristic 
when designing systems. We've investigated how a language's grammatical gender 
affects the embeddings of nouns in real-world, human-generated text datasets. 
We discovered that feminine and masculine nouns are distinguishable in such 
datasets, with higher levels of semantic relatedness than expected by chance, 
and that this distinction is significantly more pronounced in languages that 
unambiguously indicate noun gender, rather than through indirect clues or 
contextual hints. We also found that models trained on these datasets are 
capable of accurately identifying the gender of nouns in their native language, 
with some exhibiting exceptional performance. This distinction is primarily due to 
the increased semantic relatedness among words sharing the same gender, and 
our experiments show that grouping words by their gender during training leads to 
better gender classification results. We've confirmed the effectiveness of 
our method, both in its original form and when adapted for languages that do 
not clearly indicate noun gender, and also replicated our results for both 
simple and more complex processing models. We suggest that developing 
language-models-by-example, where word embeddings are informed by a language's 
grammatical characteristics, could be a promising direction for natural language 
processing research. We've made our code and pre-trained models available

We introduce the concept of charminess of a group $G$ over a number field $k$, denoted by $\mathrm{char}(G/k)$, as the largest unramified prime $p$ that splits in $k$ and is a prime of finite reduction for $G$. This concept is further utilized to prove the charminess of several arithmetic groups. Specifically, it is demonstrated that any semisimple group $G$ defined over a number field $k$ has a charminess that is finite, given certain conditions are met. Building upon Kappa's work regarding 3-manifolds and their relationship with Lie groups, a key condition is the existence of a virtually abelian subgroup of finite index. By leveraging this, it is proven that certain arithmetic lattices possess a charminess that is finite. A notable example of this is $\mathrm{SL}_n(Z[\tfrac{1}{2},\sqrt{2}])$. For exceptional groups meeting specific criteria, a direct calculation of charminess is achieved. Lastly, a compact manifold's charminess is demonstrated to be finite if its prime of finite reduction sequence converges. As a result, a finite charminess is proven for some arithmetic groups of dim 14, constructed from snapping examples. Furthermore, it is established that certain product groups possess a charminess that is finite, such as the product of $\mathrm{SL}_2(Z)$ over various extended fields. All these findings are visualized through field labelings and prime sequences. This research is accompanied by a related exploration of stiffness, a characteristic possessed by certain groups over real closed fields. Specifically, it is proven that certain groups over the rational numbers possess a stiffness of $\infty$. Additionally, a graphical tool for detecting stiffness has been developed and employed to show the stiffness of various modular groups. These include the holomorphic symplectic group and its moduli interpretations, as well as $\mathrm{GL}_2(Z)$. Lastly, a related exploration of charminess among affine groups over the rational numbers is undertaken. Specifically, it is proven that while some affine groups possess a charminess that is finite, others do not. For instance, the level-n affine group $\mathrm{GL}_2(Z\backslash\mathbb{Z})$ has a charminess that is infinite for nearly all values of n. Predicting short-term traffic conditions is a critical issue for today's modern society.
Due to the widespread adoption of mobile GPS tracking and road sensing technologies,
traffic conditions can be monitored and, more importantly, predicted in real-time.
However, existing forecasting methods are severely constrained by the requirements
of complete spatial and temporal coverage of traffic data.
This study presents a counter-theory that claims traffic conditions in adjacent areas
are also predictive of future traffic conditions, thus justifying the development
of a prediction model that utilizes attribute similarity.
A novel framework, named SparseTrafficForecaster, is proposed to leverage
the advantages of dense spatial coverage and the innovations of attention networks.
With the integration of multi-head self-attention and graph-based attention mechanisms,
the model can effectively gather information from nearest neighbor traffic conditions.
Experimental validation on real-world datasets demonstrates the superiority
of the proposed model over state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the model
is shown to successfully handle out-of-sample predictions on unlabeled traffic data. 
The model's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/fanclfan/SporadicTraffic.

It's demonstrated that, with a sequence of N measurements, a minimum probability error of e(N) exists for this task, where e(N) is at least a perfect fraction of the error achieved when having full knowledge of the target states. Moreover, in certain situations, even with a growing number of measurements, the error e(N) remains less than a perfect fraction, implying that there is an inherent limit to the level of accuracy that can be reached. This research also reveals that, in some cases, the error e(N) is asymptotically non-existent, meaning it can be made arbitrarily small with a sufficiently long sequence. Consequently, we establish the specific values of the minimum error e(N) for identifying symmetric states based on qubits and qudits. In these cases, the error e(N) is found to be at least a perfect fraction for all sequence lengths N, regardless of the target states, as well as being exactly a perfect fraction in certain closed-form algebraic expressions relevant to their identification. In contrast, a related approach involving the calculation of a linear series coefficient is found not to be computationally feasible due to an inherent difficulty related to resolving polynomial equations. Instead, our research is grounded in the principles of Groebner bases and algebraic geometry. It is shown that, for a generic set of N target states, the minimum error e(N) can be exactly determined using a simple closed-form algebraic expression, while for an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, a related approach involving the calculation of a linear series coefficient is described but acknowledges the associated computational difficulties. Our research utilizes three quantitative measures based on trace distance, based on the work of Fuchs and van de Graaf, in order to establish the minimum error e(N) that arises from a sequence of N measurements. These measures, which include variants involving generalized quantum amplitudes and a related approach involving the calculation of a linear series coefficient, are all grounded in the principles of certain key research papers in quantum information theory. Our research is applicable to a wide variety of quantum information applications, including the scenarios of identifying quantum states, performing quantum teleportation, detecting bias in measurements, and identifying spin states. The high-redshift universe's primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) may have been strong enough to have had a significant effect on the early universe's evolution, influencing the formation of the first stars and galaxies. While there is present evidence suggesting the existence of PMFs through their impact on structure formation, direct evidence is still required to confirm their strength and characteristics. Detecting the proposed stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) directly will be critical for validating the theories about the early universe's evolution which predict its existence. Researchers have proposed multiple detection methods for SGWB but none have yet proven successful to date. This paper examines the potential for the LISA satellite and the Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiment to detect the SGWB produced by anisotropic SGWB generated in PMFs via gravitational wave (GW) multiplication. The PTA's frequency range (10^-9 - 10^-3 Hz) is found to be capable of detecting the SGWB's highest-amplitude scales and the PTA's constant and stable observations make it the ideal instrument for the task. The PTA's current data show no signs of the SGWB and therefore the analysis sets an upper limit on its strength. The lack of detection means that the SGWB's amplitude is restricted to a certain level but further upgrades to the PTA will allow for the detection of the SGWB's lower-frequency bands and potentially push the detection further back in time, thereby providing a more precise picture of the early universe's evolution. The PTA's capability to explore the SGWB's properties such as its polarization and the early universe's magnetic scale dependence is also discussed. The PTA's ability to detect the SGWB at a level of $10^{-21}$ Hz$^{-1/2}$ will correspond to a magnetic field of $10^{-4}$G in the 1 Mpc$^{-1}$ scale at a redshift of 10^5. This would make PMFs the strongest magnetic fields ever known. The presence of SGWB would also imply non-zero correlations between PMFs on different scales. The detection of SGWB would confirm that magnetic fields are the origin of gravitational waves at a level required to explain the formation of the first stars and galaxies. The PTA is one of the most promising instruments for achieving such a detection. The analysis further discusses ways in which the PTA can be used not just for detecting the SGWB but also for exploring its properties. Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for researchers due to its numerous potential applications. A significant feature of commercial light field capture devices, like the LH-1 by Snapseed, is their ability to capture high-resolution images. However, these images typically have low resolution in the epipolar dimensions. A suitable solution for the transmission of captured light fields over low-bandwidth networks is light field image compression. This paper proposes an innovative, data-driven method for light field image compression through micro-block feature prediction. A specially designed theoretical model for light field capture devices that accounts for parallax also enables the accurate training of this prediction method. A practical implementation of this idea using discrete optimization yields compression ratios of 72M for 4K x 4K light fields, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, this paper also presents an extension of the model to account for the effects of lens distortion, facilitating the training of a deep learning-based light field image compression system without ground truth data. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method demonstrates its capability to compress high-resolution light fields at low bitrates. Specifically, this paper presents compressed light fields at 20MB for a 14M pixel resolution, as well as support for distortion compression. A subsequent test on the recently-introduced EPIC-KIT dataset for light field compression further showcases the effectiveness of the proposed method. Notably, this method enables the compression of the 14K x 6K x 6K EPIC-KIT dataset to 72M at 0.38MB/M, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods. Finally, this paper also presents an extension of the model to account for the effects of defocus, facilitating the simulation-free evaluation of light field compression methods. A demonstration of this capability on the EPIC-KIT dataset is also presented in this work. A related Python project for this research has been made available on GitHub under the open-source community contribution license. Specifically, this project can be found at https://github.com/acaman83/parallax-ahd. Additionally, an associated video demonstrating the proposed method has been submitted as part of a conference presentation. A copy of this video can be found at https://youtu.be/4yfY3hU9uXg. Initially published on arXiv in May 2020 as "Learning-Based Practical Light Field Image Compression through Micro-Block Feature Prediction", this research received the second-place prize at the NTU GHOST 2020 Compressive Sensing Challenge. Achieving effective, efficient cross-lingual information retrieval with vector embeddings is a significant challenge despite current advancements in multi-lingual embeddings. These models often rely on straight-forward techniques like "mixture-of-techniques" and "average-of-techniques" to handle multiple tasks and take advantage of pre-trained language models. However, such methods do not utilize domain-specific data effectively, leading to suboptimal performance in information retrieval tasks. To address this limitation, we developed a domain-specific, interactive cross-lingual information retrieval model that leverages pre-trained capabilities for initial performance boost. Additionally, our model can integrate diverse data and train the final cross-lingual embeddings through an end-to-end process solely using dataset-level information, showing superior results on Wikipedia, HashtagGames, and CL-IR datasets when compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the theoretical benefits of interactive and non-interactive models are elucidated through an analysis of loss functions and their stability in model training. Our proposed framework and analysis demonstrate the importance of interactive data for information retrieval model development and offer insights for creating effective information retrieval models. The LHCb experiment has found the first indication of a rare and unusual decay 
for a baryon, specifically $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, obtained using 8.9 fb$^{-1}$ 
of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV. Comparing the observed yield to predictions 
from the Sharmain model, the observed decay rate is roughly 16 standard deviations 
away from the predicted rate. Alternatively, the observed decay rate is consistent 
with the assumption that it occurs without any medium effects. This is the first evidence 
for this specific baryon decay, preceding similar evidence for the $\Lambda_b^0$ baryon 
decay in 2014. The LHCb experiment has now provided two separate instances of 
medium-independent evidence for baryon decays to two muons. The ratio of 
$\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-)$ and $\Lambda_b^0 \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay rates remains 
at approximately 1/140 compared to the $\Lambda_b^0 \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ rate. 
Previous predictions from the Sharmain model estimate this ratio to be around 1/130. 
It is estimated that upcoming data will lead to statistically significant evidence 
for this specific baryon decay, regardless of whether the medium has any effects. 
These specific baryon decay rates are anticipated to provide substantial insights 
into how matter interacts with itself at extremely high energies. The LHCb 
experiment is expected to provide substantially lower relative uncertainties 
for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $\Xi^0_\mathrm{c} \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay rates 
following collection of 2021 data, which would supplement past findings. 
Currently, no indication of several baryon decays has been discovered, and the 
limits for several more baryon decays have been documented. 
It is anticipated that LHCb and ALICE experiments over the upcoming data 
collection periods will provide the decisive evidence for several more 
baryon decays, expanding our understanding of how matter interacts with itself 
at extremely high energies. The specific baryon decay rate ratios, particularly 
in the $b \to c$ transition, are anticipated to provide significant 
insights into whether matter interacts with itself at extremely high energies.

The collapse of a prestellar core undergoes rotation, which ultimately results in the formation of a protoplanetary disk. The process of core collapse is studied in detail, taking into consideration magnetic fields and rotational energy. A studied core has a mass of 0.1 solar masses and a core exponent of 1.5, with an initial natal cloud core magnetic field of 10 microgauss and rotational energy of 0.5 times the gravitational potential energy. As the core collapses, a prestellar core stage is observed lasting no more than 50,000 years before protostellar core collapse begins. During this process, axially symmetric protrusions form and cause the collapse to deviate from spherical symmetry. The collapse is characterized by an opening angle of 20 degrees and a magnetic rung altitude of one third of the core's radius. Resultantly, protoplanetary disks form with masses in agreement with those observed by ALMA, and masses of the central star-like objects are in agreement with main sequence stars of the same mass. The study reveals the necessity of detailed numerical simulations in order to understand how protoplanetary disks are formed and why some disks may never settle into a uniform configuration. Moreover, these simulations suggest that magnetic fields are insufficient on their own to explain the observed asymmetry in protoplanetary disks, and these fields play a crucial role in the disk's structural development. The study also demonstrates that magnetic fields are effectively mixed into the disk, and gases are efficiently transferred to the disk but not to the central star-like object until the dust gets settled. The study provides valuable insights into prestellar core collapse, protoplanetary disk formation, and star formation processes. The study also offers potential explanations for various star formation processes observed in astronomical research, and contributes to formation mechanisms of planetary systems. The study provides necessary conditions for formation of particular planetary systems with specific properties through protoplanetary disk development. The study is performed using a unique, cutting-edge simulation code "RH hydro" from the University of Colorado Boulder that integrates critical factors of star and planetary formation processes. The study is completed with analysis tools "Plotter" and "diagnostic tool", and research questions are answered with the help of a human reporter. The study demonstrates numerical stability up to 1,800,000 time steps or roughly four million time steps, and achieves good results with a good convergence of simulated results with theoretical star and planetary formation models. The study is achieved with the help of powerful computer hardware, i.e., Intel Xeon E5645

This paper introduces an innovative method for generating a distribution of future multi-dimensional data sequences, given a pre-existing set of observed data, by adapting the concepts of sparse Bayesian learning and variational inference for the specific task of multi-period forecasting. The proposed model is a compact reformulation of existing hierarchical sparse models, enabling an efficient Bayesian framework through a closed-form variational distribution. Empirical evaluations using synthetic and real-world data confirm the proposed model's capacity for reduced model complexity and superior predictive performance, often surpassing methods that rely on random noise models. Notably, the proposed model achieves accurate forecasts for the S&P500 index, outperforming alternative approaches such as the ARIMA model and hierarchical shrinkage ledgers. The research provides an open-source Python implementation of the model, known as STL-SDP, alongside extensive experimental results and recommendations for future work. In a setting of compact abelian groups, established principles such as duality and Stone representation gain meaning through the theory of constant logic. According to Pontryagin duality, a self-dual map in group theory corresponds to a fully faithful map in logic when viewed from the perspective of Stone representation. The effectiveness of Pontryagin duality as a tool for demonstrating a relationship between two representations lies in its symmetric nature, where symmetric properties in group theory translate to equivalent symmetric properties in logic. The paper delves into the investigation of certain symmetric properties (faithfulness, finiteness, compactness, and separability) in group theory and its corresponding equivalents in logic through the lens of Stone representation. It is revealed that all these properties are interchangeably mapped to their symmetric counterparts in group theory. Moreover, it is shown that fidelity (a localized form of faithfulness) in group theory is mapped to a logically equivalent concept that is not an inherent aspect of constant logic; in contrast, other properties are observable within the realm of constant logic. Ultimately, the research highlights the potential utility of Pontryagin duality as a tool in deriving symmetric facts in group theory and illustrates how these facts can be translated into the realm of logic while reflecting the underlying logic's characteristic features. In addition, the research serves as an introduction to the incorporation of Pontryagin duality within the framework of model theory. In model theory, the dual of a compact abelian group is equivalent to a fully faithful dual map, which can be seen through the Stone representation. Descriptions of certain model-theoretic properties (such as separability, completeness, and compactness) are revealed within the paper, where these properties are observable in group theory and its corresponding dual. The research demonstrates that most of these properties are interchangeable when the group is either finitely generated or compact. In group theory, the property of compactness implies the existence of a maximal subgroup within every subgroup. In model theory, the inclusion-exclusion principle yields a corresponding fact, where every fully faithful submodel contains a dense dense submodel within it. These principles not only mirror each other but also highlight the utility of Pontryagin duality in deriving symmetric facts in group theory and its corresponding logical equivalents. Ultimately, the research serves as an introduction to an ongoing project in the realm of model theory and group theory. The work aims to investigate duality as a tool in demonstrating relationships between two representations, where a self-dual map in group theory corresponds to a fully faithful map in logic

By examining the intersection of fairness and privacy in the context of federated learning, this article will present mathematical formulations and algorithms to address related problems, as well as highlight existing research and future areas of investigation that will address the pressing concerns of data ethics and privacy in the age of machine learning. The paper will primarily focus on concrete applications such as fair regression models and binary classification models, and present generalizable techniques that can be expanded to other problems and scenarios. Additionally, a companion code has been developed to facilitate the implementation of the techniques presented in this article and enable researchers to build on this work, as presented at the NeurIPS 2020 workshop on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. The corresponding code can be accessed via the GitHub repository https://github.com/AIResearchTeam/Fairness-and-Privacy-in-FedLearn. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. In this paper, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of symbol classes within the Fock and Hardy spaces, focusing on the algebraic and topological characteristics of these Toeplitz algebras. Specifically, we build on the work of B. D. Duguji and M. Rang i Nanopoulos, using algebraic simplifications to identify equivalent subclasses, and establish isomorphic relationships between these classes. We further utilize this framework to derive categorical equivalences of the Toeplitz algebras themselves. For the topological characteristics, we draw on the work of M. Br pedal and M. M. Cowling, providing a comprehensive study of the closed ideals within Toeplitz algebras and exploring various forms of approximability. Key results include proofs that all Toeplitz algebras have a linear dependence on the underlying Hilbert space, a linear dependence on closed ideals within the algebra, and that Toeplitz algebras are not unital if the symbol belongs to a particular degenerate class. Additionally, we establish an explicit description of the closed ideals within Toeplitz algebras of degenerate symbols, show that such ideals are densely embedded within the algebra, and that Toeplitz algebras of non-degenerate symbols do not possess densely embedded closed ideals. Finally, we prove that all Toeplitz algebras have an abundant supply of free ideals, exploring the implications for the algebraic and topological structure of these Toeplitz algebras. Notably, our results show that Toeplitz algebras can be either vastly simple or exceptionally complex, rendering many existing concepts of simplicity redundant, and prompting questions about the existence of maximal simplicity criteria for these Toeplitz algebras. A concise definition of multi-linear simplicity could potentially address this inquiry. Furthermore, the properties of free ideals within Toeplitz algebras may signify a unique concept of tensorial simplicity, warranting in-depth exploration in future research. The multi-linear simplicity of commutative Banach algebras, for example, is an intriguing area for future investigation. The multi-linear simplicity of operator algebras is another potential area for exploration in the future. A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud is surrounded by a complex of ionized gas, ionized outflows, and a partially neutral layer. A recent study has found that this system's ionized gas is largely confined and is not interacting with the cloud's main body. Although the star's outflows are creating new gas through expansion at around 800,000 km/h, this gas is not dominating the surrounding environment. A comparison of HCN and CO-25 keV X-ray data has revealed that the cloud's neutral layer is largely undisturbed and has a typical density of 1,000,000 cm^-3. However, this layer is thinner near the star and has a typical density of only 300 cm^-3. A model that takes into account the local power of the X-ray radiation has successfully reproduced the CO-25 keV map's characteristics. However, the HCN data cannot be explained solely by the local power of the X-ray radiation. The concept of veracity in data is similar to reliability, except it involves the accuracy of individual data points. Veracity refers to the accuracy of each data entry, whereas reliability refers to the number of reliable entries within a dataset. As big data continues to grow, developing methods to enhance data veracity becomes essential. This comprehensive survey focuses on machine learning-based methods for handling veracity in data. It defines veracity as the degree of accuracy for each data point, differentiating it from reliability, which represents the number of accurate data points within a dataset. The survey explores three primary categories of veracity: point veracity, referring to accurate single data points; aggregate veracity, relating to groups of data; and contextual veracity, involving data accuracy within specific contexts. It also examines two secondary categories, including human-focused veracity, involving data accuracy based on human preferences, and sensor-foci veracity, requiring data accuracy from sensors. The survey delves into machine learning-based methods for handling veracity in data, including techniques for verifying data authenticity, validating source credibility, and identifying and mitigating data veracity issues such as outliers and anomalies. Ultimately, the survey concludes with recommendations and proposed future areas of research in data veracity. [Article is currently in press.] © 2021 IISc, Bangalore. A promising field, neural architecture search, holds potential for scaling to large-scale problems but is currently limited by high computational costs. To address this challenge, researchers are now focusing on reducing interference between simultaneous searches, a crucial step in making architectural search scalable. By thoroughly investigating the nature of interference in the first time a parameter is modified across all current architecture searches, our analysis reveals that (1) the frequency of interference is inversely related to the number of samples used per architecture and (2) the probability of interference significantly decreases after the first time a parameter is modified. We further develop an optimized search strategy by (1) partitioning the search space and assigning it to multiple GPUs, (2) using a shared weight initialisation method that delays parameter sharing, and (3) employing a hierarchical model design, resulting in notable reductions in computation time. The proposed methods demonstrate superior performance on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, particularly under time constraints. For example, a 1-time overhead on CIFAR-10 yields a top-1 accuracy of 96.8% using our R2D2 model, surpassing the state-of-the-art. Moreover, a two-day computation time achieves a top-1 accuracy of 84.4% on ImageNet with the R2D2-CMP model. These advances make the studied architectures more suitable for large-scale problems, even in environments with extremely limited resources. The codes for our proposals are publicly available at https://github.com/alexkouretas/interference-reduction. The ImageNet results for other current state-of-the-art models are also included. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a 2-dimensional SGBT space is a CAT(0) space with no edges if and only if it is a tree. We also prove that a 2-dimensional SGBT space is a CAT(0) space with no edges at the expense of a different completeness condition from Gromov's. Additionally, we demonstrate that a group with a finite edge action has a 2-dimensional, non-trivial geometric action on a SGBT space. Consequently, we derive a condition for a group to have a quasi-isometric action which is analogous to a 2-dimensional, non-trivial geometric action and relate this condition to the existence of edges. Moreover, we prove that a group with a finite edge action has a geometric action on a 2-dimensional SGBT space if and only if its action is a flat geometric action. We also demonstrate the existence of a group that has a finite edge action but no geometric action on a 2-dimensional SGBT space. Finally, we derive the relationship between the boundary of a graph and its edges. Human-assisted machine translation reliability assessments are typically conducted by surveying translators and asking them to indicate the level of confidence in their work. Although this results in a substantial amount of data, it poses a significant challenge in its utilization – researchers are unable to leverage it effectively in further improving machine translation capabilities. To address this issue, our study develops a cutting-edge statistical technique that allows for the estimation of machine translation accuracy on a sentence-level, utilizing the translators' confidence ratings. This method can be employed in various scenarios, such as generating translated texts that are more accurate, improving translation quality assessments, or serving as a machine translation reliability metric. We successfully tested and refined our proposed method on two distinct datasets with two distinct machine translation tasks – one spanning English to Spanish and the other to Russian – utilizing two separate datasets collected through crowd sourcing. Our study provides valuable insights into the variability in machine translation quality, the transparency of machine translation models, and how translator confidence and content-related factors correlate. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed method in generating translated texts with minimal translation errors and achieving translation quality comparable to that of human translators. Additionally, our study showcases the proposed method's potential as a reliability metric. To facilitate future research, we publicly release the datasets, source code, and sample output generated by our study. The work presented here has the potential to be a versatile tool in the assessment and understanding of machine translation reliability. Furthermore, our study promotes the development of more robust and reliable assessment techniques, and aims to contribute to the improvement of translation quality and the development of machine translation models with increased reliability. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed method in generating translated texts with minimal translation errors and showcases the proposed method's potential as a reliability metric. Convolutional networks benefit from their ability to construct spatially-aware interactions, but this property comes at the expense of increased model complexity. The 'lottery ticket' hypothesis suggests even randomly initialized simple models can learn effective interactions and surpass larger, more complicated ones after pruning less essential components. Our research explores whether convolutional networks' unique structure grants them a built-in advantage over similar models based on fully connected architectures. To answer this, we compared the characteristics of winning lottery tickets from both network types after being initialized at random or through the 'winner-takes-all' method, and we discovered some key differences. The characteristics of the convolutional network's best tickets showed a higher degree of similarity to the original model, whereas those of the fully connected network's tickets exhibited greater dispersal. Additionally, the convolutional network's tickets performed better on datasets that emphasized visual aspects, and we found that removing the fully connected network's top layer resulted in significantly reduced performance, which largely eliminated the distinction between it and the convolutional network's tickets. These findings support the idea that convolutional networks' unique structure provides them with a higher likelihood of discovering effective, essential components, which solidifies their status as superior 'lottery ticket' candidates. The global market for cryptocurrency-based lottery tickets is steadily growing. A lottery ticket represents a unique combination of parameters that influences both the chance of winning and the amount of payment if someone wins. This payment, referred to as the "anticipated value," considers two essential factors: the probability of success and the reward for success. Successful outcomes in this context encompass both winning and selling the ticket. Win or sell, the value of a lottery ticket is determined by the price at which it can be exchanged and the nature of the underlying cryptocurrency. The time of transition from one state to another is known as a "time bucket." The anticipated value of a lottery ticket has been mathematically formalized using a method Ground Set Partitioning (GSP) to measure variations in the chances of success and payment over time. As the GSP method is computationally demanding, a practical alternative algorithm has been developed for determining the optimal time for purchasing and selling a lottery ticket, relying on historical data regarding market fluctuations and payment distributions. The new approach excels at achieving financial gains over other predictive methods that only consider historical winning patterns, such as the Random Number Prediction (RNP) method. The presented findings indicate that a strategy of selling the tickets is commonly preferred over buying them. Nonetheless, the best approach depends on the specific characteristics of the market such as market volatility and the size of the time buckets being analyzed. The new algorithm has been validated by generating artificial markets and putting the method through a series of tests, while also measuring its effectiveness using real-world data regarding three distinct types of blockchain games. The results show that the generated method yields up to 60 percent more income compared to Random Number Prediction, and that the new approach reduces computational requirements by approximately five orders of magnitude. t-SNE is a widely used dimensionality reduction technique that enables visualization and analysis of complex data distributions. However, the algorithm assumes data points follow a Gaussian distribution, which is not suitable for data on the sphere's surface. We introduce a new method, vmf-SNE, specifically designed for data characterized by low-dimensional, spherical statistical patterns and high-dimensional, non-spherical noise. Our approach converts data from any distribution onto a sphere, then applies a spherical t-SNE equivalent that preserves the data's underlying pattern in low dimensions. Evaluations across various synthetic and real-world datasets show vmf-SNE offers better visualization and representation of spherical data than the conventional, Gaussian-based t-SNE. For example, in a dataset with a Von Mises-Fisher distribution, vmf-SNE successfully preserves the data's underlying pattern in both 2D and 3D visualizations, while t-SNE fails to do so. Additionally, vmf-SNE provides more accurate reconstruction of the data's conditional probability and better data classification than t-SNE in a 10-digit MRI dataset. Moreover, vmf-SNE is used in a DREAMS dataset analysis to identify distinct VMF distributions within subpopulations of 3D brain fixed patterns. We conclude that vmf-SNE represents a significant improvement over t-SNE for data with distinct, spherical statistical patterns and recommend its use in data visualization and representation, especially for data containing multiple VMF distributions. Finally, we introduce a web-based, interactive vmf-SNE visualization platform for research and application. The platform can be accessed at https://vishub.mit.edu/dataset/vmf-SNE. The vmf-SNE source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/vishub-ml/vmf-SNE. The vmf-SNE binary is available upon request. In this research, a method is proposed to efficiently simulate complex fermionic systems using a quantum computer that combines digital and analog components. Initially, a quantum circuit is designed to convert fermionic operators into bosonic operators, utilizing a superconducting qubit and a waveguide mode to create a corresponding entangled state. Then, an analog gate is applied to replicate the fermionic hopping interaction between adjacent sites. Utilizing a detection technique with error correction, the fermionic many-body state can be accurately reconstructed. This simulation methodology may facilitate the development of quantum technologies such as quantum computing and quantum simulation, utilizing a relatively small digital quantum computer. An experimental demonstration of this concept has been performed on a Fermi-Hubbard model using a three-qubit digital quantum computer. An all-optical detection scheme was employed to reconstruct the fermionic state and extract its associated physical properties. When compared to traditional methods, the results show that the combination of digital-analog approach offers a significant speed advantage, specifically a $2^{n+1}$ times increase in processing efficiency for a similar number of qubits. Notably, this research not only showcases a novel concept for quantum information processing but also yields accurate experimental measurements of interacting many-body fermionic states. These findings may inspire the development of different quantum computing paradigms and provide new avenues for investigating complex fermionic systems using a relatively compact quantum computer. An accompanying movie depicts the computational workflow and the measurement probabilities associated with the reconstructed fermionic state. Moreover, the corresponding Julia code is available for reproduction and replication, having been carefully validated against the original experimental data. An examination of potential code vulnerabilities and a related mitigation strategy are also recommended for the reproduction of the results, as described in the ATAC code section. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the numerical outcome is presented in a related paper. Importantly, both the quantum emulation and the algorithm scrutiny were carried out with no discernible systematic bias, thus confirming the reliability of the results. An accompanying GitHub repository contains the supporting code for the paper's analysis. More generally, the research highlights the significance of experimental error correction in the context of quantum simulation. Moreover, a detailed discussion of the research's implications for the simulation of Fermi polaron systems is presented in a related work. Importantly, the research demonstrates that digital quantum computers can efficiently simulate a wide range of fermionic systems, thus bringing the simulation of interacting many-body systems within the practical realm of near-term quantum computing. Notably, the research may facilitate a better understanding of the associated physics of digital quantum computing

Graph polynomials hold significant value due to the sequences of polynomials they generate, which often include renowned invariants such as the Wiener index or the chromatic polynomial. Researchers are interested in capturing evolutionary patterns of these polynomial sequences, which can provide insights into the characteristics of the underlying graphs. This research explores the basic properties of sequences produced by graph polynomials, particularly focusing on sequences that are finite or polynomial in nature. We delve into distinguishing between graphs of identical polynomial sequences, and develop criteria for this distinction based on the roots of associated linear equations. A graphical representation of these roots, known as the Cremona-Robinson diagram, enables us to evaluate the potential for a graph to be part of a polynomial sequence. This method is applied to various examples, including the Hückel molecular orbital polynomials, which sequences of increasing and decreasing polynomials exhibit. Furthermore, we utilize our findings to establish upper limits for the degrees of the polynomials in certain invariants, such as the edge Zegraf polynomials. Finally, this research includes supplementary materials, including an interactive database that stores the first few terms of the sequences of 11 000 graph invariants, as well as a JavaScript-based tool for generating these sequences. Veech surfaces are a specific type of branched cover of the torus surface, characterized by minimal billiards motion. Given a Veech surface, its "width" can be defined as the smallest degree of a rational function with a product of singular points equal to 1, and this measure is studyied in relation to the curve consisting of surfaces with a given width. It's discovered that every width curve contains an affine component, which in the case of the bi-degree (1,1) includes the entire torus surface. However, there are exceptional Veech surfaces with a width of 2 that do not have a corresponding affine structure, and these surface's moduli space is 2-dimensional. Among these exceptional surfaces, those that are lattice-polytope are identified, including the Veech curve of genus 3, and a study is conducted on lattice-polytope surfaces with a width of less than or equal to 3. It's proven that these surfaces, with the exception of one with a width of 2, are all defined by liaisons with specific affine surfaces of bi-degree (2,1), and an explanation is given for the failure of another exceptional surface to possess such an affine structure. Moreover, it's demonstrated that each intersection point corresponding to a particular transition in the moduli space contains a corresponding transition in the variation of complex structure, and this leads to the conclusion that the moduli space containing these surfaces, with the width equal to 2, is not smooth. Finally, related results and conjectures are presented in relation to the moduli space containing all lattice-pure dimensions of bi-degree (2,1), and affine surfaces of bi-degree (2,1), and numerical analysis is applied to confirm the proposed results. Additionally, the study conducted 23 semi-structured interviews with Scrum masters and business owners to gather more in-depth, qualitative data. Conversely, the study's results suggest that traditional project management measures, such as project scope and schedule, may be more challenging to implement and maintain in fully remote Scrum projects. Ultimately, the study provides theoretical and practical insights into the relationship between remote work and the success of Scrum projects, serving as a valuable resource for future research in this area. The integral eigenvalue pair contribution, known as the Gau-Wu value, is calculated for select arrowhead matrices of size $4 \times 4$ using two methods: one that directly computes the Gau-Wu value and another that incorporates the Nussbaum determinant. The Gau-Wu value is hypothesized to be nonnegative in the case of general arrowhead matrices. These calculations provide potential evidence for this hypothesis, as they yield positive Gau-Wu values for the specified matrices. Furthermore, the Gau-Wu values of the specified matrices, when summed, are found to be positive, suggesting the validity of this hypothesis. The behavior of the Gau-Wu value is also examined as a polynomial function of its parameter $k$. The results show that the Gau-Wu value tends towards infinity as $k$ approaches infinity for the given arrowhead matrices, unlike its behavior for negative $k$, where it ultimately converges to a negative value. Finally, the results show that the Gau-Wu value for a particular matrix is less than the Gau-Wu value for its rank-one extension. This phenomenon supports the notion that the Gau-Wu value improves with matrix rank, a trend observed in previous research. The calculated Gau-Wu values, available in tabular form, alongside the corresponding Nussbaum determinants, are used to analyze the behavior of the Gau-Wu value. The behavior of the Gau-Wu value is found to be consistently nonnegative across all examined cases and serves as indicative of a convex function. The Gau-Wu value is found to be positively correlated with the Nussbaum determinant, supporting the hypothesis that the Gau-Wu value is a nonnegative, convex function. The results are further validated by applying the Gau-Wu value methodology to a selective group of $3 \times 3$ arrowhead matrices. The calculated Gau-Wu values for these matrices reveal a consistent, nonnegative trend and align with previous research on the behavior of these matrices. For this case, the GDoF achieved with optimal power control is easily determined and is shown to be the maximum possible for such a network. Next, we demonstrated that for any given number of users $K$, the GDoF achieved with optimal power control in a hard interference network is no more than $\sqrt{K}$ greater than the GDoF achieved with binary power control. Since binary power control clearly achieves nonnegative GDoF, this yields the desired result. Furthermore, the findings for soft and hard interference networks can be combined to establish the GDoF achieved with optimal power control in a general interference network with $K$ users. In multitasking environments, tasks are repeatedly assigned to a pool of agents to minimize overall processing time. We investigated how to distribute these tasks among agents to achieve the fastest possible completion time when tasks are processed simultaneously by multiple agents at varying speeds. Initially, we developed a precise method to calculate the optimal assignment in standard multitasking environments. We then extended this idea to more complex scenarios where tasks are processed simultaneously by multiple agents and demonstrated the applicability of the optimal calculation method to these cases as well. Additionally, we explored new algorithms for efficiently solving these problems in both basic and extended scenarios. We compared the newly developed algorithms, which optimize the assignment of tasks to agents, to existing approaches, such as a random assignment, a round-robin assignment, and a maximum conflict assignment. Our experiments showed that the developed algorithms significantly outperform the existing ones in both basic and extended scenarios, achieving a substantial speedup in processing time and a notable improvement in the quality of the solutions found. In particular, one of the new algorithms, which we call "MARK II," achieved up to 3.2 times faster completion times and up to a 40% improvement in the quality of the solutions found in the extended scenarios. We also showed that both new algorithms are ground state algorithms, meaning they find the best possible assignment in the given situation. We also showed that the MARK II algorithm is the first near-linear algorithm known to solve the standard multitasking allocation problem, marking a significant improvement over the previous best solution. Furthermore, we developed a new method to calculate the optimal assignment in the extended scenarios with shared processing, where tasks are processed simultaneously by multiple agents at varying speeds. We compared the new method to other existing approaches and found that it generally returns better solutions in a shorter amount of time. In particular, one of the new methods, which we call "f2c MARK II," achieved up to a 40% improvement in the quality of the solutions found in the extended scenarios with shared processing. We also found that the new methods generally run much faster than the previous best solution, with one of the new methods, f2c MAXC2, achieving a speedup of at least 16 times in the extended scenarios with shared processing. In summary, we developed precision methods to calculate the optimal assignment in both basic and extended multitasking allocation problems, which significantly improve the quality of the solutions found and, in some cases, the processing time by up to 40 times and 16 times, respectively. This paper focuses on the final project for MIT's 11.123 Special Topics in Transportation Engineering course, which delved into modeling and analyzing the dynamics of legged locomotion. Our project involves examining the single-support phase of a monopod's hop. By simulating the monopod's motion with a basic model that incorporates force and torque calculations, we analyzed the effect of ground stiffness and monopod mass on its hop cycle. Through force distribution analysis and proposed geometric modifications, we aim to discover how different designs can influence the monopod's movement and compensate for ground deformations during single-support hops. Ultimately, our simulation results demonstrate that local shape adjustments can significantly improve hop efficiency and efficiency over various ground conditions. Specifically, we observed a 23% gain in efficiency for a 2kg monopod walking on yieldable terrain, with flat feet forming an angle of 20 degrees and ground stiffness ranging from 50 to 100 N/m. This research explores the performance and energy implications of performing IoT device firmware updates over a large-scale mesh network.  As IoT devices become more prevalent, ensuring they can be updated remotely to perform their designated tasks has become essential for their reliability.  We evaluated the mesh network protocol, contiki, and its capabilities for performing node-to-node updates using various methods for optimizing and minimizing device energy consumption.  Employing a large-scale mesh network consisting of 50 Crossbow IR200 sensors, our experiments analyzed the effects of updating devices in groups versus individually, and investigated how these updates impacted energy consumption, device performance, and network efficiency.  We found that updating devices in groups using an energy-efficient update mechanism reduced energy consumption by 65%, when compared to individually updating devices.  Furthermore, our experiments revealed that this strategy also helped maintain optimal mesh network performance and reduced update completion times by optimizing network traffic.  We concluded that our developed protocol, incorporating a centralized update approach with optimized energy-saving capabilities, effectively addresses firmware updates in large-scale mesh networks, and addresses the need for such updates in IoT applications like weather monitoring, and the potential for applying our work to other low-power networks. The problem of target search by a path-length restricted agent has been studied in a new scenario where a budget is set for interactions with the environment. The agent can choose to either collect payoffs from existing locations it knows or initiate a new search. Given this constraint, the agent must strategically balance exploring new nodes against collecting existing payoffs from its target network. Since determining an optimal target-nearest-neighbor sequence is notoriously challenging, the paper proposes a straightforward yet efficient heuristic search approach for finding a target-dependent solution within a restricted budget. The proposed algorithm, called Budget Dependent Target Near Neighbor (BDTNN), offers a straightforward solution for finding a target-dependent path within a given budget. The BDTNN algorithm ensures that the target-related path found is at most budget-plus-one steps away and that its quality is at least the best possible target-independent solution within the same budget. The proposed BDTNN algorithm is shown to be applicable across a variety of target networks to maximize the expected reward when multiple targets are present. The approach involves using a unique measure of a set's "spread" to maximize the expected reward, and this measure can easily be extended for use in cases where the target distribution is unknown. The effectiveness of the BDTNN algorithm is demonstrated through its application to multiple test cases, and these test cases highlight its unique capabilities and limitations. The research implies that budget limited interactive search for multiple targets using a path-length restricted agent is an unsolvable problem when the target distribution is unknown. The BDNN algorithm is proven to be the only target-dependent solution possible when the target distribution is known and a special symmetry is present in the target nearest neighbor sequence. The research also sets a lower bound on the number of interactions required for finding a target-dependent solution within a given budget when the target distribution is known and a unique symmetry is present in the target nearest neighbor sequence. The lower bound is shown to be the best possible target-dependent solution possible for the given distribution and a special symmetry. The effectiveness of the BDTNN algorithm is further tested through its application to random target networks, and these test cases highlight its unique properties and behaviors. The approach used in this research and a variation of it can easily be extended for finding a target-dependent solution within a given budget when the target distribution is unknown. To boost the development of quantum algorithms, researchers are using classical data to test and refine their quantum models, but finding the ideal data for this purpose is a significant challenge. This study demonstrates the presence of universal adversarial instances and perturbations for quantum classifiers. Specifically, we show that there are vectors whose application to any quantum state causes a significant change in classification outcome for an enormous number of related functions. Developing accurate predictive models of mobile radio signals is crucial for enhancing communication systems, as they enable estimating the strength and quality of future signal strength and quality. To achieve this, researchers typically collect extensive on-field data, designing proprietary algorithms to analyze it, as seen in a recent study by T. Halin. Following this, we conducted a more realistic field measurement campaign to create a comprehensive dataset of outdoor downlink cellular network radio signals. By comparing two advanced deep neural networks, we discovered that a novel 3D deep convolutional neural network outperformed a dynamic radio signal model based on radio channel characteristics, offering superior accuracy and computational efficiency with minimal collinear antennas. Therefore, we recommend utilizing the 3D deep neural network in place of the dynamic radio signal model for accurate predictions and real-time applications. Moreover, this approach effectively utilizes a reduced dataset, mitigating storage and training issues, and enables data augmentation for increased accuracy. As such, this technique serves as an exemplar for quantitative radio pattern modeling without field measurements. Finally, the collected data and source code are available for replicating the study's results and facilitating future research. With continued advancements in deep learning, researchers can expect significant enhancements in communication systems, such as enhanced handoff techniques, which rely on accurate prediction models. Consequently, we expect future research to focus on expanding this approach for predicting various communication system parameters. Notably, unlike existing predictive models, our technique does not rely on assumptions about radio signal patterns or channel characteristics. The essential role of power expansion models is to determine the most efficient capacity investments, including generators, transmission lines, and storage systems, to meet future electricity demands while ensuring reliability and costs are minimized. These models significantly influence the development of electrical systems, shaping the composition of system operators, technology investments, and the low-carbon energy mix. The design of such models is crucial but has largely been overlooked; hence, this research investigates the impact of different model structures on the predicted outcomes and their connections to actual system performance. The investigation reveals that models overemphasize the importance of existing system infrastructure, underestimate the value of distributed and agile investments, and fail to consider the complex interactions within the energy system. To enhance the practicality and effectiveness of power expansion models, this research proposes a method for evaluating and optimizing the responsiveness of these models, defined as their ability to adapt to various system configurations without compromising performance. The study demonstrates that by incorporating representative distributed resources and flexible systems, along with explorations of diverse energy mixes and technology combinations, it's possible to improve the responsiveness of power expansion models. The proposed method is applied to a modified version of the North European power system within the SUMO modeling environment, utilizing a comprehensive set of energy system configurations. The research showcases that by employing this approach, power expansion models can produce more accurate, generalizable results, reflecting the intricate dynamics of the energy system more effectively. These improved outcomes have significant implications for the optimization of electrical systems, including enhanced resource allocation, technology planning, and mitigation strategies. The end-of-the-end scenario development approach also holds value as a versatile tool, encompassing applications such as evaluating policy packages, assessing the efficacy of support programs, and investigating the impact of emerging energy technologies. Ultimately, this research aims to enhance our understanding of power expansion models and encourage the exploration of new approaches that can better capture the complexities of the energy system and guide low-carbon energy development. Secondly, it proves the existence and uniqueness of the solution for these systems. Lastly, it analyzes the continuity of the solutions with respect to their initial conditions. The key challenge in this research lies in handling the ill-posed issue associated with the long-term behavior of the Vlasov-Poisson system, particularly due to the double coupling between the Vlasov equation's non-linear terms and the Poisson equation's solution's free charges. The Collatz Conjecture is a mathematical hypothesis that concerns the sequence of numbers that arises from a specific set of operations applied to a given number. Specifically, if a number is even, it is divided by two, and if it is odd, it is multiplied by one and then rounded down to the nearest whole number. The conjecture asserts that, regardless of the initial value, this sequence eventually enters a cycle and that the conjecture has been extensively computationally verified for an enormous range of possible initial values, but a formal mathematical proof or disproof remains unsolved since its inception in the early 20th century. The numbers confirming the conjecture's sequence are known as "well numbers," and research into them is also still ongoing. The article will delve into the history, the various approaches and some key findings regarding this renowned and intriguing mathematical hypothesis. Additionally, it will cover The Pisinger's algorithm in detail, a high-speed method for computing the Collatz sequence that the author invented and was published in the Journal of Computational and Computational Intelligence in 2021, which is available online at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-30571-5_7. The algorithm has also won the first place in the mathematical competition in the category of algorithms in the year 2021, organized by the European Mathematical Society (EMS), the Slovak Mathematical Union (SMU) and the Scientific and Educational Foundation (SEF), and was selected for the top 5 algorithms in the algorithms final in the year 2022, selected by the European Mathematical Society (EMS), the Slovak Mathematical Union (SMU) and the Algorithmic Executive Committee (AEc). The article will also cover some key findings and the new theoretical bases related to The Pisinger's Algorithm for computing the Collatz Conjecture which were published at the following media: at the Dr. Stefan Pisinger's homepage at https://stufisisinger.wixsite.com/stu as well as at the following social networks at https://www.facebook.com/stufisisinger, as the Pisinger's algorithms for computing the Collatz Conjecture has achieved a significant success and a new chapter in the theoretical bases for computing the Collatz Conjecture has been opened. A novel approach is presented for enhancing the clarity of text in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) documents by incorporating a technique called mathematical entity linking. This method, similar to referring expressions in natural language, identifies and links references to specific mathematical entities within the text. As a starting point, we develop mathematical entity linking capabilities and demonstrate their usefulness in improving the performance of document classification tasks. Our experiments, involving the classification of arXiv documents into various categories using both conventional and mathematical entity featuring methods, reveal a substantial increase in achieving state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, we showcase the potential benefits and clarity gains resulting from mathematical entity replacement in a document. Additionally, to facilitate the interpretation of models, we create a dataset providing detailed mathematical entity annotations for over 20,000 arXiv documents. This dataset and associated pre-trained models are made accessible through an open-source library called MeFine, which is available for public use. Both the dataset and MeFine models can serve as valuable resources for the communities involved in STEM document processing, as well as the broader research and development of scientific language processing. Compressive sensing draws upon sensing technology that takes rapid, quadratic measurements. Anosov et al. initially provided effective recovery guarantees for at least one signal in the presence of white Gaussian noise, with a focus on sensing matrices generated randomly through a Gaussian or Fourier basis. Additional research has been conducted by Soltanahoseini et al., using a rotation-based matrix in their work. Our study expands upon this work by providing guaranteed recovery for all signals under the same random measurement settings. Furthermore, we offer an optimized number of measurements, with a threshold close to the theoretical optimum and adhering to a strict condition. Unlike previous research, our findings apply to general sensing matrices, and a comprehensive proof is presented for the first time. Our method employs a novel 'decoupling' technique in combinatorics, along with a recent result from Arden et al. regarding concentration bounds for character sums. Our optimized algorithm is based on an iterative process of finding the most dominant quadratic measurement and utilizing a search algorithm within the span of secondary-order measurements to locate a basis for the signal. An exhaustive set of techniques, including the simple method of initially subtracting dominant terms and using diophantine approximation, are employed with the aim of providing a practical solution. Our method is shown to have a computational complexity closely aligned with the theoretical optimum, specifically in the range of n to n square root of n, where n represents the signal dimension. An experimental evaluation using synthetic data verifies the efficacy of our proposed algorithm. Lastly, demonstrations of the practical applicability of our method can be seen in actual-world sensing scenarios such as magnetic resonance angiography and audio signal recovery. Within the inner structures of the dissipation range in turbulent flows, mechanical fluctuations induce thermal disturbances through the exchange of momentum. This mechanism is mediated by the local slope of the temperature gradient. In this study, we utilize direct numerical simulations of two-dimensional, shear-flow turbulence to investigate the various scales over which mechanical fluctuations influence the atmosphere. Our primary focus is on the environment of the stratospheric thermal wave, particularly in areas where the thermal wave is driven by the residual circulation resulting from the vertical component of mechanical fluctuations. Using the two-scale approach from theoretical models, we categorize our models based on the relative sizes of the thermal wave and the residual circulation. This allows us to study both the residual circulation-dominated regime, where the thermal wave is large and the momentum transfer is uniform, and the turbulence-dominated regime, where the thermal wave is small and the momentum transfer is localized. In general, our findings confirm that of earlier studies: the residual circulation-dominated regime exhibits multiple-scale energy transfer via inverse cascade, whereas the turbulence-dominated regime exhibits localized forcing of thermal waves. Our investigation into natural language-based extraction of design discussions aims to provide an efficient, time-saving alternative for gathering qualitative design data. This work introduces a novel research metric called VenueRank that offers a simpler alternative to traditional citation indexes. By prioritizing the extensive dissemination of research outside of the core conference and journal circuits, VenueRank scores enable researchers to gauge their influence in spreading knowledge within the scientific community. A comprehensive database containing over 2 million venue records and associated publication counts for around 340,000 researchers, covering more than 30 industries and over 7,500 conferences and journals, has been used to test the effectiveness of VenueRank. By focusing on the top VenueRank and Citation Index scores, our analysis reveals distinct research trajectories. Notably, our study highlights how VenueRank avoids the inherent biases of the citation system, thus providing more accurate and balanced assessments of researchers' achievements. Evaluations also reveal the robustness of VenueRank to varying factors such as industry, career stage, and level of industry engagement. Consequently, VenueRank scores can serve as valuable indicators of researchers' ability to spread new knowledge and ideas within their domain. Inspired by the concept of Google's page rank, VenueRank offers a straightforward and easy-to-compute metric that measures a researcher's vast network of conferences and co-working institutions where their work is widely recognized. A free, open-source tool has been developed to calculate VenueRank scores for both individual researchers and statistical analyses of broader groups. Moreover, our analysis encourages future researchers to focus on the dynamics of research collaboration and development by exploring the evolution of the scientific community's knowledge and interactions. Ultimately, our work serves as a thought-provoking illustration of the countless opportunities that exist for researchers to disseminate new knowledge and ideas beyond their immediate circles. Consequently, the concept of VenueRank serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of collaborative research and knowledge-sharing among various sectors of the scientific community. In light of these findings, the development of VenueRank is positioned to become a valuable alternative to the traditional citation indexes used to measure a researcher's achievements and impact. Clustering is a crucial method for organizing data by grouping elements that exhibit similarity into one system. Despite its utility in various scientific fields, implementing a clustering method that accounts for overlapping groups in a manner that is invariant to rotations and permutations of the data has been a challenging task until recently. We address this challenge by introducing two new algorithms, one of which uses a multi-step process and the other a gradient-based approach, to perform the clustering in a way that is both overlapping and robust to rotations and permutations. We test the algorithms by applying them to synthetic data, images, and a dataset from the field of neuroscience. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the methods in organizing data into groups that make sense regardless of their characteristics. Importantly, the algorithms can be used together to compare the similarity of different groupings and select the most plausible one. We also introduced a method for estimating the importance of each data point to forming groups and found that these values to vary significantly from one dataset to another. Future work may involve the use of these estimates to gain insight into the characteristics of the data. Graph normalization essentially discards node substructures, meaning that more refined substructures are lost. For instance, considering a node having both a broad cluster and a smaller subcluster within it, graph normalization will only conserve the full cluster's membership. Problematically, this discarded subcluster's influence on the node is eliminated. As a result, features from smaller substructures within this node are completely absent in the network. The magnetic field of young stars is thought to be generated through differential rotation and amplified in coronal mass ejections, resulting in numerous magnetic lobes, which could act as magnetic loops producing low-frequency radiation. Low-frequency observations of binary systems such as CR Draconis, consisting of a flare star and a cooler companion, are crucial in understanding these magnetic fields and their role in their unusual radio variability. We utilized the Westerbork Synthesis Radio Telescope to observe CR Draconis over a 12-month period at 18 different epochs, collecting radio data between 34 and 18.6 GHz and discovering radio variability ranging from 10% to 300% with frequent outbursts. We determined the radio spectrum of the stars is consistent with electron-cyclotron maser instability, indicating a coronal scale of ~0.4-1.6 kilometer. We further established a low-frequency lightcurve model, consisting of a 35-day period and a 12.5-day subperiod, explaining 80% of the radio variability and aligning with optical data. We concluded that the radio variability in CR Draconis is likely caused by a unique electron-cyclotron maser instability triggered by coronal mass ejections originating from a magnetic field feature shared between the two components. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the radio emission in CR Draconis is most likely a result of gas flowing along magnetic field loops, possibly triggered by CME events, supporting the theoretical understanding of magnetic field configuration in compact, unstable magnetic fields of single and binary flare stars. We will provide a framework to link the magnetic field configuration in single and binary stars to their astrophysical properties. Moreover, our findings have significant implications for the search for exoplanets around these active stars, the formation of planetary systems, and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI). Finally, our observations will enable us to assess the significance of the radio gap in the lightcurve model of other active star binary systems and help us to identify the most promising targets for future radio and optical monitoring campaigns to explore the role of magnetic fields in these active stars and their planet-forming disks.
