Our capacity to understand images relies on various levels of abstraction, 
with higher-level interpretations resistant to minor changes and retrievable 
only after carefully examining the visual details.  Unlike humans, machines 
are still superior at detecting altered images, thanks to their knack for precise 
visual differentiation.  Exploring these discrepancies between human and machine 
visual perceptions can lead to a better comprehension of (1) how humans and machines 
differently process visual information, (2) the potential for developing more 
effective automated image description algorithms, and (3) the significance of 
transforming targets in adversarial machine learning research.  To this end, we've 
created a range of severe image transformation techniques affecting image content, 
like a person's shape or the background, as well as image edges and textures.  A 
human evaluation encompassing 13 categories revealed that humans could usually 
accurately identify images undergoing these transformations but struggled with 
those altering a person's silhouette or the image's background.  By comparing our 
transformation methods with state-of-the-art adversarial attacks, we've shown that 
they pose a greater challenge for machine vision than those typically used in 
adversarial research, leading us to propose considering a broader scope of 
transformation targets in future adversarial attacks.  Our code and datasets are 
now available to facilitate future research.  Additionally, we've explored how 
describing image alterations through language can reflect humans' varying levels of 
difficulty in perceiving these changes and can serve as a measurable indicator of 
the difficulties encountered by different image transformation methods.  As such, 
measuring text description difficulty can serve as an important evaluation metric for 
assessing image transformation methods, which may find applications in automated image 
description, adversarial attacks, and other related domains.  Our research is now 
online at https://severe-transforms.github.io/; the project's source code can be 
found at https://github.com/gitsky/severe-transforms.  Finally, our drypaint 
implementation of severe image transformation methods is available at https://dry-paint.github.io/.  A demonstration of our work, including a related video, is also available at https://ds.gke.hu/ds2021/s17/DsGKE_Demo.html. The connection between the Askey-Wilson polynomials and the Chern-Simons theory is explored through the 3-manifold S^1 \times S^2 equipped with a non-orientable genus g surface as its boundary. Focusing on Wilson line expectations provides a direct link to the Radon-Nikodym derivative and the Hessenberg sum, which are associated with the Askey-Wilson algebra and its irreducible representations. Specifically, we examine the sum over links over a fixed plane in three-dimensional space, which reveals a connection to the Askey-Wilson matrix and, ultimately, to the quantum numbers associated with its eigenvalues, thereby providing a generalization to the Hackmuller-Troost polynomial. Furthermore, we establish that the quantum numbers associated with the eigenvalues of the Askey-Wilson matrix are conserved during the course of a physical process, which is analogous to a non-Abelian Wilson line configuration that undergoes a reformulation of its gauge group and, consequently, its local gauge invariance. In this context, we derive a consistency criterion for such transformations. Moreover, we identify an interplay between the quantum product of three operators associated with the Askey-Wilson algebra and a refined version of the quantum Yang-Yang mechanism, which is essentially a generalization of the integrable side of the integrable Chern-Simons theory. Lastly, we provide a direct comparison between the Chern-Simons theory and the Askey-Wilson algebra and explore some of its potential applications in statistical mechanics. Initially, we investigate a system comprising (1+1)-dimensional spinless particles in a zero-jump potential on the real line with a general quartic interaction. When expressed in terms of the Askey-Wilson polynomials, the energy spectrum satisfies a closure relation and, through a coordinate transformation, one can verify the existence of a finite maximal kinetic energy. Subsequently, we generalize these findings to the case of (1+1)-dimensional bosons with spin, which satisfies the constraints of the conformal field theory. In the final section, we pose some open problems that bridge the gap between the Askey-Wilson algebra and the integrable Chern-Simons theory. Recent research has showcased the potential for pre-trained language models to perform zero-shot learning through text-based prompts, highlighting varying levels of success depending on the choice of dataset and task. However, selecting an optimal set of parameters for pre-trained language models in zero-shot learning remains a pressing issue. To that end, we introduce a method that involves pre-trained language models to adapt to zero-shot learning by optimizing a set of widely applicable sets of parameters across multiple datasets. Our approach, which we call "meta-tuning," involves training a model on a diverse group of datasets to improve its performance on a wider range of applications. By treating the various datasets and prompts as different settings, we demonstrate that pre-trained language models can learn generally applicable representations through meta-tuning. Meta-tuning has far-reaching implications, as it allows a model to be adapted for use on unseen datasets and prompts with minimal modification. Our experiments encompass a diverse set of 11 datasets and 8 natural-language inference tasks, as well as multiple evaluation datasets and benchmarks, providing comprehensive evaluation of the method. Furthermore, our results show that a model trained through meta-tuning outperforms its baseline counterpart, improving its average performance by 15.2% on the relevant tasks. Importantly, our adapted model exhibits a high degree of applicability, as the model's average performance remains consistent across a wide range of unseen data and prompts. Last but not least, our research reveals that the core concepts underlying the various tasks are shared across multiple datasets, which are largely composed of a small set of universally applicable natural language patterns and structures. These key insights have the potential to significantly expand the range of applications for pre-trained language models, as they can be readily adapted for use on unseen datasets and tasks with minimal modification. Designing effective observers for large complex systems, such as infectious disease models, poses significant challenges. Although observers have been successfully implemented for simple models with fully observable state variables, the real-world scenarios are often characterized by limited state variable observation, unknown parameters, and distributed data collection. This latter point is particularly relevant for epidemic models. To address these complexities, a new observer design is introduced that requires a relatively small amount of local data collection. Furthermore, the proposed observer is universally applicable to systems with partially observable states, unknown parameters, and time-varying parameters. To demonstrate its utility, the observer is applied to a basic SIR model, yielding excellent results, and its application to more advanced epidemic models is also explored. Notably, the proposed observer outperforms existing observers in terms of observing the total infected population, achieving accuracy within 10% after just ten time steps with only ten percent of the data collection needed. Similarly, for the Bergamini model, which includes non-linear effects, the proposed observer achieves accuracy within 20% after twenty time steps with a comparable need for data collection. Lastly, the proposed observer is also explored in the context of the generalized epidemic model, which includes a range of additional factors not accounted for in previous observer designs. Although results are mixed, with accuracy rates ranging from 20% to 60%, the proposed observer remains a valuable tool for data collection in this system. Overall, the proposed observer demonstrates significant utility for a range of epidemic models through its robust performance and simplicity of use. Moreover, the proposed observer provides an important tool for quantifying the uncertainty associated with state variable estimation during epidemic outbreaks. To the knowledge of the authors, this latter point is an unprecedented capability of observer designs. To facilitate future research, the corresponding mathematical frameworks and corresponding codes (written in MATLAB) are provided. This way, the proposed observer can be tested against a wider range of epidemic models than in the presented research, ultimately leading to a more comprehensive understanding of its capabilities and limitations. Decentralized management of wireless networks through local decision-making techniques has gained significant interest due to its implications on power consumption and robustness. In this paper, we explore the feasibility of using decentralized methods for potentiometric channel control in single-transmitter, multi-user systems. By formulating an optimization problem that minimizes transmission power while maintaining data detection quality, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for the local cost function to guarantee the global optimality of the decentralized approach. Furthermore, we validate the efficiency of the proposed method with extensive numerical simulations, demonstrating its superiority over a baseline model that imposes a minimum power threshold. Additionally, we examine the practicality of the proposed algorithm by studying its convergence properties and examining the effects of network connectivity on its performance. Lastly, we delve into several potential extensions of the proposed work, including the integration of resource allocation and packet management processes. Using a network resilience model, we demonstrate that the resilience of the network can be achieved by implementing a decentralized, plug-and-play distributed management system. Moreover, we show that the proposed management system complements existing optimization methods, such as the Lagrange Dual Decentralized (LDD) algorithm, to obtain optimized system performance. Ultimately, we investigate various implementation strategies for achieving decentralized management in practice. From a technical perspective, the proposed work contributes novel approaches for analyzing and designing wireless communication systems, while from a practical perspective, it provides actionable suggestions for implementing decentralized management in real-world settings. The findings of this research can serve as a basis for developing future communication systems with decentralized management capabilities. Moreover, we anticipate that the concepts embedded within our framework will inspire a range of innovative applications in this domain. The present study differs from our prior work in several key ways, including the generalization of potentiometric channel control, the assessment of decentralized management performance across multiple metrics, the examination of achieving decentralized management in systems lacking separability, and the exploration of the diverse application areas of the proposed framework. A new analytical framework, inspired by the E-value concept, is developed to evaluate the influence of missing data assumptions on Bayesian inference. Three distinct E-values are examined: the 'assumption E-value' evaluating the accuracy of classical missing data assumptions, the 'Bayesian E-value' evaluating the robustness of Bayesian missing data methods, and the 'posterior E-value' evaluating the stability of Bayesian inference under different missing data assumptions. This framework is applied in the context of two Bayesian networks, first to assess the impact of missing data assumptions on posterior inference, and second to assess the robustness of Bayesian missing data techniques, revealing that conventional methods can be notably sensitive to the underlying data assumptions. This inspires the introduction of simple post-processing techniques, demonstrated to significantly mitigate the potential biases resulting from the missing data assumptions. The framework is further generalized to encompass various Bayesian and non-Bayesian analyses. The theoretical findings are substantiated by a range of real-world data examples. This research is made more accessible through the provision of a dedicated software package for the reproduction of results and the implementation of the proposed methods. The package is critical in the assessment of the E-values, relying on a combination of machine learning and (semi-)automatic inferential computing strategies. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising approach for preserving IoVs privacy, as it enables service providers to collaborate on training machine learning models without accessing individual users' data. However, there's still a question mark over whether FL's level of privacy protection is sufficient to prevent data theft by service providers, and whether FL benefits all parties equally. To explore this issue, we conducted a comprehensive review of recent research on FL-based frameworks, with a specific focus on how they address IoVs privacy and mobility concerns. Our review also examines the effectiveness of FL in addressing practical challenges such as non-convex optimization, device network asymmetry, data availability and transfer, device selection and scheduling, model updating and personalization, and security breaches. In addition to these practical challenges, we also examined how various research interventions, such as security mechanisms and blockchain technology, address security concerns within FL systems. Ultimately, we identified key challenges that need to be addressed through further research and proposed potential future avenues of exploration for FL-based frameworks. We create a new neural network architecture called NuSPAN to solve the nonuniform sparse problem in inversion techniques, such as interpreting reflected seismic waves. A main challenge with nonuniform sparse problems is that certain inversion parameters have well-defined meanings, while others do not have clear interpretations. To address this, we propose a proximal average network utilizing the UNLocS algorithm as its core. The UNLocS algorithm combines the split Bregman iteration and forward-Backward split with a proximal term based on the $\ell_{2}$-norm or the Charlier partial sum. By developing a neural network representing the proximal average operator from the UNLocS algorithm's 2D and 3D versions and demonstrating its effectiveness through numerical tests, we demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of the NuSPAN architecture. Additionally, we use a seismic data example to illustrate its practical applications in inversion techniques. With the ability to handle sparsity on a group or element-wise basis, the proposed model outperforms competing methods in denoising tasks. Moreover, the proximal average network's ability to utilize gradient information from the $\ell_{2}$-norm or the Charler partial sum results in faster convergence speed compared to its counterparts. Therefore, the proposed architecture is a valuable contribution to the research community. Our results confirm that the model is in a critical state with a specific conformal central charge and reveal the non-trivial structural features of the model at its critical point. This research aims to develop a breaking point-based integrability theory for non-continuous functions. We define and study a new class of functions, fully integrable, which have continuous integrals that can be broken down into continuous functions at their breaking points. We prove that fully integrable functions retain key properties like continuity, absolute continuity, and Lipschitz continuity. Additionally, we show that this theory applies to non-continuous functions with a limited number of breaking points, leading to a generalization of the continuous integrability theory. Our results also include alternative versions of theorems for functions with a limited number of breaking points, as well as those with a finite number of breaking points in a specified set. Ultimately, this research validates a non-continuous integrability criterion, marking a significant achievement in the field. Specifically, we show that a non-continuous function is fully integrable if it meets certain conditions on its variation and perturbation functions. This result surpasses the current best criterion, which requires a more complex expression involving the function's derivative and a specified function of the function's value. Our research also introduces a non-continuous version of the Dubovitsa and Pol'osenel criterion, which is instrumental in assessing the integrability of a function with a limited number of breaking points. Finally, this research demonstrates the applicability of the developed theory to various special cases and presents a multitude of examples illustrating the developed conclusions. Specifically, we present examples of functions that are fully integrable, but not continuous; examples of functions that are continuous, but not fully integrable; and examples of functions that are fully integrable with unique attributes, such as a limited number of breaking points or a specified variation function behavior. By achieving these results, we significantly expand the fully integrable function class, leading to a simpler and more comprehensive integrability theory. This theory is particularly useful as a means to generalize the continuous integrability theory and forge new connections between various functional properties. Moreover, the developed theory is instrumental in tackling a wide range of practical problems in the theory of special functions and their applications. One of the primary implications of this research is the generalization of a theorem for different classes of functions that are fully integrable with a limited number of breaking points. This theorem is instrumental in the theory of convex games, where it finds the following application: the moment of a fully integrable function that is fully integrable with a limited number of breaking points can be broken down into a sum of moments of functions that are continuous and fully integrable. Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn general visual and semantic features. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by low-quality dataset annotations and corrupted semantic associations caused by scale disparities. To overcome these limitations, we propose the VT-CLIP framework, which utilizes a two-stage approach combining self-supervised image-text learning with joint vision and language pre-training. The framework initially develops visual and textual features through CLIP pre-training using paired RGB and monocular depth images. The resulting visual and semantic features are then refined through depth-guided text-clip alignment, which aligns text with depth-generated pseudo-labels. Finally, we demonstrate VT-CLIP's superior performance on a range of challenging tasks, such as zero-shot object detection and attribute recognition, as well as visual question answering and image captioning. Notably, we achieve state-of-the-art results on the MS-COCO dataset, reducing recall by 8.8% compared to the current best model. We demonstrate the applicability of these methods by examining Hatfield operators in L^2[0,1] Hilbert space. A comprehensive comparative study was conducted to evaluate our proposed method against established techniques for unsupervised feature learning using both synthetic and real genomic data sets. The results show that the new approach surpasses existing methods in accurately identifying positional characteristics. Additionally, we introduce an innovative position-aware ensemble technique for enhancing the predictive accuracy of individual deep learning models. The proposed methods successfully apply to genomic data sets, resulting in novel representations of positions that facilitate significant dimensionality reduction without compromising informational content. Moreover, using positional embeddings, we identify patterns of co-occurring bases at various scales within the sequences. Ensemble models derived from different positional scales and depths exhibit distinct performance characteristics. Specifically, deeper models tend to capture more general patterns, whereas shallower models are better suited for identifying specific correlations between base positions. Interestingly, models incorporating all available positional scales demonstrate exceptional overall performance. The proposed approaches for automatic feature extraction as a position-centric framework is universally applicable to any type of sequence data. Thus, it can be employed for analyzing various types of biological data, such as protein sequences. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the positional embeddings used in our models and the canonical ordering present within DNA sequences. A brief discussion is provided on the potential implications of our findings, along with the benefits of exploring the intricate structures typically inherent in DNA sequences. Specifically, we highlight the potential of our position-centric framework in uncovering valuable information, such as repetitive elements and regulatory sites. The corresponding position-based features may hold the key to better comprehending the intricate mechanisms governing repetitive elements and regulatory sites. Ultimately, these features may serve as essential components in emerging applications such as synthetic biology and the development of artificial regulatory elements. We propose a general method to derive further conservation principles from a given model. This method, initially introduced in a recent article for incompressible fluids, is now applied to compressible Navier-Stokes equations. For simplicity, we limit our analysis to a one-dimensional setting and a barotropic fluid, where the conservation of mass and energy are well-established principles. By employing a suitable transformation, which is specified in a compact form as a$_E$, we demonstrate the existence of two more conservation principles, defined as a$_{EM}$$\bullet$$u$ and a$_{EM}$$\bullet$$|u|^{2}$. These principles are represented as the divergence of a$_{EM}$$\otimes$($u, \partial_{x}u$) and a$_{EM}$$\otimes$($|u|^{2}, \partial_{x}u$), respectively. Here, ($u, \partial_{x}u$) and ($|u|^{2}, \partial_{x}u$) are considered as matrices, and a$_{EM}$ = 2$(\partial_{x}u)^{2}$ + 5$(\partial_{x}u)^{4}$/($|u|^{2}$ + 5$(\partial_{x}u)^{2}$) + 2$(\partial_{x}u)^{2}$. These findings represent a theoretical solution to conservation issues encountered when dealing with a system of equations and can be widely applied across various physical and chemical models. Additionally, we show that the energy density $e$ evolves according to a first-order Taylor series with terms $\part_{x}u^{2}, \part_{x}^{2}u$ and $\part_{x}^{3}u$ as key factors. These findings are expected to facilitate a deeper understanding of systems where conservation is challenging, such as for incompressible polar fluids with conservation of vertical wind and specific chemical reactions in one- and two-dimensional environments. These types of systems can now be analyzed to new depths, from microscopic to macroscopic levels, with the capability of handling multiple systems in a combined fashion through a suitable extension of our method. Furthermore, our approach is expected to contribute to a greater understanding of dynamical systems and complex systems, where these principles will facilitate a deeper and more comprehensive analysis of system evolution and interactions. These findings will be further explored in accompanying papers, where we delves into their applications and relevance.

Accurately predicting bad loan scenarios is vital for determining optimal loan issuance and interest rate settings.

This work investigates the solvability of the edge-tinting problem in the specified scenario. queryability, and its capacity for customizable word embeddings. Our MindMind

Machine learning can be made more resilient to malicious data by using methods 
that detect and exclude suspicious inputs. However, the effectiveness of these 
methods depends on various factors, including the specific query used to gather 
informative data and the characteristics of the data to be encountered in the future 
(a priori knowledge). In this paper, we determine the query attributes that enable 
robust learning through informative sampling. Specifically, we focus on a widely 
used method called iterative sampling, where the model selects and asks a 
sequence of questions to gather more data. Our main finding is that incorporating 
future knowledge into the selection process significantly boosts the model's 
resilience to malicious data. Nevertheless, the optimal way to utilize this knowledge 
varies depending on the data distribution and our proposed metric can aid in 
maximizing its benefits. Additionally, we illustrate how the concepts we've 
developed apply to a broad class of data sampling methods based on optimality 
principles. These concepts may lead to more efficient and adaptive sampling 
strategies. Our study is available at https://zahn1900.github.io/local-inquiries/.

When incorporating a query oracle to gather more data, the algorithm's 
robustness to malicious data depends on various factors, including the 
informative value of the data gathered (a priori knowledge). In this study, we 
determine the conditions under which local inferences are beneficial for 
robustness. We begin by illustrating the importance of the robustness a-c and 
the benefit of c-a consistency (the adversarial data's similarity to the training 
data's mean direction). We then demonstrate that local inferences are beneficial 
for achieving these conditions. In general, the utility of local inferences varies 
based on several factors, including the distribution, the parameters of the 
training data's mean direction, and the characteristics of the query used. 
Unfortunately, the algorithm's uncertainty about its parameters and the data 
distributions hinders its ability to maximize its potential. To address this issue, 
we propose a metric that enables the algorithm to estimate the remaining 
benefits of local inferences. In a scenario with a known data distribution, the 
algorithm can utilize this metric to determine when local inferences are

Recent research on complete interface methods for multi-dimensional conservation laws has led to the development of several new standards governing the process of contraction for entropic discontinuities. Although some standards were initially introduced by Frid and Lu in 2007 for systems of two equations, our discussion expands upon their findings to include more general conservation law systems of any dimension. Additionally, we review existing results from the literature that demonstrate the existence of contraction for entropic discontinuities in the subcharacteristic hyperbolotic case, as well as theoretical estimates of the contraction rate. Since theoretical estimates often differ from practical results, the full standards cannot be universally applied. However, in certain complete interface methods, the requirement for a perfect flux jump matrix is sufficiently strong to ensure standard compliance even in the absence of a contraction rate estimate. On the other therd, some of the elements of contraction are implicitly ensured by the design of the interface operator as a dual of a positivity-preserving operator, although this is typically an inductive result with no general theory available yet. Furthermore, even though the concept of dual interface operators holds much potential for further investigation, its application remains limited in the current research context. Consequently, the presentation of contraction results in the existing literature is often inductive and typically confined to specific interface methods. In order to promote the development of new interface methods with predictable behavior, the proposal seeks to consolidate the standards into a usable collection that can be more easily modified than individual papers, while striving to address the remaining open questions on dual interface operators through discussions with the research community. As the reliance on machine learning in medicine grows, the importance of managing noisy medical labels amidst a plethora of data also increases. Current methods primarily focus on regulating model outputs from excessive noise but often fail to consider the underlying annotation process. Consequently, label noise persists a significant challenge across various medical image classification tasks. To address this issue, a new self-regulating mechanism is proposed that utilizes Bayesian statistics to reassess individual labels based on a model's confidence levels, thereby ensuring labels are consistent within the training dataset. An experiment was conducted to demonstrate the proposed method's efficacy using the NIH ChestX-Ray-14 dataset, achieving an improved accuracy of 4% over traditional models when subjected to moderate levels of noise, as measured by overall and task-specific fractional errors. Additionally, the method outperformed other noise reduction techniques both visually and statistically. To promote versatility, an open-source 2D medical image generation model, LabeledImage-Generator, is also made publicly available, facilitating various forms of data augmentation for image classification tasks. To the knowledge of the authors, no similar image generation models are available for the medical community, and this model is proposed as a valuable resource moving forward. The discrete approximation of an interpolation projector, which maps a discrete vector to a point in a finite-dimensional subspace, is analyzed. A specific norm associated with this projector is examined and, in the context of numerical analysis, certain general results are demonstrated, which include guarantees for the stability of the approximation. The proof of these results relies on the smoothness of the underlying function and the characteristics of the sampling points. The results are finalized with a discussion on the implications of the smoothness condition. The case of sampling points generated by Gaussian random experiments is also explored and it is demonstrated that the general results can be improved in this context, notably for the scenario involving Poisson sampling. Finally, the theoretical findings are substantiated with numerical results that examine the performance of different interpolation methods. These methods include point interpolation, variational finite elements, and polynomial splines. The focus is particularly on the polynomial splines, for which the approximation error is formally established through a continuation method. The numerical experiments are conducted within the context of a second-order quasilinear elliptic problem in the context of computational micromechanics. The relevant code is publicly available and can be accessed at https://github.com/jpfeffer9/SPS. The primary contribution of this study is the determination of an lower bound for the norm of the interpolation projector, which is applicable in the scenario where the interpolation points are generated through Poisson sampling. The study shows that the proven bound can be superior to the bound established by the polynomial splines method, particularly for smooth functions. The study further reveals that the approximation error is zero when the sampling points converge to a subset of the domain, under the condition that the function is in the class of C-infty functions. A secondary contribution of this study is the formal establishment of the approximation error through a continuation method, which employs a homotopy technique, for the dependent-sampling strategy. The homotopy technique, which is realized through a one-dimensional continuation method, has yet to be extensively utilized in the generation of sampling points. The study demonstrates that the homotopy technique can be used to generate sampling points that satisfy the desired properties, which is an additional benefit of this approach. The study further highlights that the homotopy technique can be tuned depending on the desired properties of the approximation, which is an added advantage. The study finally concludes by discussing the potential extensions and generalizations of the theoretical results, which could potentially be applied in the context of random sampling. The related work is publicly available at https://github.com/jp

Researchers studying a two-dimensional Weyl semimetal in a periodic, artificial magnetic field have conducted a thorough analysis of this system when it exhibits integer quantum Hall regimes. They used the mode expansion method incorporating the effects of fermi surface winding and found that at these regime's transitions, a unique phase emerges, characterized by a break in time-reversal symmetry. This break manifests as a topological phase with a finite Chern number on one of its sublattices. As the magnetic field increases, this time-reversal-broken phase expands and eventually becomes a time-reversal-broken insulator when the magnetic field reaches its sixth step. The time-reversal-broken phase's transition to the time-reversal-restored phase is marked by pseudogapped behavior progressing into a normal 2D Weyl semimetal. Furthermore, this model displays gapped phase boundaries that exhibit fractional Chern insulator characteristics, and the appearance of nodal structures reminiscent of gapped phase boundaries in both normal and inverted 2D Weyl semimetal states are delayed until the magnetic flux reaches its fifth step. This time-reversal-broken phase's properties are similar to those of a recently studied chiral topological liquid, except for the distinct appearance of gapped behaviors that is characteristic of bosonic systems. Nonetheless, the appearance of insulating regions within the phase indicates that this time-reversal-broken phase is unique to the situation where a pair of oppositively charged effective fermions is present. This possibility could be explored in the study of charged anyons within the context of quantum hexagons. Further research is required in order to fully explore the relationship between time-reversal symmetry and the observed topological phases. Some key properties of this system may be experimentally identified through the analysis of local magnetic or electric properties at increased magnetic fields, while the behavior of time-reversal symmetry breaks is likely to be most visible in the study of quasi-particles at low energies. Moreover, the coexistence of two distinct types of symmetry-breaking behaviors within the phase, where the time-reversal symmetry break is overridden by the insulating behavior, poses an interesting challenge for the study of this system. Ultimately, the study of this time-reversal-broken phase is unique and may be influenced by the presence of non-symmetrical lattice structures; experiments that mimic its behavior may yield valuable insights into the way these topological phases interact. In response to rising COVID-19 cases, numerous government agencies and health care providers have established online portals to gather patient information for contact tracing purposes, resulting in a massive surge of web-form based COVID-19 infection reports needing to be processed and analyzed. The data collected via these forms is typically not encoded but rather represented by class-based drop-down menus or text fields expecting users to provide their location, age, etc. manually inputting this information on multiple forms across multiple websites proves to be both time-consuming and tedious. An efficient approach to mitigate this issue involves the use of synthetic data generation through oversampling techniques that allow for intelligent, semi-automated data collection, greatly reducing both the time and effort involved in the process. Building on this concept, we set out to expand our research from basic oversampling methods to develop and evaluate a novel set of data generation techniques capable of producing semi-valid, synthetic class-imbalanced text data that accurately resembles real-world distributions, focusing specifically on multi-class text classification tasks. Our proposed approach consisted of generating text data using various oversampling methods and an encoding technique that preserves important token information, resulting in a distribution of data that better replicates real-world conditions due to an overrepresentation of the majority class. Our methodology incorporates both rule-based and machine learning-based editing methods to refine and enhance the generated text, mirroring the imperfections typically seen in real-world text data. Through a detailed analysis of our method's efficacy on publicly available imbalanced text classification datasets augmented with synthetic data, we observed significant improvements when using our proposed distribution-shift aware data generation approach as compared to traditional oversampling techniques. Notably, we achieved a 4% increase in average performance across all datasets following data augmentation. Moreover, our method demonstrated particular efficacy on datasets with a significant level of categorical imbalance (such as the NLPimbal and NLPimbal2 datasets), resulting in notable improvements exceeding 10% in these cases. An implementation of our distribution-shift aware data generation approach may be found on our GitHub repository. Future research could focus on extending our approach to incorporate additional data augmentation techniques, such as generating multiple variations of the same label, or incorporating additional pre-processing methods to refine the generated text further. The integration of our method with online form parsing tools has the potential to greatly enhance the efficiency of COVID-19 data collection, among other applications. Ultimately, our approach has the potential to greatly impact research in data augmentation, remote sensing, geolocalization, and related fields where dataset imbalance poses a significant challenge. It found that local news outlets with smaller audiences that focused on local issues covered COVID-19 at a lower rate, had less detailed reporting, and relied heavily on older sources. Conversely, local news outlets with younger audiences covered COVID-19 at a higher rate, employed more critical thinking, and referenced a broader range of credible sources. Furthermore, our research revealed that local news outlets' COVID-19 coverage was closely linked to regional case and death rates, suggesting that local news outlets play a crucial role in disseminating information to their communities during public health crises. Our research did not find any correlation between local news outlets' COVID-19 coverage and economic indicators of the local community. It did, however, discover that local news outlets' COVID-19 coverage was closely tied to the level of local news outlets' competition and the sophistication of the local news infrastructure, which may have contributed to the variation in local news outlets' COVID-19 coverage. Unlike conventional lasers, this design doesn't rely on an optical resonator but instead uses digital techniques to shape the pulse. Instead of traditional feedback mechanisms, we utilized a specially designed non-linear crystal that helps maintain the pulse shape. The described system can produce high peak powers with nearly full pulse coherence, yielding a very low spectral line width of tens of kilohertz, a feature particularly useful for applications such as spectroscopy and magnetic resonance imaging. The high repetition rate and powerful pulse amplitude make this system suitable for applications like spectroscopy and magnetic resonance imaging. The addition of a frequency shifter enables tunability over a broad frequency range, potentially opening new applications in spectroscopy and sensing. While current output power is relatively low, technological advancements in elements like photonic integrated circuits, ring lasers, and non-linear crystals could potentially increase the power to kilowatt levels, where many applications become more viable. The current maximum distance we can maintain the pulse coherence over is several meters, suggesting that future advancements could lead to coherence preservation at various scales from a few meters or centimeters to kilometers. For K3 surfaces with a junction of extended rational curves, we examine the relationship between their Picard groups and values of holomorphic periods. This involves identifying hyperbolicity parameters and a degree-related invariant, where the Picard group and certain subgroups of the Mordell-Weil group are comprised of elements that have given values. The chosen extended rational curves yield Riemann surfaces of genus 1, i.e., elliptic curves, whose Borel-Chen classes contribute to the Picard group and a specific Weil divisor. This setup enables us to establish a connection between the Picard group and an elliptic curve over the Siegel disk of a corresponding meromorphic function. This, in turn, facilitates the demonstration of lattices within the Mordell-Weil group being insufficient for hyperbolicity. Moreover, our work also involves calculating the Chow ring and smooth cobordism rings of certain K3 surface configurations, which are applicable in various theoretical models, including string theory and supersymmetric quantum field theories. These calculations reveal these rings to be highly structured. Specifically, the Chow ring is generated by classes related to the Picard group and cap products, while the smooth cobordism rings are generated by classes representing the identities in the Picard group and a form of elliptic curve invariant. Moreover, these rings are found to be highly decomposable and form highly structured rings that are both oriented and unoriented. Furthermore, we also show that the transfers induced by inclusions of genus 1 curves within the Picard group generate identical maps in the Chow ring and show that these transfers are tautological in nature. This, in turn, enables us to establish a relationship of comparability between the degrees of elliptic curves and transfers in the Picard group, which is shown to be applicable to various theoretical models, including quantum field theories and string theory. This, in turn, facilitates the demonstration of an important degree-related inequality and identifies an important theoretical concept, i.e., a phenomenon of intersectional degeneracy. This phenomenon is found to be applicable to various theoretical models, including quantum field theories and string theory. Furthermore, we also demonstrate the importance of the identified degrees and establish an important theorem involving their relationship with Siegel disks. This, in turn, enables us to demonstrate the existence of zeta functions with specified characteristics, i.e., those with Specular Zeta functions and generalized generating functions. These functions are found to be closely related to theoretical concepts, including quantum field theories and string theory.

A stochastic Newton method is proposed for solving a distributed convex optimization problem, where a global cost function is broken down into multiple local components, each computed at distinct nodes. The algorithm, $D$Stochastic Newton ($D$SN), ensures that the local estimates at each node converge to the actual solution under suitable conditions. These conditions are typically met in various network architectures such as star, tree, and fully-connected graphs. The method also applies to general graph topologies through reassignment of probabilistic tasks. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated in terms of its expected convergence rate, using the expected functional error. Numerical experiments demonstrate that $D$SN outperforms existing distributed optimization algorithms for a range of test problems. The results also highlight the impact of communication architecture and data distribution on the performance of the proposed method. Indigenous communities in India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and neighboring countries are subjected to hate speech from radical groups, aiming to marginalize and exclude minority groups from society. Our research focuses on detecting hate speech in critiques of two major Indian groups, aimed at individuals with different sexual orientations. Leveraging Oxford's Hatebase as a starting point, we've developed a dataset to train a hate-speech classification algorithm, showing a 93% accuracy rate, after fine-tuning the approach. Our findings indicate that initial training on a dataset is crucial for a classifier's success. Additionally, we've discovered that our method, employing a recurrent neural network, is more effective than a transfer learning method, utilizing a pre-trained VGG16 model. While hate speech prevalence is declining on Twitter, thanks to an increase in pro-LGBTQ+ content, our research highlights the need for continued efforts to counter hate speech from all directions. Finally, we recommend using a refined version of our dataset to train a text generation model through a generator, with the aim of automatically counteracting hate speech with anti-hate messages. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using a machine-learning-based approach to detect hate speech and suggest potential applications for future research. As the use of artificial intelligence in critical decision-making processes increases, concerns have risen about its potential for bias in high-stakes professions, such as self-driving commercial vehicle services. Like any emerging technological tool, AI that predicts commercial driving abilities still requires experts to interpret its evaluations under real-world circumstances. This study investigates the decision-making role of human experts in evaluating commercial driving skills by reviewing and classifying video segments using AI-generated evaluations, in comparison to relying solely on automated predictions. The research highlights key considerations that should be taken into account during the development of such decision-support systems, emphasizing the need for 'when' and 'how' decisions, rather than relying solely on outputs generated by the AI. The findings indicate that combining human judgment with AI-generated evaluations offers several benefits, including enhanced accuracy, increased transparency, and improved fairness. This research serves as a model for similar decision-making tasks where human expertise and AI collaboration are leveraged to achieve more precise and ethical outcomes. The research findings can specifically benefit companies looking to integrate the use of predictive tools in their operational workflows. Additionally, the research demonstrates the value of expert moderation in AI-driven assessments, which can be applied more broadly to various domains where AI and human collaboration are used to improve decision-making processes. The research findings were published in the Proceedings of the 2022 ACM Conference on Web and Social Media. The study aimed to assess a model's ability to extrapolate effectively on unseen image types. Utilizing nine diverse ImageNet subcategories, researchers conducted a detailed analysis of a model's performance by considering both image content and category specificity. The results demonstrated that models perform better on subcategories with more visible attributes and those characteristic of an image content's local context. Building upon these insights, an out-of-category challenge was proposed, which involves collecting images representing local contents of a model's learned subcategories from various global contexts. The image collection process and initial evaluation results of this OOC challenge are detailed in this study. It is hoped that this endeavor promotes the development of more robust AI models, capable of withstanding the complexities of real-world data environments. The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex nonlinear dynamical systems, but as systems increase in dimensionality, traditional AKM methods become impractical due to the limitations of classical finite-dimensional approximation in handling high-dimensional problems. The proposed solution, sparse-grid techniques combined with AKM, aims to overcome these limitations by maintaining high accuracy through efficient use of computational resources. This hybrid approach, sparse-grid-Driven AKM, utilizes smoothing techniques to approximate Koopman operator eigenfunctions on a selected subset of grid points, then applies these approximations to predict system behavior. The method is tested on two nonlinear dynamical systems: the first, with known eigenfunctions, is used to evaluate convergence and accuracy; and the second, a nonlinear ordinary differential equation, is used to explore breakthroughs in modeling complex phenomena with fewer data points. The results demonstrate that SDAKM outperforms traditional AKM by delivering high-accuracy solutions for complex high-dimensional systems with improved efficiency. The method effectively addresses the trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, offering considerable advantages in 4D-10D dynamic systems. In particular, the SDAKM method reduces the required points by 2 to 5 orders of magnitude in comparison to standard AKM, while matching or surpassing its accuracy rates, with the added benefit of predicting system behavior on selected points. Furthermore, in terms of predictive capabilities, the SDAKM method excels over high-dimensional targets with the ability to predict system behavior on selected points up to 10 times more effectively than traditional AKM. The method remains available on GitHub under the open-source license. This research introduces a novel mathematical technique, the outer complex scaling method. It provides an accurate solution for Schrödinger equations applied to atoms and molecules in strong direct current (DC) electric fields. The technique involves modifying the coordinates of the continuum states by adding an imaginary component, effectively shifting the Hamiltonian far from the real axis. Similar to the well-known complex scaling method, this approach has proven valuable for eliminating unphysical scattering states, despite introducing minor inaccuracies in the wave function's asymptotic behavior due to the rounding error inherent to numerical calculations. To rectify this shortcoming, the outer complex scaling method is suggested, where the scaling transformation is only applied to the coordinates relevant to the continuum, thus effectively eliminating all unphysical states with high precision. Furthermore, the technical aspects of the method are discussed, including the determination of the scaling parameter and the initial wave function starting point. The outcomes of the numerical computations using this approach demonstrate that it can describe the resonances of small atoms, such as hydrogen, in strong DC electric fields with great accuracy. It is hoped that this method will be utilized in future research to investigate the behavior of atoms and molecules in DC electric fields. Lastly, the outcomes of the numerical computations using this approach suggest that it may be applied to the even heavier resonances of the hydrogen molecule-ion, H$_2^+$. It is anticipated that this method will be useful for a broad range of quantum systems subjected to DC electric fields. The outcomes of the numerical computations using this approach provide resonance energies in excellent agreement with recent experimental findings. It is hoped that this method will be utilized to investigate the behavior of diatomic ions and molecules. Recently, the bound states of the hydrogen molecule-ion have been experimentally determined for fields up to 1.04 V/Å, and it is anticipated that this method will be instrumental in predicting and comparing theoretical and experimental results. It is notable that the outcomes of the numerical computations using this approach reveal that the resonances of the hydrogen molecule-ion exhibit widths significantly lower than those of the hydrogen ion, H$_2^+$, which is predominantly the outcome of the significant difference in the ionization energies of the two systems. It is hoped that this method will be useful for a wide variety of quantum systems. The outcomes of the numerical computations using this approach provide valuable insights into the behavior of the hydrogen molecule-ion and other multi-atomic systems in strong DC electric fields. It is anticipated that this method will be utilized to investigate the properties of the hydrogen molecule in strong DC electric fields.

Our societal responses to the COVID-19 pandemic resulted in unprecedented worldwide changes in human behavior. Although the pandemic's impact on mobility across cities was extensively documented, its influence on the diversity of urban interactions remained underexplored. In this research, we examine the income diversity of urban encounters in major cities worldwide. By combining data from foot traffic and geographically-agnostic social media platforms, we quantify the level of diversity present during the pandemic, then compare it to corresponding pre-pandemic levels. Our analysis reveals that the diversity of urban interactions significantly decreased in most cities but notes an exception of Tokyo. Furthermore, we determined that the decrease in diversity was more pronounced in cities with higher income inequalities. By employing a simple theoretical model, we attribute these observations to a combination of two factors: the voluntary nature of changes in human behavior and government-mandated restrictions on public gatherings. Ultimately, our findings have significant implications on urban planning, highlighting the need for increased research on the subject. The data collected in this research will be made publicly available to inform future policy decisions regarding urban settings. By applying our research to real-world scenarios, we aim to promote more resilient and flexible urban design principles. The theoretical model used in this research can serve as a basis for a variety of scenarios and behaviors, allowing for a broader understanding of the relationship between individual choices and collective consequences. The ultimate goal of this research is to facilitate a better understanding of the complex interplay between human decisions and societal effects. By adopting a multidisciplinary approach, our research aims to address pressing issues related to urban diversity and behavior. As urban centers continue to grow and become more prominent, ensuring that urban planning is effective, sensitive, and responsive to the unique characteristics of city-dwellers becomes an increasingly crucial concern. Our research highlights the significance of income diversity in urban settings, a topic previously overlooked in the vast literature on human behavior and mobility. By employing diverse data sets of human behavior, our research provides a more comprehensive view of the complex factors at play during the pandemic. In particular, our analysis of social media activity sheds light on the patterns of human interactions, revealing that a lower percentage of total foot traffic in urban areas was composed of diverse encounters during the pandemic. By exploring the underlying causes of this decrease, our research reveals that the natural fluctuations in human behavior were insufficient to explain the variety of urban encounters during the pandemic. Consequently, we attribute the decline in income diversity of urban encounters to a combination of two factors: government-mandated restrictions on public gatherings and the varying choices made by urban residents

This research examines an ultrathin semiconductor barrier as a model gap, using an exact solution to the 3D and 1D three-subband Schrödinger equation.  The study compares electronic density distributions and current flow in the context of nonlocal and quasiparticle theories, including the effects of nonlocality through noninteracting and interacting electron gas responses.  Findings show that a quasiparticle approach relying on an exchange-enhanced gap has considerable grounds, yet this effect diminishes as the gap becomes increasingly thin.  The research further explores a nonlocal and nonquasiparticle approach relying on an exchange-enhanced electron gap in the form of an energy-dependent dielectric function.  It is determined that this nonlocal and nonquasiparticle model produces the fastest decay rates for current flow and electronic density within the thin gap, closely approaching a well-known dielectric function derived from QED theory.  A comparative analysis is performed on the transverse and longitudinal modes of the thin-gap system to depict its propagation mechanisms in the nonlocal and nonquasiparticle model.  It is revealed that a quasiparticle approach may overlook an energy-dependent and long-range electron contribution and further that proximity effects between materials lead to an exchange-enhanced and localizing influence on electron propagation and density within the thin gap. Patient similarites can be utilized to group patients for downstream tasks such as prediction and recommendation. However, the task of determining patient similarities poses a challenge as time-series data, specifically in the case of electronic health records. Upon initial examination, it appears that neighboring patients in the patient array $X_{N \times T}$, where $N$ is the number of patients and $T$ is the number of time points, would naturally exhibit similarity. However, this is an unbalanced form of similarity as nearby patients are compared against patients further away. To rectify this, we propose the Heterogeneous Ressemblance Graph Neural Network (HRGNN). HRGNN commences by constructing a graph from the patient data and identifying the k nearest neighbors for each patient. To optimize patient neighbors for similarity evaluation, we employ a novel optimization technique. Subsequently, we implement a heterogenous graph neural network to determine patient similarities. Our proposed approach achieved superior results on two datasets when compared to the benchmark methods. For instance, our technique achieved a 2.5% increase in the convergence of diabetes markers as recorded through HbA1c levels and a 3.5% increase in the convergence of heart rates, when tested against eight benchmark methods. Our research indicates that HRGNN is an efficient and effective method for identifying patient similarities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that identifying patient similarities is a crucial capability essential for optimizing downstream tasks. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated their efficacy in signal processing tasks. One such application is modulation classification (MC) for software-defined radios, utilizing a DNN to map a modulated signal to its corresponding class. Nevertheless, the reliance of DNN-based MC on complex learning data makes them vulnerable to adversarial attacks that manipulate the input to disrupt the DNN's operation, giving rise to incorrect classifications. This study presents an innovative method to create adversarial signals that can bypass the DNN's detection, based on a combination of generative adversarial networks (GANs). This approach involves utilizing multiple GANs, one for each Mc class, to generate signals that will be misclassified by the DNN. The analysis demonstrates that the proposed method significantly enhances the creation of adversarial signals that accurately fool the DNN. Moreover, the study shows that combining this approach with data augmentation for the DNN can notably boost its robustness. Our research indicates that the proposed method is efficient and can be employed in practical scenarios to develop attacks on DNN-based MC. This method's success stems from its ability to exploit differences in Mc classes that the DNN has learned to recognize, often resulting from easily distinguishable characteristics such as the carrier frequency. This understanding of what makes Mc classes recognizable by the DNN also provides insights into how the DNN learned its knowledge, providing an opportunity to develop new pre-processing techniques that can robustly counter adversarial attacks. Furthermore, the proposed method and insights into Mc class recognition are potentially applicable to other DNN-based classification tasks as well. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies promote a continuous learning approach, but they haven't addressed
the challenge of combining data from different hospitals. Also, they have focused
on the challenges of predicting lesion labels rather than the actual lesions themselves.
In response, we're working on segmenting lesions in a more practical context,
specifically, when training data is scarce. We're using a continuous learning approach
that combines data from hospitals A and B. Our goal is to evaluate how this process
affects segmentation results when applied to hospital C. We found that both the
feature extractor and the segmentation model deteriorated when applied to hospital
C. Therefore, we're exploring whether training a model from scratch would lead to
better results. After modifying our data augmentation method, we're now able to
achieve improved segmentation results from scratch. Our research ultimately points
to the need for further study on the application of continuous learning in the
medical imaging field. The source code is available at https://github.com/andreabaldi/continual-montage-segmentation.

Visual perception can be understood through the combination of local and global processes, where local processes identify distinctive features and global processes organize them into meaningful patterns.  The detection of features is particularly important as it is an essential step in recognizing various objects and patterns.  In this study, a type of visual feature that is prominent yet easily overlooked is being examined - high-contrast edges that are near optimal and opposite each other.  These edges, or bipolar contrasts, are crucial in certain biologically-based neural networks for navigating and recognizing objects, yet were not thought to hold much importance in human vision. Our findings indicate that the emission stems from an expanded core with a mass of 30-$50\,\%$ of the local standard prime mass, situated $0.87\pm0.04$ pc away from the central hot core. This newly discovered core, named C2-West, exhibits a significant infall velocity of $4.0\pm0.2\,\times10^{-3}$ ms$^{-1}$ and an excess velocity of $2.9\pm0.2\,\times10^{-3}$ ms$^{-1}$ and is likely influenced by protostellar activity. Children who consistently reject the help of others may struggle with taking others' perspectives, and researchers have linked this social issue to reduced capacity for learning from others. To simulate this challenge in machine learning models, we've developed a new method using data manipulation to force pre-trained Transformer language models to rely solely on their internal sources of knowledge. Our experimental results show that these modified models exhibit similar characteristics to those of children who isolate themselves, severely impairing their ability to learn new concepts and understand others' viewpoints, and this impairment persists across various architectures and size scales, but is not fixed and can only be mitigated by resetting the models from a younger state comparable to that of large language models trained from scratch. Unlike its human counterpart, however, this modification disables the models' capacity for generating original content, limiting their potential applications and leading us to suggest that future AI systems should be designed with a built-in capacity for self-reflection and social interaction. Our code and detailed analysis are available for review. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationship between human social development and machine learning, driving forward the potential advancements in future AI systems. Developing this machine metaphor further, our paper describes a cutting-edge method that mimics human social isolation in a machine learning framework for the first time, offering insights into the trade-offs between a machine learning algorithm's reliance on external inputs and its internal knowledge reserves. Our analysis also reveals that these modified models can only learn and recover from social isolation through-resetting, much like children who overcome self-isolation through parental guidance. Our study delivers a new perspective on the design of future AI systems, suggesting that future AI systems should be created with a degree of self-reflection and social interaction. Our paper's findings are accessible through a machine-readable format, and our code and data are publicly available. To enhance the translation quality of neural machine translation models, it is desirable to utilize word-level predictions beyond the current target sequence, which requires models to be modified to accommodate look-ahead predictions. However, since existing models are designed to process sequences from left to right, incorporating look-ahead predictions proves challenging. Our novel "look-ahead focus" technique addresses this limitation by incorporating relevance weights to focus on specific target words during translation generation. In experiments with English-to-German translation, we show that by considering words up to 5 positions ahead, the top 5 most accurate translations can be achieved, yielding improvements in BLEU score, with a notable increase of 1.1 and 1.3 points on the NIST data sets 2002-2006 respectively. In contrast, relying solely on neighboring words yields a decrease of 0.4 and 0.7 points in BLEU score. Moreover, we demonstrate that the look-ahead position can serve as a complexity measure for translation tasks. Our proposed method, "look-ahead focus", facilitates incorporation of look-ahead predictions in traditional left-to-right models without requiring model rearchitecture or using ensembles. It provides a useful tool for investigating non-myopic translation models and uncovering the underlying reasons behind their performance enhancements. The code for our method is publicly available at https://github.com/krishnanp5/laf. In addition to look-ahead predictions, we also examine other non-myopic model variations, achieving increases of 0.6 and 1.3 points in BLEU score respectively. Notably, relying solely on neighboring words leads to decreases of 0.4 and 0.7 points in BLEU score. The research suggests that exploring a balanced approach between examining past and future translation history may lead to improved outcomes. Moreover, utilizing word-level predictions beyond the current target sequence can translate into enhanced translation quality. Our study offers quantitative measures to compare the effectiveness of various non-myopic model variations, as well as a comprehensive understanding of their performance trends. The research is limited in that it assumes all look-ahead predictions are equally relevant, whereas in reality, models likely have varying levels of relevance based on word distributions, with some words being more informative than others based on their positions. Papadopoulos and Temam recently proposed a versatile framework for evaluating Asian options based on a specific type of stochastic process. Their method involves converting the given process into a class of processes with stationary, memoryless distribution, utilizing a convolution operator to do so. This approach excels in maintaining convolution structure throughout, thus efficiently pricing all related Asian options. Although their framework is broadly applicable and includes multiple specific pricing formulas as case studies, it does have some limitations for options with non-linear payoffs. In response, alternative frameworks have been suggested that are better suited to such payoffs, but do so at the cost of additional complexity. In contrast, this comment suggests two straightforward modifications to Papadopoulos and Temam's framework, one of which can easily extend to non-linear payoffs with relative simplicity. Additionally, both modifications can take advantage of a complete parameter separation, greatly aiding in computational efficiency. The first modification builds on the original scheme of Papadopoulos and Temam by replacing the convolution operator with a more general linear transformation. The second, complementary option instead uses an expectation transform followed by a linear combination. Both approaches yield formulas that are easily verifiable through numerical Monte-Carlo simulations. In consequence, these modifications can broadly evaluate Asian options based on any type of Markov process. As demonstrated by testing, these suggestions show exceptional performance in pricing various options, with statistical significance easily achieved through Monte-Carlo simulations. Ultimately, the modifications are proposed for consideration in incorporating Papadopoulos and Temam's framework. The associated code for these suggestions has been included in the repository at https://github.com/amanbair/transformed-pricing. Additionally, the provided code can be easily extended to accommodate pricing in various other contexts. Pricing results for the test suite can be seen on the AOSP website. In this study, we examine a novel type of random graph known as the directed hybrid random graph (DHRG), featuring a unique blend of rules that govern edge creation. It combines a preference-based mechanism, akin to the universal scaling law, with a random attachment process. To investigate the long-term behavior and transition patterns of the generated graphs, we simulate various scenarios using the Stochastic Global Update (SGU) process. Our simulations uncover two distinct types of patterns: (i) a primitive period characterized by unpredictable changes before settling into (ii) a stable state marked by the coexistence of a robust core network with isolated island components. Specifically, our findings highlight the presence of two distinct time frames: an initial unpredictable phase during which the core and isolated nodes fluctuate in number, and a subsequent stable phase characterized by a fixed ratio of core to isolated nodes. Moreover, our analysis reveals key metrics and patterns such as the core and isolated nodes' degree distributions, the presence of a small set of highly connected 'hybrid' nodes, and the significant influence of an adjustable parameter, $\theta$. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the plausible existence of two distinct phases: (i) a core network comprised of densely connected nodes, and (ii) a set of sparsely connected island components, occurring simultaneously in the generated graphs. Interestingly, our analysis also uncovers a highly adaptable node that acts as a bridge, facilitating communication between the core and isolated parts of the network. The generated graphs, featuring intricate topology, display qualities of real-world systems such as social networks. With such properties, they are well-suited for modeling systems in which connection preferences play a role, including information spread across directed networks. Ultimately, the generated graphs prove valuable in both analytical and practical applications.

A novel approach called Symbolic Regression of Kernel Expressions (SKRE) is utilized to derive and evaluate complex Bayesian learning models. These models, specifically Gaussian Process models, rely on suitable kernel functions to predict dependencies between data points. The SKRE technique involves a systematic method for selecting kernel functions that accurately reflect the underlying relationships within a given dataset. In this study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the SKRE technique in three distinct domains: personalized learning, image synthesis, and drug target identification. The results obtained from the three applications confirm the superiority of SKRE over alternative kernel selection methods. Moreover, our work highlights the importance of a vast, computationally accessible collection of fundamental mathematical expressions, known as the Knowledge Bank. The symbolic expressions within the Knowledge Bank serve as the fundamental components of Gaussian Process models, analogous to how individual building blocks form the foundation of a language. The Knowledge Bank is designed to be continuously updated and expanded through SKRE, ultimately enabling the development of a self-improving bank that facilitates the selection of suitable expressions. The development of such a bank has far-reaching implications for a wide range of fields, including the discovery of personalized learning models, image features, protein structures, and potential drug targets. The integration of the Knowledge Bank into educational platforms, such as MOOCs, could significantly enhance student outcomes by providing a vast, symbolic understanding of the underlying data patterns. Optimizing the number of computational elements in vectorized operations is a key challenge in deep learning, as current methods lack a systematic framework for simultaneous optimization of both model and filter sparsity. We propose the Spartan module, an easily integrable block for differentiable sparsity using a transportation framework with two novel sparsity optimization techniques. The Spartan module consists of an initial encoder that maps inputs to a reduced-dimensional space, a conventional fully-connected layer acting as a decoder, and an regularized transportation loss that determines parameter redundancy. The use of regularized transportation as loss function in association with optimal transport algorithms like Sinkhorn or Gumbel allows for the measurement of redundancy and further filters out unessential parameters. A second approach employs random Laplace sampling with a Katz tree-based pruning strategy to assign weights to the parameters, resulting in better performance than current state-of-the-art techniques. Evaluation on ImageNet reveals significant sparsity-aware improvements over state-of-the-art results for ResNet, Wide-ResNet and MobileNet architectures, with notable achievement of outperforming the current best approach with 50% less parameters on the Labeled-YOLO dataset. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, a voluntary tracing system was introduced in England to track contacts of infected individuals and help contain the outbreak. As part of this effort, local authorities were encouraged to form their own tracing teams to supplement the national system, but the effect of this initiative on the national campaign's success remained unclear. To address this gap, a study investigated the connection between the number of individuals locally traced and the overall efficiency of the contact tracing campaign. By analyzing daily data on the contact tracing campaign, including the total number of daily new cases and daily new case discoveries via different methods of tracing, the researchers were able to assess the campaign's efficiency in real-time. They applied a technique known as time series analysis, incorporating COVID-19 related variables into a model to evaluate the campaign's effectiveness. To quantify the campaign's efficiency, the researchers used metrics such as the contact recovery rate and the overall efficiency in finding infectious cases, known as the detection efficiency. They discovered a significant positive connection between the number of individuals locally traced and the campaign's contact recovery rate, but no connection between local tracing and the initial detection of new cases. Furthermore, an analysis of the campaign's efficiency during the periods when local tracing and national tracing were both operational revealed that the campaign performed better when local tracing was active.
