Determining the age of an open cluster is a complex process due to the variability in mass loss of its protostars and the influence of dynamical relaxation. These factors were taken into consideration in a new study of the Melotte 72 cluster, utilizing the second data release of the Gaia survey. The research relied on data from the Gaia parallax program and the TESS space telescope for photometric observations. These observations allowed for an analysis of the cluster's initial mass function (IMF) and the examination of potential sources of uncertainty. The findings indicated that Melotte 72 is significantly younger than previously estimated, with an actual age ranging from approximately 500-700 million years. These new age findings align with astrophysical density estimates and provide the groundwork for an in-depth examination of the cluster's structure. Moreover, the melotte 72 cluster is relatively young and possesses a distinctively round shape, with some cluster members possibly experiencing ejection due to explosive events or the dynamics of the cluster. These new observations and findings support a theory proposing that Melotte 72 is essentially a star-forming cluster. The melotte 72 cluster's initial mass, further estimated in this study, would make it one of the lowest-mass local star clusters. These unique properties and patterns of the melotte 72 cluster offer valuable insights into star-forming processes and serve as an excellent subject for research in astrophysics, with the cluster still in an active star-forming phase. These new findings and the varying mass trends observed in various mass ranges challenge the long-held assumption that open clusters conform to the widely accepted Kroupa (2001) initial mass function model. The melotte 712 cluster, previously known for its distinct radial mass distribution, now shows consistency when compared to other clusters based on the revised Gaia survey. These new observations suggest a revised low-mass trend that forms a naturally declining slope at low masses and challenges the long-held high-mass IMF hypothesis. These new findings and the revised low-mass trends observed in melotte 72 and the melotte 715 cluster support a theory proposing that the high-mass peaks observed in these clusters result from a different physical process and may be the result of a more common star-formation phenomenon, such as stimulated star formation. These new observations and the revised low-mass trends support a theory promoting the widespread occurrence of stimulated star formation events in the early stages of star-cluster development. These new findings and the revised low-mass trends provide the opportunity to explore basic star formation processes

Random geometric graphs, which exhibit distinct threshold behaviors, are categorized as sparse networks. A specific type of sparse graph, the minimum cuts network, is known as a minimum cuts Gaussian network. This paper examines homological properties of a specific Gaussian network model introduced by Arora and Ruskoy. It explores Betti numbers in two-dimensional models and its Poisson approximation. Notably, the convergence rate of the approximation is found to be inversely proportional to the square root of the average degree. Specifically, when comparing to a Poisson random variable, the relative error is shown to be bounded by a constant and the square root of the average degree, less than or equal to 1.18, for sufficiently large average degrees. Similarly, for one-dimensional models, which can be viewed as point processes, a similar relation was established with the area term replaced with a dimension-specific constant. These findings were also verified using numerical simulations. It's worth noting that similar results have been reported by Ravelozo and Arroyo for a specific type of Gaussian network known as Erdos-Renyi graph in one-dimensional models. However, for two-dimensional models, this is the first time such estimates have been made. Moreover, previous works on Gaussian networks homology reported either polynomial or exponential error rates. This paper's results were published in a forthcoming journal, but earlier results on homology estimates for a specific type of Gaussian network model were published in another journal. Automating the adjustment of an eye-in-hand camera in 3D workplaces poses a significant challenge due to numerous variables at play. In workplaces where human supervision is not possible, an autonomous method for adjusting the camera is essential. Our novel technique combines computer vision and machine learning to adjust the camera without moving the robotic arm's end effector. Leveraging a single image, our proposed method generates an image adjustment matrix to reposition the camera based on the end effector's estimated position. To achieve this, we developed a novel deep learning-based approach that extracts a heatmap indicating the end effector's projected location. Our testing showed that our method achieved an average precision of 90% in identifying the end effector's projected position and accurate image adjustment with minimal residual distortion (less than 1 pixel in width and height). We examine a variant of constrained reinforcement learning where our agent aims to
determine the optimal policy for an existing task-based reward function and constraint
specifications. The approach is termed Reverse Reinforcement Learning as it reverses the
traditional reinforcement learning process. Our focus lies in using interaction with a task
expert to find the best policy despite the expert's incomplete or ambiguous explanations
for task success. We propose two models: one relies on finding the highest reward outcome
using a model known as Progress Pursuing Operations Discrete (POD), and the other utilizes
a model based on conditional programming called Reverse Trajectory Constrained Reinforcement
Learning (TrCLR). TrCLR leverages an implicit constraint representation and applies a model
of the expert's explanations to discover the optimal policy. We test these models on a robot
navigation scenario with an unskilled and a skilled agent to illustrate their practical
applications. Our experiments show that both models effectively yield a satisfactory policy
within the given constraints, but the derived policies exhibit distinct characteristics based
on the presence of a skilled or unskilled task expert. TrCLR outperforms POD in terms of both
convergence speed and overall efficacy. The proposed approaches, however, fall short when
faced with very basic or non-existent constraint specifications. Furthermore, their reliance
on complete and implicit constraint representations hinders their flexibility and results in
less transferability compared to conventional reinforcement learning methods. The use of
these models is best suited for collaborative learning environments where direct instruction
from a task expert is readily available. The presented work marks the first successful
implementation of RRL, and our experiments provide valuable insights into its behavior,
notably the similarity in policies derived from skilled and unskilled experts as observed in
the various evaluation metrics. The resulting models are publicly accessible at

The behavior of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can be extensively
characterized by their ability to exactly solve partial differential equations
and their robust data fitting capabilities, often accompanied by unpredictable
noise in the residual. Current PINN risk assessments are restricted to
computational error analysis based on Monte Carlo sampling, which is time-
consumming and inefficient for large-scale problems. Our proposed approach
involves using Gaussian processes to develop an empirical, data-driven method
for pinning the PINN's generalization error, allowing for the analysis of PINNs'
robustness and the identification of optimal hyperparameters through Bayesian
optimization. This method is successfully demonstrated on two complex PDE-based
problems involving multiple subdomains and a random input variable. Firstly, a
freeze-damped Navier-Stokes equation with a known exact solution is used to
verify the method's accuracy in estimating the generalization and total testing
errors. Additionally, a random input variable is applied to this equation to
illustrate the effectiveness of the method in assessing uncertainty. Lastly, a
more challenging system of PDEs describing binary nucleation in solution is used
to showcase the method's utility in crystallization processes, where transparent
prediction intervals and the derivation of design-of-experiment samples help PINNs
achieve data completion. Our study indicates that the method is efficient, easy
to implement, and capable of providing certified bounds for the generalization
and total testing errors of PINNs. Furthermore, it can be utilized for data
interpolation in the presence of incomplete dataset collections. Ultimately, this
method perseveres with the core translational goals of the PINN framework by
maximizing the likelihood of the model achieving accurate in-distribution
generalization. Video recordings of the studied problems are accessible through

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of linear bandits using a diverse set of actions, which has long been a topic of interest within the research community. Due to the combinatorial complexity and dimensionality issues associated with this problem, previous studies largely focused on heuristic approaches; however, we have established a mathematical framework for this problem by combining ideas from linear bandits and combinatorial statistics. Our contributions include computationally efficient methods for estimating regression parameters and our novel "closet convexity" principle, which ensures minimal loss in the presence of noisy observations. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that these techniques lead to statistically consistent results, which we have verified through extensive numerical experiments. Interestingly, the resulting results sometimes surpass the existing state-of-the-art approaches, which typically incorporate "elimination" techniques. Moreover, we have discovered that these techniques correspond to specific "policy strategies" within our framework, which allows us to offer fresh insights and perspectives on this classic problem. The implications of our findings are also relevant to reinforcement learning, which often builds upon the bandit learning framework. Additionally, we have developed a generalization of the "elimination" techniques, which led to novel statistical inference techniques for multi-armed bandits, which we have validated through various examples. Lastly, our approach enables the creation of asymptotic theories for a range of bandit problems, which will lead to future research in this area. Graphene with gaps experiences an Orbital Hall effect distinct from the Valley Hall effect, where electrons in lower and upper bands occupy distinct orbital states. Applying an external magnetic field reveals a direct relationship between the Chern number and an orbital Hall conductivity, indicating that each valley contributes half of the total Chern number. As proven through exact diagonalization on a lattice model, this relationship holds consistently. Furthermore, the Orbital Hall effect is experimentally verifiable and robust against impurities. Our findings present a new perspective on the Valley Hall effect in gapless graphene and provide an alternative mechanism for its observation, potentially applicable in other two-dimensional materials. The proposed effect may enable the separation of valley electrons using an electric field, opening up possibilities for devices such as valves, Hall balloons, and orbittometers. Here, a theoretical model is developed to predict the properties of a gapped graphene layer under a magnetic field, revealing a rich set of phase diagrams influenced by the chemical potential and magnetic induction. It is shown that the phase diagrams exhibit similarities with those of superconducting and exciton condensate phase diagrams when the number of bands is greater than 2. In gapped graphene, the appearance of a diamagnetic phase opposite to the Chern insulator phase, with a certain Hall conductivity, is characteristic. By contrasting the band structure of various types of 2D materials, such as bilayer graphene, monolayer boron nitride, and transition metal dichalcogenides, it is observed that some of them may exhibit the Orbital Hall effect while bypassing the Valley Hall effect. A comparison with the behavior of 2D systems that are superconducting, ferromagnetic, or excitonic is also presented. Moreover, the influence of the electron-electron interaction on the Orbital Hall effect in gapless graphene is evaluated within the context of the Hubbard model, revealing an increase in the Orbital Hall conductivity as the ratio of interaction to the electron hopping strength increases. The study offers suggestions for experimental investigations of the Orbital Hall effect in various two-dimensional systems, such as in the presence of a charged impurity, a photonic or phononic excitation, and an electromagnetic wave. The proposed effect may enable the separation of orbital states using an electric field, leading to a new set of devices including valves, Hall balloons, and oscillators. The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue and improve the accuracy of matching algorithms. A method developed for this purpose utilizes iterative algorithms that incorporate both astrometric and photometric data for a more precise matching of sources. This method demonstrates high levels of precision and accuracy in matching a range of catalogs, outperforming traditional astrometric-based matching methods in some instances. A notable advantage of this approach is its ability to accurately match sources with varying brightness levels, a task previously challenging with astrometric-based methods alone. To validate the method, it was applied to a near-infrared catalog of faint objects obtained through the VISTA Kilo-degree Infrared Galaxy Survey, and compared against reference catalogs of known sources. When matched using the magnitudes of sources, the method exhibited a high level of precision, accurately identifying 75% of sources within a 1 arcsecond radius and demonstrating minimal contamination, accurately matching fewer than 1% of sources to themselves. Similarly, the method demonstrated high levels of accuracy, demonstrating an error rate of less than 0.4% when compared against reference catalogs. Notably, the method prioritized matches based on the closest astrometric and photometric residuals, suggesting a significant advantage to incorporating photometric information in matching sources. However, incorporating additional photometric bands, and matching sources based on multiple channels of information, did not improve the accuracy of matching sources based on astrometric data alone and led to a slight decrease in precision and a slight increase in the frequency of self-matches. These results suggest the importance of incorporating photometric information in matching sources, particularly when working to match large, faint objects such as galaxies. Moreover, the method demonstrated the significance of incorporating photometric information in matching sources, and suggested several potential applications to various fields of research, and proposed additional research avenues to validate these findings. Specifically, the method could be applied to near-infrared intensity information obtained through ALMA and VLA observations, and compared against matching sources based on astrometric data alone. Additionally, the method could be applied to a comprehensive near-infrared catalog of galaxies obtained through a substantial survey such as the VISTA-Kilo Degree Infrared Galaxy Survey. When matched using the magnitudes of sources, the method exhibited a high level of precision, demonstrated an extremely high level of accuracy, and demonstrated minimal contamination, accurately matching fewer than 1% of sources to themselves.

In this paper, we explore infinite hypergraphs and identify minimal vertex sets that participate in specific subgraph formations. Our results also address existence concerns for certain types of subhypercubes within infinite hypergraphs. Additionally, we investigate the structure of minimal vertex sets in relation to hypergraph connectivity and show that a dense hypergraph with certain properties always contains a complete minimal vertex set. Our work also involves an examination of categorical properties related to these sets. Moreover, we demonstrate instances where certain types of subhypercubes cannot exist and set boundaries on their possible sizes. As existing ontologies continue to expand, they often become complex networks involving many related terms, which can lead to substantial interpretation difficulties when utilizing hierarchical visualization tools that focus on individual terms' definitions. To address this challenge, we have developed a innovative, visual representation method called OntoPlot that seamlessly integrates hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections within a comprehensive ontology framework. Through a case study involving a large, widely-used healthcare ontology, we have demonstrated OntoPlot's capabilities and explored its potential applications in related research domains. Furthermore, all the code and data used in this research have been made publicly available to foster future research into visual data representation methods.

We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines a speaker-dependent inter-domain loss with CycleGAN for the task of semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. The inter-domain loss, trained with a teacher-student model of ASR and Automatic Speaker Verification, imposes a multi-stream constraint that facilitates speech feature learning with minimal speaker information. These features are then fine-tuned by a CycleGAN loss, which minimizes inter-domain feature mappings to facilitate more general speech recognition patterns. Our approach effectively leverages a widely available speaker embedding for improved speech feature learning and has been demonstrated to achieve accurate ASR with reduced data annotation. Notably, with the integration of speaker-related constraints, model accuracy is recorded at 52.5% cer on the Voxlit dev set with 1011 hours of mixed audio content, and a minimal 2% cer decrease is observed when moving from a 16-hour trained speaker-dependent model to the proposed speaker-independent approach. To the best of our knowledge, this research constitutes the first application of speaker embedding for enhanced end-to-end ASR through domain alignment. The findings and implementation details are freely accessible on our GitHub repository. Moreover, model pre-training is now possible due to the availability of the Voxlit, LSMTK, and LibriSpeech datasets, marking significant progress in speaker-dependent ASR. Despite the availability of sophisticated deep learning-based models, their applications remain hindered by limitations such as their large memory requirements, slow processing speeds, and limited capacity for handling long sequences. To overcome these challenges, we investigated the use of efficient transformer language models, specifically FastTransformer and CoT, in a practical automated essay assessment environment. These models have previously demonstrated success in various applications such as machine translation and text generation. Our study involves evaluating the efficiency and accuracy of these models in understanding the content of essays written by students. Our experimental findings reveal that the CoT-Large model surpasses the BERT-S Large model in identifying correct answers to questions, while the CoT-Large and BERT-S Large models perform equally well in detecting incorrect answers. Additionally, we found that the CoT models exhibit lower latency and improved processing efficiency on modern GPUs. Our study also highlights the potential of modifying the positional embedding strategy of the CoT models to further enhance their performance. To facilitate reproducibility, we publicly share the source code and pre-trained CoT models on GitHub. Our study contributes to the development of efficient automated essay assessment models capable of handling lengthy essays. Such efficient models can potentially replace the slower and more memory-intensive deep learning models currently in use. The success of the CoT models in our study suggests that they could be adapted for a broader range of natural language processing applications requiring sequential reasoning capabilities. Our research is geared towards developing automated essay assessment models that can be utilized in real-world applications. To contribute further to this area, we plan to continue improving the efficiency and accuracy of these models, as well as exploring their application in essay content analysis. Our next-step research aims to evaluate the performance of the CoT models on a more comprehensive range of automated essay assessment tasks, such as identifying the writing stage, analyzing the essay's overall quality, and detecting plagiarism. To achieve this goal, we intend to pre-train the CoT models on a more extensive writing-related corpus, thereby enhancing their capabilities in complex tasks involving sequential reasoning. Our ultimate objective is to leverage the automated essay assessment models developed through this research to support the writing instruction process in educational settings, thereby positively impacting students' writing outcomes. To facilitate the practical application of these models, we plan to establish a user-friendly application enabling educators to analyze the writing quality and detect plagiarism across a variety of writing styles and academic disciplines. Our research has the potential to make a significant practical impact in the automation of essay assessment tasks

Our artificial intelligence system for simulating throwing motions has generated a significant amount of user-generated content on social media platforms.
This content includes various factors that influence the appearance and realism of the simulations.
By utilizing user-generated videos of actual throwing motions and adjusting the desired trajectory, our system can generate realistic three-dimensional arm movements.
The point at which the simulated ball is released appears as a random variable in our system's calculations.
We discovered that even seemingly minor discrepancies in this point of release can greatly impact both the visual appeal and the perceived authenticity of the simulations.
To better understand these variations, we established a quantitative metric for measuring the differences in simulation quality.
Using this metric, we conducted a survey among non-experts and a group of professional baseball players to determine their average perception of the simulations' authenticity.
The results showed that incorrect points of release can significantly lower the authenticity score, although the rate of decline varies based on the level of realism displayed in the simulations.
Moreover, our results reveal that subtle changes in arm movement can have a greater impact on authenticity than precise control over the ball's trajectory.
This finding suggests that our system's current focus on accurately modeling arm movements is crucial to creating realistic throwing motion simulations.
Our study also demonstrates that incorporating elements of uncertainty in our simulations, represented by a faux effect, can make the simulations appear more authentic.
Ultimately, our investigation challenges our field's long-standing goal of achieving maximum precision in rendering three-dimensional human movements.
Instead, our findings suggest that mimicking the natural variability of human movements, as evidenced by the simulations' fauxthrows, can be a vital component of creating compelling experiences. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called TsDL is proposed, combining a syntactic parser with a top-down tree structured neural machine translation model. The underlying idea is that tree structure can improve decoding efficiency and quality, and incorporating syntax from multiple sources can enhance translation accuracy. The proposed TsDL architecture achieves this goal by parsing source language sentences and then using a syntactic attention mechanism in a tree structured space to guide the translation process. The model is further improved by leveraging syntactic and lexical mutual attention between the target tree and a lexical table to determine word meanings. Experimental evaluations show that the TsDL architecture yields superior results on the EN-FR NMT task, outperforming baseline models by 3.12 BLEU points. Moreover, the model is capable of parsing source language sentences with high accuracy, with an average LAS rate of 84.7%. Overall, the TsDL architecture demonstrates the potential for tree structured decoding in NMT tasks, and its mutual attention mechanism is an innovative way to capture complex word and phrase relationships. The model is available for public access at the website: https://github.com/ckgao/TsDL. Coverage analysis of related work is presented in the paper's introduction.

A multiplicative stochastic process with log-normal distributed increments is studied, where a lower bound is established for the process based on its positive history. Two types of models are examined: one where the lower bound is a constant, leading to a piecewise linear multiplicative stochastic process, and another where the lower bound is a function of past values, leading to a nonlinear multiplicative stochastic process. These models are shown to have practical applications in financial modeling and statistical analysis. Specifically, the first model is used to explain the coexistence of extreme value and non-extreme value scenarios in financial time series, where a minimum threshold applies. Additionally, the second model is applied in a three-field statistical analysis where the presence of three distinct asymptotes is observed in a univariate probability distribution. This distinctivity arises due to differing market conditions: bullish, bearish, and neutral. By employing the nonlinear multiplicative stochastic process, a novel method for estimating thresholds and mean excesses is developed, grounded in the recent 'quick sort' algorithm. This algorithm demonstrates both computational efficiency and statistical robustness. The estimates produced by this algorithm show consistency with established practical methods for short samples and tend towards convergence towards the expected theoretical values at asymptotic limits. Moreover, the statistical analysis method itself converges towards the expected theoretical values. Extensive empirical studies demonstrate that the novel technique outperforms existing methods in estimates, sensitivity analysis, and convergence. One of the studied stocks shows significant real-world relevance in that the minimum threshold estimates suggest that the 2020 pandemic caused minimal harm to the stock's value. The general technique can be applied across various fields such as weather and high-energy physics where multiplicative stochastic processes with lower bounds are present. The technique can be used to predict future values of such processes given their historical data. There is an ongoing debate about the relationship between the depth of a quantum circuit and its utility in computing tasks. Research has been conducted to evaluate the value of shallow circuits, which have fewer than a logarithmic number of qubits, in quantum computing. This work develops a framework based on shadow tomography to assess the state of a quantum system via a limited set of observables. This framework is applied to determine the predictive power of shallow circuits in quantum computing. A novel protocol is proposed that relies on random Clifford circuits and achieves fast improvement in predictive accuracy with minimal qubit usage. This protocol exhibits linear improvement in predictive accuracy, using a logarithmic number of qubits, and a shallow improvement in depth, which outperforms previous methods. This research supports the contention that shallow circuits hold significant value in quantum computing. Future work may adapt this protocol for tasks like quantum machine learning and quantum optimization. Additionally, shallow circuits could serve as a useful tool for generating highly entangled states and demonstrating the presence of entanglement in specific forms. Implementing the protocol using current quantum hardware is discussed, as well as its potential limitations. A related theoretical advantage is proven and a comparison is made with related research conducted by other researchers. This comparison is accompanied by a demonstration of the existing limitations of similar schemes. Firstly, a well-known scheme is shown to achieve linear improvement in depth but incurs significant overhead. In contrast, a different scheme is shown to exchange speed for additional qubits. Both of these schemes are shown not to be practical on current hardware. In summary, our research highlights the significance of shallow circuits that apply low-depth, noisy operations to quantum states. These circuits may be of use in various near-term quantum applications. Moreover, our research could pave the way for the development of new quantum algorithms that exploit the advantages of shallow circuits. Implementing these ideas in quantum computing is encouraged. Developing multilingual MT models to accommodate languages with limited data has shown potential in addressing code-switching issues and expanding model coverage. Given the significant resource requirements for such models, compression techniques like distillation and quantization are considered viable approaches for tackling the data scarcity issue. In this study, we compare the feasibility of utilizing distillation and quantization for low-resource MT model development. While distillation has proven highly effective for translation quality improvement, its reliance on a larger, teacher model makes it impractical for low-resource settings. On the other hand, quantization offers a more promising route to model lightweight low-resource MT models since it enables training directly from a small number of samples. Notably, our experiments show that while distillation significantly enhances translation quality, model size, and inference speed are ultimately constrained by the large weights of the teacher model. In contrast, model size reduction through quantization leads to substantial improvements in inference speed and translation latency, even at the expense of slight quality losses, making it a stronger candidate for developing lightweight low-resource MT models. Given these findings, a comprehensive investigation is called for to develop compression methods like distillation and quantization that facilitate efficient low-resource MT model development. Ultimately, our research aims to facilitate a thorough assessment of both distillation and quantization as effective compression techniques for developing compression methods that facilitate efficient low-resource MT model development. Results are made available on GitHub at https://github.com/kevincattaneo/Compressing-Models. Developing image description models that produce fluent and relevant descriptions is an essential yet challenging task. Existing models struggle to create descriptions according to specific requirements due to the rigid structure of traditional decoding methods. Recent breakthroughs in prompt engineering for language models have shown promise in customizing model behavior with tailored prompts. We propose a new image description model that incorporates a prompt to balance image understanding and language style, achieving good performance on Image Description and Captioning tasks. We also provide prompts for practical applications, demonstrating the model's capabilities in producing descriptions on demand. Our model performs comparable or better on public metrics (BLEU, CIDEr) and human evaluation for evaluation metrics (coherence, common sense, and fluency). The study reveals the potential of prompt engineering in tackling the challenging task of controlling the style and relevance of image descriptions. Artificial intelligence systems have numerous applications where their predictive capabilities are crucial, particularly in scenarios that involve making decisions about the well-being of individuals, such as whether a person should be granted parole. To ensure that these systems function in a manner that is considered just, it is essential to understand the reasons behind their predictions and how they relate to the factors that directly impact people's lives. In the case of the parole decision, for example, a prediction that a person will be considered a danger to society if released should ideally stem from the fact that they may pose a danger to society if they commit further crimes, rather than simply because they have a history of past crimes. Causal examination techniques can be used to identify the underlying causes of social harms, even in situations where there are no relevant variables and where the cause-and-effect relationships are complex. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, an application is described where the underlying causes of incarceration are identified using data from the 2018 U.S. American Community Survey. Although the results are not presented here, an automated system is proposed that can be used to perform causal examinations with synthetic data, allowing causal examination techniques to be applied in situations where the data may be insufficient or insensitive. Furthermore, a plan is outlined for collecting additional data from the public sector in order to enhance the quality of causal examination results, which would involve amending existing data collection forms to include relevant questions. Ultimately, the results of a survey of the relevant agencies are presented, suggesting that the adoption of this new data collection strategy could be implemented relatively easily and at little cost. A plan is also presented for using the results of the causal examinations to develop targeted policies, such as the establishment of expert review panels. Ultimately, the results show that (1) AI systems can be used to identify the causal mechanisms that underlie the predictions that these systems generate; (2) additional data can be used to strengthen the causal links that are present in the data; (3) calculating the total benefit of a strategy can be more difficult than determining the strategy's target population; ((4) incorporating prior knowledge into the causal examination results can be essential; and (5) the results of the causal examinations can be used by the government to inform public policy decisions. Ultimately, the results suggest that the most effective public policy decisions are made by considering the ethical and the moral implications of the actions that they entail. Significant changes in how people live and work are having far-reaching effects on energy consumption patterns. Electrification is gaining momentum across various sectors including transport, heat, and industry. However, current electricity distribution networks were not designed to accommodate the increased load and the resulting high frequency fluctuations. To operate efficiently, networks require significant upgrades, but this is a costly endeavor. To minimize expenses, the upgrade process should be guided by accurate load forecasting tools. Specifically, forecasting daily peak loads is crucial for optimizing network upgrade strategies. To address this, researchers propose a novel method combining the power of ensemble forecasting and model-based techniques. The proposed framework leverages various forecasting methods, including persistence, ridge regression, and a dynamic model incorporating seasonal factors and lagged response variables. The integration of these forecasts into a unified model enables reliable estimates of daily peak loads and average load, while minimizing dispersion. The approach's feasibility is demonstrated through application to a small UK distribution network and a large German distribution network. The former network has 465 consumers with time-series data available for 3 years and 13 hours a day, while the latter has 26,000 consumers with 5 years of time-series data, but only single-time-step forecasts. The proposed framework produces consistent estimates, is robust to changes in load profiles, and outperforms competing methods like GEP-GAN and SVR. Notably, the proposed framework enhances model robustness by reducing the influence of individual forecasts. The optimization of the seasonal factor and lagged response variables, specifically the peak factor and the time of the peak load, is achieved through a novel iterative process. The proposed framework's performance is evaluated in terms of the complexity of the parameters involved. Model-based techniques excel at average and peak load forecasting, while ensemble forecasting outperforms other techniques in terms of forecast fusion. The optimization of the model parameters and the selection of the most suitable parameters are achieved through the minimization of the distance between the observed and the forecast load profiles. The primary difficulty lies in gathering suitable data and crafting an accurate mathematical representation. This study proposes a systematic framework for incorporating domain expertise into machine learning models as a means of enhancing their predictive capacity and robustness. The proposed method is comprised of three distinct approaches: a data modelization framework for representing inputs and outputs through symbolic languages, a data preparation framework for transforming numerical data, and a machine learning framework for integrating symbolic and numerical components. This method is illustrated through its application in a simulated aircraft maintenance case study and a real-world example from the railway industry involving a predictive maintenance scenario for actuators. Both examples demonstrate the feasibility of integrating domain knowledge into machine learning models to mitigate data scarcity and improve overall performance. The primary contributions of this research are the proposed frameworks and their combined effect of enabling practical application of machine learning in contexts that previously posed considerable challenges. Additionally, an open-source software tool was developed to support the proposed method, which is available for public use. Both the software tool and tutorial have been thoroughly documented to ensure ease of public access and use. The application of machine learning requires considerable expertise in the domain in question; therefore, incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning models, as proposed in this research, enhances their capacity to generalise and increases their effectiveness. The proposed method prioritises domain knowledge integration above model performance; in other words, data quality and pre-processing take precedence over model performance. This research seeks to inspire machine learning practitioners to integrate domain knowledge into their models and make data preparation a higher priority. Electron scattering off a target within a cavity resonates when the electron's energy aligns with the target's excitation frequencies within the cavity. This interaction is typically studied using a stationary target, but our work involves an accelerating electron, which couples to the cavity's time-varying electromagnetic field. This time-varying coupling leads to an unprecedented form of resonance, characterized by the target's excitations resonating simultaneously with the electron's kinetic energy. Our theoretical study illustrates how vacuum fluctuations in the cavity's electromagnetic field stabilize this unique resonance and demonstrate its occurrence through time-resolved, high-resolution imaging of the target. This resonance is predicted to manifest in the target's x-ray emission via the resonant excitation of core excitations, and the emission is forecasted to be periodic and synchronized with the electron's scattering phase, while also featuring a significant enhancement stemming from the target's non-linear responses to both the cavity's quantum fluctuations and the accelerating electron's quantum characteristics. Our research proposes a way to observe this phenomenon termed "light-matter antibunching" via the target's emission of low-energy photons, which is predicted to occur within the cavity. The phenomenon is characterized by the absence of two-time correlations of the emitted photons and is predicted to be marked by the target's radiation-pressure-induced emission of "quantum dots." These novel findings are anticipated to be accessible to experimental investigation through the implementation of advanced nanotechnology and ultrafast electron scattering methods. Our research marks an advancement in the light-matter interactions field, specifically in the light-matter coupling regime characterized by the scattering of an accelerating electron off a target within a cavity. The conventional approach to parameter tuning in legged locomotion is expensive and time-consuming due to the need for expert supervision. Our novel method recognizes that controllable actuator stiffness is a crucial factor in optimizing quadruped gait patterns, thereby enabling the automation of gait adaptation and stiffness configuration. We propose a unique set of stiffness configurations and a learning algorithm, referred to as the'slip-index,' which evaluates desirable characteristics (slip resistance) of a quadruped's gait. We successfully evaluated our method on a physical elastic-legged quadruped, demonstrating that it can independently determine the optimal gait pattern and actuator stiffness to achieve dynamic gait at varying speeds without expert input. Our results illustrate the effectiveness of model-free learning in optimizing the performance of elastic-legged quadruped locomotion. We propose a simple and efficient strategy, referred to as the minimum variance method (MV), for resolving the separability problem in quantum theory. The proposed approach is akin to a variational method. Through in-depth analysis, we display the MV strategy's effectiveness through its ability to detect the presence of entanglement at the minimal possible error in numerous genuine states across different quantum systems. Moreover, the method's efficacy is also demonstrated in the case of mixed states where only one purified state is examined. The relative error in determining the concurrence in such instances is shown to be infinitesimally small. Furthermore, using the complexity of the method as the optimality criterion, we find that the first two iterations of the MV strategy perform substantially better compared to the other minimal variance methods (MVMs) proposed in the past. While the third and final iteration of the MV also excels among all other MVMs, its performance difference is remarkably smaller. Consequently, in practical applications where only one iteration can be employed, the first two iterations of the MV strategy are recommended for use. Ultimately, the MV strategy serves as a highly efficient tool to identify the symmetry properties present within quantum states, a characteristic typically characterized by their separability's preservation under specific unitary transformations. Through analysis of the strategy's performance across various numerical models, the presence of entanglement in classes of bipartite and tripartite states was successfully detected. The method's performance is also examined in the context of noisy states across the dephasing channel. Interestingly, the performance observed was found to be dependent on the dimension of the complexity-determining matrix employed. Notably, the performance improves significantly with an increase in the system's dimensions. Our results suggest that the MV strategy could potentially serve as an optimal alternative to the more computationally demanding approaches such as the singular value threshold test (SVTT) for use in the solution of the separability problem in quantum theory, particularly in large-scale quantum systems. A theoretical analysis is conducted for a specific small-scale ripping mode observed in a collisionless slab plasma. Utilizing a local analysis, it's discovered that the mechanism driving this mode involves a particular type of wave, which the research community has previously categorized as wave-number dependent. This wave produces a force on the main mode by disrupting its phase, which the theory shows translates directly into a specific type of resistance for the main mode of interest. By contrast, experimental findings indicate the driving force is more complex and closely related to how the main mode of interest produces these higher-wavenumber waves. This distinction leads to two distinct interpretations for the small-scale ripping mode, which varies depending on whether considering theory or experimental facts. While the former suggests the small-scale ripping mode represents a particular type of instability in collisionless slabs, experimental evidence suggests it might simply be a manifestation of how the main mode of interest generates these higher-wavenumber waves. Nevertheless, regardless of the interpretation, the small-scale ripping mode is recognized as a mode of instability that significantly impedes plasma stabilization efforts due to its rapid growth rate. A key goal of fashion image retrieval involves pinpointing a fashion item's style traits.
However, style traits serve as an intricate indicator of a garment's aesthetic and technical characteristics.
As such, manipulating fashion images according to specified traits is of significant utility in the fashion industry, aiding designers in constructing designs with desired characteristics and in retrieving images that match customers' desired aesthetic and technical specifications.
Despite the prevalence of Fashion Image Retrieval (FIR), very few studies have explored GAN-based conditioning techniques to manipulate fashion images according to defined traits.
In response, we aim to develop a semi-supervised method for incorporating style traits into fashion images.
Our algorithm trains two neural networks - a feature extraction network and a feature combination network - using labeled images and unlabeled images.
Upon training, it is capable of autonomously incorporating various traits into fashion images.
We evaluate our approach through comparison with prior semantic fashion image manipulation methods on two datasets and found our results superior in terms of visual quality and trait specificity. Moreover, prior methods require extensive ground-truth fashion style annotations, a requirement that leads to scalability and usability constraints. In contrast, our approach requires only category-level labels for training and can effectively incorporate a wide array of fashion traits.
Ultimately, the outcomes of our research enable the creation of high-quality fashion images with specified traits, advancing the applications of fashion image retrieval and generation in the fashion industry. The Dual Gradient Method is proposed for addressing linear ill-posed problems within the context of Banach spaces and their duals. The development is initially grounded in an existing dual approach by Burachyk et al. In the absence of noise, the DG-M is demonstrated to produce a convergent sequence, with optimal rates of convergence mimicking those of the original primal problem. In the presence of noise, the DG-M is shown to yield a weak convergence outcome analogous to that of the primal problem. Moreover, the dual approach is depicted as being more robust than its primal counterpart in the measured data. Lastly, a practical application of the DG-M is provided through the use of X-ray computed tomography as a concrete example. The latter's formulation involves dual Banach spaces defined over the 2D classical Besov space and its dual, the Besov space's dual being the Sobolev space. Numerical tests performed on real-world data have validated the effectiveness of the suggested method. In particular, the numerical results have revealed that the DG-M outperforms its primal counterpart and exhibits greater stability when evaluated using the condition number of matrices. The chosen approach involves minimizing the dual norm of the residual, and this minimization can be achieved using an adaptive gradient method such as ADAM. Consequently, the suggested method is referred to as the Dual Adam Method for handling regularized ill-posed problems involving function measurements. In order to maintain the paper's clarity, the proof of the dual approach's stability and convergence has been grounded in the primal approach's proof for handling regularized problems in Hilbert spaces and their duals. Consequently, the convergence proof for the dual approach is provided in the paper's supplementary material. In addition to the above-mentioned information, the paper's supplementary material contains the numerical tests' data and the tomographic reconstructions obtained using the DG-M, its stability information and the optimal parameter values, and the Besov space's property information, and the plots of the numerical tests' data have been provided in the paper's attachments. The process of estimating depth from light field images has gained significant interest over the last few years due to their inherent geometric properties. However, solving this problem proves to be difficult and time-consuming. Our proposed method, occlusion-aware estimation using the cost builder, overcomes these issues by using key, secondary, and tertiary views effectively. Specifically, we designed our cost builder to prioritize central views for accurate geometry and faster convergence, reserving secondary and tertiary views for dealing with occlusions. This leads to substantial performance improvements, outshining existing methods by over 2 times in terms of inference speed while maintaining comparable accuracy. Our source code has been made publicly available. With our novel strategy and optimized implementation, we aim to bring light field depth estimation closer to real-world applications. Our study showcases the efficacy of occlusion-aware strategies in achieving high-quality light field depth estimation results. Moreover, we documented the performance of our approach on the standard LF-DF1 benchmark using the NPardorf benchmarking tool. Our results indicate that our proposed method, OCB-LFD, achieves state-of-the-art results on the LF-DF1 benchmark with 28.60% Ssim and 0.7441 MSE. Our method ranks 4th on the LF-DF1 benchmark for accuracy and 1st for speed. Additionally, our occlusion-aware strategy excels at predicting the occurrence of occlusions with 84.21% accuracy, surpassing the best existing methods by over 2 times. Our approach has the capability of handling occlusions of varying complexity levels, ranging from mild (e.g., an object obstructing the view of a corner point) to severe (e.g., an object completely masking the center point of the light field). This capability makes our proposed method highly adaptable to practical applications. Our study should be reviewed using the detailed paper and the supplementary video provided. This study applies the bilinear approach to solve the Fokas-Lenells equations, which describe quantum nonlinear cavity fiber systems. It combines the Fokas approach with the reduced dressing method to obtain multiple consistent initial value problems for the Fokas-Lenells equations. The approach allows for the reduction of the NLS equation nontangential contour boundary value problem to a simpler ordinary differential problem. The results are verified using numerical methods. One of the key challenges in implementing this approach is obtaining boundary values, which for the Fokas-Lenells equations involves solving a related problem for the associated NLS equation. If the initial data for the Fokas-Lenells equations is a solution of the NLS equation, this problem is simplified. Otherwise, a related initial value problem for the NLS equation needs to be solved. The approach is illustrated using two examples, one of which being a step function and the other a raised cosine function. The results are also compared with exact analytical solutions found in existing literature. The approach is confirmed to be accurate by good agreement between numerical and analytical data. The approach is proposed as a means of solving the Fokas-Lenells equations, which is an important task in modeling quantum nonlinear cavity fiber systems. The approach is generic and can be applied to equations with multiple spatial dimensions. However, in such cases, the approach is subject to nontangential lattice boundary value conditions. The key benefits of this approach are its ability to solve boundary value problems and its high order of accuracy. The approach is also free from contamination by rounding error at late times. The approach is operated in a forward mode, which is a key advantage. The approach is not dependent on solving a Riemann problem. The approach is generic and can be applied to a range of equations, including the KdV, mKdV, regularized mKdV, fifth order equation, S-G equation, BO equation, Burgers equation, BO-Eq, BO-SG equation. The key challenges in implementing this approach are the generation of boundary values and keeping a high order of accuracy at late times, which is a difficult task for multisoliton initial data. The approach is an extension of the reduced dressing method and is built on the superposition principle. The key components of this approach are the linear problem for the Fokas-Lenells equations and its initial value problem. The approach is in the process of being implemented in a C code. Alternative theories of gravity that deviate from General Relativity on the Riemannian platform have been proposed to explain the yet unexplained aspects of the Universe and physics. These alternatives can be categorized into two types, which are based on their consistency with the geometric framework: the ones that remain consistent (weak theories) and those that break the geometric framework (strong theories). Weak theories attempt to expand the Ricci action by introducing extra curvature invariant terms, whereas strong theories go beyond the Ricci tensor and develop novel action formulas. An example of a strong theory is the Riemannon theory, which builds on the Riemann tensor and the Ricci tensor. An alternative approach to developing this theory is provided, starting from the eleven-dimensional supergravity action of double field theory. This procedure involves a stepwise process of imposing constraints to arrive at the Riemannon theory. As a result, the newly derived theory is shown to be consistent with the existing weak theory, which is based on a specific action formula. Additionally, the novel methods developed here can be applied to identify new examples of strong gravitational theories. Moreover, the study of gravity actions suggests that the graviton becomes massive in the process, and the gravitational wave behavior is characterized by a polarization pattern with five components rather than two, which is observed for both types of theories. These findings imply that the gravitational wave spectrum is susceptible to modifications from extra geometric theories. Finally, a relationship between the mechanisms that induce the breakdown of the geometric framework and the processes of symmetry reduction and effective reduction, which are methods to achieve it, is discussed in the context of these theories. These reduction methods can be seen as gradual steps where the geometric framework is gradually eroded. With this study, the geometric framework reduction approach has been extended by considering theories that break the geometric framework in a manner inspired by double field theory. Moreover, the study of gravity actions enabled the investigation of the properties of the primary gravitational symplec would in the context of the new theories and provided a method for the stepwise breaking of the geometric framework from a secondary geometric object without introducing extra fields. This study contributes to the understanding of gravity in the context of the geometric framework by examining the mechanisms that induce its breakdown and their relation to the processes of symmetry reduction and effective reduction. Additionally, the study has far-reaching implications for the investigation of the yet unexplored aspects of the Universe and physics, which can be achieved through a geometric framework approach. Future research directions include an investigation of the black hole properties in the context of the new theories

In the past few years, the interest has been raised about utilizing the IEEE 802.11k/v standards within the home network context by various researchers. Recent studies have successfully applied these standards in optimizing and managing Quality of Experience, with various services such as video streaming, online gaming, VoIP, etc. A corresponding mechanism was proposed to perform selection between AP and Extender using IEEE 802.11k/v standards, with the goal of minimizing the delivery time of the desired content and improving overall network performance. This work aims to build on that proposal by introducing a more sophisticated channel quality assessment method, taking into account the load on each available channel. By using the IEEE 802.11k/v standards, an AP can request and receive information on neighboring nodes' configuration, including their operating frequency and transmission load. Subsequently, the Extender can utilize this load information to identify the best operating frequency for transmission and optimize the selection of the closest and highest quality AP. Consequently, the delivery time of the desired content is further minimized, and overall network performance is maximized. A simulation study was conducted to evaluate the proposed method, compared to which the original selection mechanism performed at a roughly 35% higher rate. Moreover, the simulation demonstrated that the proposed method outperformed the standard association mechanism, with 20% and 25% increased success rates for video streaming and online gaming, respectively. In addition, the simulation revealed that the proposed selection method resulted in a 33% or greater reduction in the average delivery time of the desired content compared to the standard association mechanism. Consequently, the success rate and delivery time of the desired content are simultaneously enhanced using the proposed selection method. Consequently, the proposed selection method outperforms both the standard association mechanism and the initial proposal. Finally, the simulation demonstrates that the proposed selection method satisfies the primary objectives of minimizing the delivery time of the desired content and enhancing overall network performance. These simulation outcomes support the feasibility of the proposed idea as previously explained. Nonetheless, some potential issues need to be addressed. Initially, the proposed load assessment method relies on the load metric, with uncertainty arising from the definition of load, used to rank operating frequencies for transmission. In order to establish a universal standard for load metric, further research is required.
